What Is CMA Intermediate?

CMA Intermediate is the second of the three stages of the Cost and Management Accountant qualification run by The Institute of Cost Accountants of India (ICMAI) — after Foundation and before Final. A candidate reaches it either by clearing CMA Foundation, or via other recognised entry routes ICMAI publishes (e.g. graduates in any discipline, or CAT-qualified students under the Institute's exemption scheme). Passing both groups of Intermediate is itself a recognised qualification and is also the gateway to CMA Final and to Practical Training.

Structure — Two Groups, Eight Papers

Paper 6Financial Accounting (FA) — this document

Group IIPaper 9Operations Management & Strategic Management (OMSM)
Paper 10Corporate Accounting and Auditing (CAA)
Paper 11Financial Management and Business Data Analytics (FMDA)
Paper 12Management Accounting (MA)

Note the renumbering versus the older Syllabus 2016: under that syllabus, Financial Accounting was "Paper 5." Under the current Syllabus 2022, it is Paper 6 — Business Laws and Ethics moved into the Paper 5 slot instead.

Exam Pattern, Timing and Passing Criteria (applies to every Intermediate paper, including this one)

Marks: each paper is 100 marks, split 30 marks Objective/MCQ + 70 marks Descriptive.

Descriptive section: typically 7 questions of 14 marks each, of which any 5 must be attempted (5 × 14 = 70).

Duration: 3 hours per paper, plus 15 minutes' reading time before writing begins. Offline, pen-and-paper mode.

Negative marking: none, on the MCQ portion.

Passing criteria: minimum 40% in each individual paper of a group, AND a minimum 50% aggregate across all four papers of that group, to pass the group.

Exam sessions: twice yearly — June and December.

Where Paper 6 Sits, and How to Approach It

Paper 6 is a pure-accounting paper — unlike Paper 5's law-and-citation format, marks here come from correctly applying a procedure: journalising a transaction, posting a ledger, preparing a Trading/P&L/Balance Sheet, computing a partner's settlement on retirement, or apportioning Hire Purchase interest. Every format reproduced in this document (Journal, Ledger, Cash Book, BRS, Trial Balance, Trading/P&L Account, Balance Sheet, Receipts & Payments Account, Income & Expenditure Account, Realisation Account, and every proforma in between) follows the exact column layout ICMAI's own Study Notes use.

The paper blends six distinct territories — core bookkeeping and adjustments (Module 1), special transactions like Bills of Exchange/Consignment/Joint Venture (Module 2), final accounts across three organisation types (Module 3), the single biggest module in the paper by far, Partnership Accounting across its full life cycle (Module 4), four compact but distinct special-topic modules — Lease, Branch/Departmental, Insurance Claims, Hire Purchase (Modules 5–8), and Accounting Standards with their Ind AS comparisons (Module 9). Each rewards precision on formats and figures over prose.

How to Use This Document

Paper 6 is a format-and-computation paper: marks come from reproducing the correct proforma, applying the correct method, and landing on the correct figure — not from prose. Every ledger, journal entry, and worked illustration reproduced here follows ICMAI's own Study Notes exactly, and every figure has been checked for internal arithmetic consistency (debits equal credits, statements foot correctly).

On sourcing: Every fact, format, formula, and worked illustration in this document is drawn exclusively from ICMAI's Paper 6 Study Notes (Syllabus 2022) as supplied for this purpose. Nothing has been fetched from any external source. Presentation aids layered around that content — never new substantive content — are: the plain-language Glossaries before each module, the Mind Maps (which only re-arrange the module's own topics visually), and the exam-strategy notes (test-taking advice, not syllabus content).

Reading This Document

1. Module and topic numbering matches the source exactly. Section 4.5 in this document is Section 4.5 in the ICMAI Study Notes — nothing renumbered.

2. Formats are reproduced, not just described. The exact column headings of every ledger/statement are shown, since the exam tests whether you know which column an item belongs in.

3. Every boxed formula IS the descriptive-answer skeleton. The 70-mark section rewards a structured working — these boxes are the structure to reproduce.

4. Worked illustrations carry the source's own figures. Follow the working line by line before checking the answer — that's how the method, not just the number, sticks.

5. One glossary sits before every module. Read it before the topics — it defines every technical term used in that module in plain words.

Exam Strategy for a 30% MCQ + 70% Descriptive, Computation-Heavy Paper

1. No negative marking on the MCQ portion. Attempt every objective question — an eliminated-down guess has positive expected value.

2. Read the requirement line before the data. Knowing exactly what figure/statement is asked for before you start computing prevents wasted work on the wrong output.

3. Show the working, not just the answer. Descriptive marking in a computation paper is largely method-based — a correctly structured Realisation Account or Trading Account with one wrong figure still earns most of the marks; a bare final number does not.

4. Attempt exactly 5 of the 7 descriptive questions — choose fast. Skim all 7 stems first (2–3 minutes), rank by which proforma/method you're most fluent in, and commit.

5. Weight your prep to Module 4. Partnership Accounting alone is worth as much as Modules 1 and 2 combined (20 of 100 marks) — if time runs short anywhere in revision, it is never Module 4's turn to be cut.

6. Distractors are engineered from classic mistakes. Wrong MCQ options are the numbers you get by making one specific error — every ⚠ TRAP block in this document names those errors.

MODULE 1 OF 9 · SECTION A · WEIGHT 15% · ≈15 MARKS

Accounting
Fundamentals

The four frameworks within which accounting operates, the principles — concepts and conventions — on which accounting theory rests, the distinction between capital and revenue transactions, and application-oriented knowledge of every stage of the Accounting Cycle from identification of a transaction to finalisation of accounts: Chart of Accounts, the Accounting Equation, the Double Entry System, Books of Original Entry and Subsidiary Books, Journal, Ledger, Cash Book, Bank Reconciliation, Trial Balance, and Adjustments & Rectifications.

MUST NOT SKIP: the Accounting Equation, Assets = Liabilities + Capital, introduced in 1.4 — it is the single foundation every later Debit/Credit rule, Journal entry and Ledger posting in this module is built on.

1.1–1.8

Module Learning Objectives

This module gives in-depth knowledge of the four frameworks within which accounting operates and the principles on which accounting theory and practice are based, plus detailed, application-oriented knowledge of every stage of accounting from identification of a transaction up to finalisation of accounts. After studying this module, you will be able to: understand the frameworks of accounting; know the principles of accounting, i.e. Accounting Concepts and Accounting Conventions; understand the concept of a transaction and its different types; understand the Accounting Cycle; get the knowledge of different books of accounts and related concepts — Journal, Ledger, Cash Book, Bank Book (1.5–1.6); learn the preparation and scrutiny of a Trial Balance (1.7); pass adjustment entries and rectification entries (1.8); and do the accounting for depreciation, amortisation, bad debts and provisions thereof (1.8).

Glossary — 1.1–1.4, in Plain Words

The technical terms this part of the module introduces, explained simply.

FrameworkA common set of rules and guidelines used to measure, recognise, present and disclose information in an entity's financial statements.
GAAPGenerally Accepted Accounting Principles — the common set of rules, conventions, standards and procedures the accounting profession has developed for uniform, consistent record-keeping.
Accounting PrinciplesThe basic rules acting as the primary standard for recording transactions and maintaining books of accounts; split into Accounting Concepts and Accounting Conventions.
Accounting ConceptAn assumption or condition that defines the parameters within which accounting operates — the foundation for accounting principles.
Accounting ConventionA custom, method or guideline associated with the practical application of accounting principles — widely accepted, but can change over time.
Entity ConceptThe business and the persons who own or manage it are two independent entities — the owner's personal transactions are separate from the business's.
Going Concern ConceptThe business is assumed to continue existing indefinitely, unless there is good evidence to the contrary.
Accounting Period ConceptThe infinite life of a business is split into smaller periods of equal duration (quarter/half-year/year) so results can be ascertained regularly.
Money Measurement ConceptOnly events expressible in terms of money are recorded, using money as the common denominator for otherwise dissimilar items.
Accrual ConceptBoth cash and credit transactions are recognised — revenue ≠ cash received and expense ≠ cash paid, whenever credit transactions exist.
Dual Aspect ConceptEvery transaction has two aspects, Debit and Credit, affecting at least two accounts — expressed as Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
Matching ConceptRevenues and the expenses incurred to earn them must be recorded in the same accounting period.
Realisation ConceptRevenue is recognised only to the extent it is certainly realisable — an order received is not revenue; goods actually supplied and billed is.
Cost Concept (Historical Cost)Assets are recorded in the books at their cost of acquisition (plus installation etc.), not at market price.
Convention of ConservatismProvide for all possible losses, but anticipate no possible gains — tends to understate income, profits and resources.
Convention of ConsistencyThe same accounting rules and practices are applied continuously, period after period, for reliable comparison.
Convention of MaterialityOnly material facts — those capable of influencing an informed investor's decision — need be recorded and disclosed.
Convention of Full DisclosureAll material facts, favourable or not, must be disclosed fully, fairly and honestly in the accounting statements.
Capital ExpenditureExpenditure whose benefit is enjoyed over more than one accounting period; non-recurring; capitalised and shown in the Balance Sheet.
Revenue ExpenditureExpenditure whose benefit is enjoyed within the current accounting period; recurring; charged against profit as an expense.
Deferred Revenue ExpenditureRevenue-natured expenditure carried forward on the presumption it will benefit a subsequent period too — part written off now, the rest shown as an asset.
Capital ReceiptMoney received from operations other than the entity's regular operations; non-recurring; not recognised as income.
Revenue ReceiptMoney received from the entity's regular day-to-day operations; recurring; recognised as income.
Capital Profit / LossA gain or loss arising outside the entity's regular operating activities — e.g. sale of a fixed asset, or raising capital.
Revenue Profit / LossA gain or loss arising from the entity's regular, day-to-day operating activities.
Accounting CycleThe complete, sequential process from identifying a transaction through recording, posting and trial balance to the financial statements.
EventAny happening — financial (e.g. purchasing a book) or non-financial (e.g. going for a walk).
TransactionAn event with a monetary impact on the entity's financial position, involving at least two parties and a monetary exchange for goods or services.
Chart of Accounts (COA)The numbered, indexed listing of every account in the general ledger — the foundation of financial reporting.
Accounting EquationAssets = Liabilities + Equity — the identity that stays in balance before and after every transaction.
Double Entry SystemEvery transaction is recorded with an equal Debit and Credit, in at least two accounts.
Books of Original Entry (Day Books)The journals in which transactions are first recorded, chronologically, before being posted to the ledger.
Special Journal / Subsidiary BooksA book of original entry dedicated to recording one specific type of transaction only (e.g. Cash Book, Purchase Journal).
General Journal (Journal Proper)The book of original entry for transactions that have no dedicated Special Journal.
PostingRecording a summary of the journal's entries into the relevant accounts of the ledger.

Module 1 Mind Map — read it now, redraw it from memory once you finish the module

CONCEPT

1.1 Four Frameworks of Accounting (Conceptual, Legal, Institutional and Regulatory) ★★ MED

In accounting, a “framework” provides a common set of rules and guidelines used to measure, recognise, present and disclose the information appearing in an entity's financial statements.

The framework of accounting has four pillars.

The Four Frameworks ★★★ HIGH

  • (a) Conceptual Framework — a body of interrelated objectives (the goals and purposes of financial reporting) and fundamentals (the underlying concepts that help achieve those objectives). It guides preparers on selecting, recognising and measuring transactions, events and circumstances, states the objectives of General-Purpose Financial Reporting, and guides on the qualitative characteristics financial statements must possess. It plays an important role in developing the Institutional Framework and assists preparers in developing consistent accounting policies when no accounting standard applies to a situation.
  • (b) Legal Framework — the statutes under which a business is formed and controlled. In India: partnerships under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 or the LLP Act 2008; co-operatives under the Co-operative Societies Act 1912; companies under the Companies Act 2013; banks under the Banking Regulation Act 1949; insurance companies under the Insurance Act 1938; electricity companies under the Central Electricity Act 2003. These statutes (and the Rules framed under them) govern administrative set-up, use of resources, financing, maintenance of books of accounts and treatment of specified transactions — e.g. the Companies Act 2013 and Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014 govern accounting records, issue/redemption of securities, investments, consolidation and winding up; Companies (CSR) Rules 2014 govern accounting of CSR expenses and carry-forward/set-off of excess amounts spent; the Act's Schedules also prescribe the form and content of financial statements.
  • (c) Institutional Framework — pronouncements issued by institutions entrusted by sovereign authorities to develop standards, to ensure comparability and consistency of accounting information. In India, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) is entrusted with this role; its Accounting Standard Board develops quality accounting standards. Two sets currently exist: Accounting Standards under Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules 2021, and Ind ASs under Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules 2015. In addition, the Cost Accounting Standards Board (CASB) of the Institute of Cost Accountants of India has, so far, developed 24 Cost Accounting Standards.
  • (d) Regulatory Framework — the regulatory ambit of sector regulators shaping accounting and, more importantly, reporting. In India: RBI (money market operations — BASEL Norms and accounting of NPAs, Non-Performing Assets), SEBI (capital market operations — shapes accounting/reporting by a listed firm), IRDAI (insurance sector), PFRDA (pension funds), plus the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and the Competition Commission. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations 2009 affect tariff determination and accounting in an electricity company.

Together, these four frameworks provide the foundation on which accounting — and, more specifically, corporate accounting — is based in India: they streamline the accounting process, improve the quality of reports generated, and contribute to the overall development of accounting.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Conceptual = the underlying “why/what” theory (ICAI-level, fills gaps when no standard applies). Legal = the statute that formed and controls the entity (Companies Act, Partnership Act, etc.). Institutional = the standard-setting body's own pronouncements (ICAI's AS/Ind AS, ICMAI's CAS). Regulatory = the sector watchdog's rules layered on top of all the above (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, TRAI).

Institutional vs. Regulatory — the recurring confusion

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING SEBI/RBI/IRDAI AS PART OF THE INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK

THE TRAP: since SEBI, RBI and IRDAI also issue binding pronouncements, a question wrongly files them under the Institutional Framework.

THE TWIST: the Institutional Framework is specifically the accounting/cost standard-setting bodies — ICAI's Accounting Standard Board (AS, Ind AS) and ICMAI's CASB (24 Cost Accounting Standards). RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, TRAI and the Competition Commission are sector regulators layered on top — that is the Regulatory Framework, a separate, fourth pillar.

CONCEPT

1.2 Accounting Principles, Concepts and Conventions ★★★ HIGH

To ensure uniformity and consistency in record-keeping, the accounting profession has developed rules, conventions, standards and procedures that are generally accepted and universally practised — this common set is called Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). GAAP indicates how to report economic events, and is followed so that users of accounting information have an optimum level of consistency across the financial statements they analyse. In India, financial statements are prepared on the basis of accounting standards issued by ICAI and the law laid down in applicable statutes (e.g. Schedule III to the Companies Act 2013, followed by all companies).

Accounting Principles are the basic rules acting as the primary standard for recording business transactions and maintaining books of accounts. To be accepted, an accounting principle must be: (1) objective, (2) usable in practical situations, (3) reliable, (4) feasible (applicable without incurring high costs), and (5) comprehensible to a person with a basic knowledge of accounting and finance.

Accounting Principles split into [A] Accounting Concepts (assumptions and conditions that define the parameters and constraints within which accounting operates — the foundation for accounting principles, ensuring recording on sound, logical bases) and [B] Accounting Conventions (customs, methods, procedures or guidelines associated with the practical application of accounting principles — widely accepted common practices that may, unlike concepts, change over time as general opinion/practice shifts).

The Nine Accounting Concepts

  1. Entity Concept: the organisation is distinct and separate from the persons who own or manage it — two independent entities. Enables recording of transactions between the entity and its owners/stakeholders. Example: if the owner pays personal expenses from business cash, that transaction is recorded in the business's books — it takes cash out of the business and reduces the owner's claim (Capital).
  2. Going Concern Concept: the organisation is assumed to continue existing for an indefinite period — unless there is good evidence to the contrary. Lets the accountant carry forward asset/liability values from one period to the next without questioning their usefulness/worth or the recoverability of receivables. Forms the basis for preparing the Balance Sheet.
  3. Accounting Period (Periodicity) Concept: the infinite life of an organisation is split into smaller periods of equal duration (a quarter, half-year or year), so operating results are ascertained and financial position (via the Balance Sheet) is reflected at regular intervals.
  4. Money Measurement Concept: only events expressible in terms of money are recorded — money is the common denominator letting heterogeneous items be added together. Example: cash, raw material, vehicles and computers can only be combined into total assets once each is expressed in money. Limitation: only the absolute money value is considered, though real value may fluctuate with inflation, exchange rates etc.
  5. Accrual Concept: recognises both cash and credit transactions. In a cash transaction owner's equity is instantly affected; a credit transaction creates a mere obligation. When credit transactions exist (the general case), revenues ≠ cash receipts and expenses ≠ cash paid during the period.
  6. Dual Aspect Concept: every transaction recorded is based on two aspects — technically “Debit” and “Credit” — affecting two (or more) accounts on their respective opposite sides; hence every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts. Example: goods purchased for cash has two aspects, “paying cash” and “receiving goods.” Expressed as an equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
  7. Matching Concept: revenues and expenses must be recorded at the same time as they are incurred — revenues earned should be matched with the expenses incurred during the accounting period, via adjustments for prepaid expenses, accrued incomes etc. Operating result can be measured only when incomes are compared with the related expenses.
  8. Realisation Concept: revenue is recognised only to the extent it is certainly realisable — merely getting an order from a customer is not revenue. Reasonable certainty of realising the money comes only when the goods ordered are actually supplied to the customer and billed. Ensures unearned/unrealised income is never treated as revenue.
  9. Cost Concept: business assets are recorded at the cost incurred for their acquisition, including capital costs of installation — not at market price. This recorded amount is also called “Historical Cost.” Example: a packing machine bought for ₹40,00,000, with ₹30,000 transportation and ₹20,000 installation, is recorded at the aggregate ₹40,50,000.

The Four Accounting Conventions

  1. Convention of Conservatism: assumes an uncertain future and advocates providing for all possible losses, but never for possible future gains — applying it always results in an understatement of incomes, profits and resources.
  2. Convention of Consistency: advocates continuous observation and application of the same accounting rules and practices — vital for profit/loss calculations and for comparing company performance over time. Frequent changes in treatment make accounting information less reliable.
  3. Convention of Materiality: advocates recording and reflecting all material facts (information that can potentially influence an informed investor's decision) and eliminating insignificant information. What is material for one organisation may be immaterial for another, and materiality in one time period may not carry into a later one.
  4. Convention of Full Disclosure: advocates full disclosure of all material information, whether favourable or otherwise, in the accounting statements — requires that statements be prepared honestly. Holds particular importance where ownership is separate from management.
⚡ SHORTCUT: 9 Concepts (assumptions defining the boundary of accounting): Entity, Going Concern, Accounting Period, Money Measurement, Accrual, Dual Aspect, Matching, Realisation, Cost. 4 Conventions (customary practices, can shift over time): Conservatism, Consistency, Materiality, Full Disclosure.

Accounting principles, concepts and conventions bring uniformity to the recording process. This uniformity makes it possible to reliably compare financial results, financial position and cash flows of different organisations, and of the same organisation over different periods — standardising the financial reporting process.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CALLING EVERY ACCOUNTING RULE A “CONCEPT”

THE TRAP: Materiality or Conservatism gets classified as an Accounting Concept, or Going Concern gets classified as a Convention.

THE TWIST: Concepts are foundational assumptions defining the boundaries within which accounting operates (they don't change) — Entity, Going Concern, Accounting Period, Money Measurement, Accrual, Dual Aspect, Matching, Realisation, Cost. Conventions are customary practices that evolved from usage and can shift over time — Conservatism, Consistency, Materiality, Full Disclosure. The 9-vs-4 split is fixed; mixing a name across the two groups is the most common error in this topic.

CONCEPT

1.3 Capital and Revenue Transactions ★★★ HIGH

Proper distinction between transactions of capital and revenue nature is one of the fundamental requirements of accounting — without it, the very objective of accounting is affected. Applying the concepts of periodicity, accrual and matching leads to identifying a transaction as either capital-natured or revenue-natured. Correct classification achieves three purposes:

  1. Ensures proper accounting of transactions by identifying them as income or liability, and expense or asset.
  2. Determines the true operating result, via correct identification of incomes and expenses.
  3. Ensures proper disclosure of financial position in the Balance Sheet, via correct disclosure of assets and liabilities.

1.3.1 Capital and Revenue Expenditures ★★★ HIGH

Capital Expenditure is expenditure whose benefit is enjoyed over a number of accounting periods; non-recurring in nature; incurred when an asset/service is acquired or a fixed asset is improved, and the resulting asset is not intended for resale in the ordinary course of business. Examples: purchase of machinery, construction of a building, development of a website, heavy repairs of a non-current asset. Treatment: not written off completely against income in the period it is acquired — capitalised as an asset, reflected in the Balance Sheet, and gradually charged against profit over time (e.g. buying machinery is capital expenditure, but charging regular depreciation on it is revenue expenditure).

Revenue Expenditure is expenditure whose benefit is enjoyed in the current accounting period; recurring in nature; incurred to carry on the regular course of operations. Examples: purchase of goods for sale; recurring expenses like salaries, wages, rent, depreciation, conveyance charges, monthly internet charges; repairs and maintenance of non-current assets. Treatment: charged as an expense against profit in the period it is incurred or recognised.

Capital ExpenditureRevenue Expenditure
Economic benefit enjoyed over more than one accounting period.Economic benefit enjoyed for only one accounting period.
Non-recurring in nature.Recurring in nature.
Reflected in the Balance Sheet.Debited to the Income Statement.
May be incurred before or after the commencement of business operations.Always incurred after the commencement of business operations.
Tends to increase earning capacity, or reduce operating costs.Helps in carrying on business activities in the current period.
Only a portion gets matched against revenue to determine the operating result (e.g. via depreciation).The entire amount is matched against revenue to determine the operating result.

Four rules govern recognising Capital Expenditure.

  1. Expenditure to acquire long-term assets (useful life more than one accounting period), for use in the organisation and not meant for resale. Example: a second-hand car dealer buying furniture for own use — capital; the same dealer buying second-hand cars for resale — revenue, since he deals in second-hand cars.
  2. Expenditure to improve a machine's condition or put an old asset into working condition — capitalised and added to the asset's cost. Any expenditure to put an asset into working condition is also capital expenditure — e.g. a building purchased for ₹40,00,000 with ₹2,00,000 spent on registration and stamp duty gives total capital expenditure of ₹42,00,000.
  3. Expenditure to improve the earning capacity of the organisation — e.g. expenditure incurred for shifting the factory for easier supply of raw materials.
  4. Preliminary expenses incurred before the commencement of business — e.g. legal charges for drafting the Memorandum/Articles of Association, brokerage paid to brokers, or commission paid to underwriters for raising capital.

Deferred Revenue Expenditure

Deferred Revenue Expenditure is expenditure for which payment has been made or a liability incurred, but which is carried forward on the presumption that it will be of benefit over a subsequent period or periods.

Examples: heavy advertisement expenditure incurred prior to launching a new product; development expenses of a product. Treatment: the expense portion (benefit consumed this year) is debited to the Income Statement; the unwritten-off portion appears as an asset in the Balance Sheet.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: AS-26 KILLED “DEFERRED REVENUE EXPENDITURE” FOR ADVERTISING/R&D

THE TRAP: heavy launch advertising, promotional spend, training or research expenditure gets carried forward as a deferred revenue expenditure asset.

THE TWIST: after the issuance of AS-26, any expenditure incurred for research, training, advertising and promotional activities has to be recognised as a simple revenue expense of the period in which it is incurred — not deferred.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: “INCURRED BEFORE THE BUSINESS STARTS ⇒ MUST BE REVENUE”

THE TRAP: assuming any expense paid before the business commences operations must be revenue in nature, since there is “nothing yet” to benefit from it.

THE TWIST: preliminary expenses (MOA/AOA legal charges, brokerage, underwriting commission) incurred before commencement of business are explicitly Capital Expenditure. The correct rule runs the other way: Capital Expenditure may be incurred before or after commencement of operations; Revenue Expenditure is always incurred after commencement.

1.3.2 Capital and Revenue Receipts ★★★ HIGH

Capital Receipts are receipts obtained from operations other than the entity's regular operations; they have no effect on the operating result. Example: a company issues 1,000 new shares at ₹50 issue price to raise funds for expansion — Total Capital Raised = 1,000 × ₹50 = ₹50,000. Treatment: credited to the respective capital-nature account, reflected in the Balance Sheet.

Revenue Receipts are receipts obtained from the entity's regular course of operations; they increase profits or decrease losses and are set against revenue expenses to ascertain the period's profit. Example: a company sells 1,000 units at ₹20 per unit in the normal course of business — Revenue Receipt = 1,000 × ₹20 = ₹20,000. Treatment: recognised as income, credited to the Income Statement.

Capital ReceiptRevenue Receipt
Obtained from operations OTHER than the entity's regular operations.Obtained from regular day-to-day operations.
Irregular, hence non-recurring in nature.Recurring in nature.
Not recognised as an income.Recognised as an income.
Reflected in the Balance Sheet.Credited to the Income Statement.

1.3.3–1.3.4 Capital and Revenue Profits, Capital and Revenue Losses

The matching of revenues and expenses results in either profit or loss — this extends the capital/revenue distinction to profits and losses too.

TypeArises FromAccounting Treatment
Capital ProfitNon-operating activities; non-recurring — generally the sale of assets other than inventory, raising capital, or purchasing an existing business. Examples: profit prior to incorporation; premium received on issue of shares; profit on re-issue of forfeited shares; redemption of a debenture at a discount; profit on sale or revaluation of a non-current tangible asset.Generally capitalised — transferred to a Capital Reserve Account.
Revenue ProfitRegular operating activities; recurring. Examples: profit from selling the merchandise the business deals in; profit from rendering regular services to clients; surplus earned by a non-profit organisation.Determined in the Income Statement, then distributed to the owners or transferred to a Reserve Account.
Capital LossDoes not arise in the regular course of operations. Examples: sale of assets other than inventory for less than written down value; extraordinary loss/elimination of assets (e.g. by flood, fire); raising debt capital at a discount (debentures issued at a discount); settling a liability for more than its book value (debenture issued at par but redeemed at a premium).Charged against revenue (debit side of Income Statement), or reflected on the asset side of the Balance Sheet as a fictitious asset.
Revenue LossArises in the normal course of business. Examples: discount allowed to customers for prompt payment; loss due to bad debts.Recorded on the debit side of the Income Statement.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Classify as Capital or Revenue Expenditure, with reasons

(i) Extension of railway tracks in the factory area → Capital — benefit yielded for more than one accounting period.

(ii) Wages paid to machine operators → Revenue — benefit yielded for the current period only.

(iii) Installation costs of new production machine → Capital — benefits the business for more than one period.

(iv) Materials for extension to foremen's offices in the factory → Capital — benefits the business for more than one period.

(v) Rent paid for the factory → Revenue — benefits only the current period.

(vi) Payment for computer time to operate a new stores control system → Revenue — incurred to carry on normal business.

(vii) Wages paid to own employees for building the foremen's offices → Capital — benefits the business for more than one period.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — State with reasons: Capital or Revenue Expenditure

(i) ₹10,000 incurred obtaining a licence for starting the factory → Capital — incurred to acquire a right to carry on business for a long period.

(ii) ₹1,000 paid for removal of stock to a new site → Revenue — does not enhance asset value, and is needed for starting business at the new site.

(iii) ₹5,000 incurred for changing rings and pistons of an engine → Revenue — restores the engine's efficiency only, adds nothing to its capacity.

(iv) ₹2,000 spent as lawyer's fee to defend a suit claiming the firm's factory site belonged to the plaintiff (suit unsuccessful) → Revenue — defending title to the firm's own assets.

(v) ₹10,000 spent advertising a new product, benefit effective over four years → Revenue — as per AS-26.

(vi) Factory shed constructed at a cost of ₹1,00,000; ₹5,000 for temporary huts to store building materials → Both Capital — the factory shed and the temporary huts for construction materials are both capital expenditure.

CONCEPT

1.4 Accounting Cycle — Charts of Accounts, Accounting Equation, Double Entry, Books of Original Entry ★★★ HIGH

The Accounting Cycle is a sequence of activities performed by an accountant to document and report an organisation's financial transactions during an accounting period — the entire process from identifying transactions, through recording and processing them, to their representation in the financial statements and closing the accounts.

The accounting cycle follows eight sequential stages (Fig. 1.1).

  1. Identifying Transactions — analysing events to determine whether they are transactions.
  2. Recording in Books of Original Entry — recording identified transactions in the relevant journal, as journal entries.
  3. Posting to the Ledger — recording a summary of the activities in the relevant ledger accounts.
  4. Drafting the Unadjusted Trial Balance — drawn from ledger data at period end, to identify errors made during posting.
  5. Passing Adjustment Entries — identifying and passing the necessary adjustments.
  6. Drafting the Adjusted Trial Balance — the last step before preparing financial statements.
  7. Closing of Books — ledger accounts are closed and balanced (“zeroed out”) at period end.
  8. Drafting the Financial Statements — in order: Income Statement, Statement of Retained Earnings, Balance Sheet, Statement of Cash Flows. The Income Statement is prepared from the closing balances of nominal accounts, while real and personal account balances are reflected in the Balance Sheet.

Events & Transactions

Transactions are the starting point of the accounting cycle — transactions are created through events, but not all events are transactions.

  • Event: any happening — can be financial (purchasing a book, paying cab fare, receiving a cheque) or non-financial (visiting a book store, going for a morning walk). An event may involve any number of parties and may be complete or incomplete.
  • Transaction: an event which has a monetary impact on the financial position of the organisation. To qualify as a transaction, an event must involve at least two parties, and must involve a monetary exchange for goods or a service.

Analysis of Transactions means observing the changes in financial position an organisation's transactions cause. A change in financial position means a change in one or more of the five basic elements of accounting: Assets, Liabilities, Capital/Equity, Expenses, and Revenue. This analysis identifies which accounts a transaction involves, and its Debit and Credit aspects.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING EVERY EVENT AS RECORDABLE

THE TRAP: assuming any business-related happening — a client meeting, appointing a manager, visiting a supplier — gets entered in the books.

THE TWIST: only events that qualify as transactions get recorded — a monetary impact on financial position, at least two parties, and a monetary exchange for goods/services. A non-financial event, or an event with no monetary impact, is never a transaction and is never recorded.

ILLUSTRATION — Mr. Suman De's Trading Business: Analysing Transactions

1. Commences business, investing ₹5,00,000 cash → Cash (Asset) +5,00,000; Capital +5,00,000.

2. Opens a current account, depositing ₹2,00,000 → Cash (Asset) −2,00,000; Bank (Asset) +2,00,000.

3. Borrows ₹1,20,000 from the bank, interest @10% p.a. → Bank (Asset) +1,20,000; Bank Loan (Liability) +1,20,000.

4. Purchases equipment worth ₹80,000 for cash → Equipment (Asset) +80,000; Cash (Asset) −80,000.

5. Purchases goods worth ₹1,00,000 for resale, 60% cash / 30% cheque / balance credit → Purchases (Expense) +1,00,000; Cash −60,000; Bank −30,000; Creditors (Liability) +10,000.

6. Goods sold in cash, ₹1,70,000 → Cash (Asset) +1,70,000; Sales (Revenue) +1,70,000.

7. Goods sold on credit, ₹80,000 → Debtors (Asset) +80,000; Sales (Revenue) +80,000.

8. Wages incurred, ₹20,000 → Wages (Expense) +20,000; Cash (Asset) −20,000.

9. Interest on bank loan charged, ₹3,000 → Bank Interest (Expense) +3,000; Bank (Asset) −3,000.

10. Cash collected from a debtor, ₹20,000 → Cash (Asset) +20,000; Debtors (Asset) −20,000.

11. Cash paid to a creditor, ₹8,000 → Cash (Asset) −8,000; Creditors (Liability) −8,000.

12. Withdraws ₹7,000 cash for personal use → Cash (Asset) −7,000; Capital −7,000.

Every transaction changes at least two elements, and Assets = Liabilities + Capital stays true throughout.

Illustrative Accounting Equation Transactions — Quick Reference

TransactionAssets + Expenses + DrawingsLiabilities + Capital + Revenue
Cash introduced by proprietorCash (Asset) increasesCapital increases
Purchase of goods in cashInventory (Asset) increases; Cash (Asset) decreases—
Purchase of goods on creditInventory (Asset) increasesCreditors (Liability) increases
Sale of goods in cashCash (Asset) increases; Inventory (Asset) decreases—
Sale of goods on creditDebtors (Asset) increases; Inventory (Asset) decreases—
Salaries paidSalaries (Expense) increases; Cash/Bank (Asset) decreases—
Rent receivedCash/Bank (Asset) increasesRent Received (Revenue) increases
Goods withdrawn by proprietorInventory (Asset) decreasesCapital decreases

Chart of Accounts (COA) & Codification Structure

A Chart of Accounts (COA) is a listing of all accounts in the general ledger, each accompanied by a reference number — a financial organisational tool giving a complete, sub-categorised index of every account, and the driving force / foundation behind an organisation's book-keeping and financial reporting.

A chart of accounts typically lists asset accounts first, followed by liability and capital accounts, then revenue and expense accounts. Setting one up follows three steps.

  1. Define the accounts: each account gets a name, a brief description and an identification code/number.
  2. Order the accounts: Balance Sheet accounts list the most liquid assets first; Revenue and Expense accounts list items closest to operations first (e.g. Sales before non-operating income).
  3. Design the numbering: begin with an initial design reflecting the major headings, then add detailed descriptions later as future references.

For a small business, a three-digit code may suffice; complex businesses with thousands of accounts require longer reference numbers, assigned in a logical order.

Number RangeAccount Category
1000–1999Asset accounts
2000–2999Liability accounts
3000–3999Equity accounts
4000–4999Revenue accounts
5000–5999Cost of goods sold accounts
6000–6999Expense accounts
7000–7999Other revenue (e.g. rent received, bad debt recovery)
8000–8999Other expenses (e.g. depreciation, income taxes)

Equivalently grouped as Balance Sheet Accounts (Assets 1000–1999, Liabilities 2000–2999, Owner's Equity 3000–3999) versus Income Statement Accounts (Operating Revenue 4000–4999, Operating Expense 5000–5999, Overhead Costs 6000–6999, Non-operating Revenue/Gains 7000–7999, Non-operating Expenses/Losses 8000–8999). Numbers are deliberately spaced apart so new accounts can be inserted later without renumbering.

The Accounting Equation ★★★ HIGH

Assets represent valuable resources controlled by the company (cash, receivables, fixed assets, inventory); Liabilities represent the organisation's obligations to external stakeholders; Equity represents the owner's net claim on the assets. Liabilities and Equity together show how the assets have been financed. All three components appear in the Balance Sheet.

Assets = Liabilities + Equity
Assets = Liabilities + [Capital + (Revenue – Expenses) – Drawings]
Assets + Expenses + Drawings = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue

This equation is the foundation of the double-entry system — at a general level, recording any transaction always involves keeping the accounting equation in balance.

Double Entry System

The Double Entry System of Bookkeeping is an accounting system that recognises that every transaction has two aspects, both of which are recorded in the books of accounts — a fundamental concept encompassing accounting and book-keeping in present times.

“Debit” (Dr.) is from Latin debitum, “what is due”; “Credit” (Cr.) from credere, “what is trusted.” A debit entry in one account gives the opposite effect in another via a credit entry, so the sum of all Debit balances must equal the sum of all Credit balances. Based on the accounting equation, the system requires: (1) every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts; (2) total debits recorded for a transaction equal total credits recorded.

The rules of debit and credit for recording transactions can be explained by applying two methods: (1) Golden Rules (based on classifying accounts as Personal, Real or Nominal); and (2) the Accounting Equation approach (based directly on Assets/Liabilities/Capital/Revenue/Expense movements).

The Double Entry System proceeds through four successive stages.

  1. Transactions are first recorded in the Books of Original Entry (Journal and other Subsidiary Books).
  2. The transactions are classified suitably and recorded in the Ledger.
  3. Arithmetical accuracy of the books is checked by drafting a Trial Balance.
  4. The result of the period's operations is ascertained via the Income Statement, and the entity's financial position at period end is reflected in the Balance Sheet.

Books of Original Entry, Subsidiary Books & Finalisation of Accounts

Books of original entry (technically called Journals, also “Day Books” since transactions are recorded daily) are the accounting books in which transactions entered into by an organisation are initially recorded, in the form of individual Journal Entries, in chronological order, with description and reference to supporting documents. The information is thereafter summarised and posted into the ledger accounts. Books of original entry are broadly classified into two categories: Special Journals (Day Books) and the General Journal.

After the transactions of a period have been recorded in the journal/subsidiary books, they are posted to the respective accounts in the Ledger (the Book of Final Entry). At the end of the accounting period (quarter/half-year/year), the ledger accounts are balanced and closed. Closure depends on the nature of the account: Nominal accounts (incomes, expenses, gains, losses) are closed by transfer to the Income Statement — Trading A/c and Profit & Loss A/c for a profit-oriented organisation, or Income & Expenditure A/c for a non-profit organisation — to ascertain the operating result (profit/loss or surplus/deficit). The balances of Real and Personal accounts are carried forward to the next accounting period and reflected in the Balance Sheet, which shows the organisation's financial position — assets owned, liabilities and equity — at the end of the specific accounting period. This closing and drafting of financial statements is the finalisation of accounts.

CONCEPT

1.5 Journal (Day Books and Journal Proper), Ledger ★★★ HIGH

Journal is the book of original entry in which financial transactions are first recorded, after their occurrence, in chronological order. The word derives from the French jour (“a day”) — a daily record. Recording a transaction in the journal is called Journalising; the entry itself is a Journal Entry; every entry is followed by a short summary called the Narration.

Format of a Journal, with a Worked Entry
DateParticularsVoucher No.Ledger Folio(₹) Dr.(₹) Cr.
09.02.2023Purchase A/c ……Dr.
  To Cash A/c
(Being goods purchased for cash)		315 / 1750,00050,000

Worked from the source's own example: per Voucher No. 31 of Roy Brothers, on 09.02.2023 goods worth ₹50,000 were purchased and cash paid immediately; the folios of Purchase A/c and Cash A/c in the ledger are 5 and 17 respectively.

Each entry rests on a source document — purchase invoices (inward invoices), sales invoices (outward invoices), debit notes, credit notes, etc. Recording does not end at the journal: with the objective of classification, transactions are thereafter summarised and posted to the respective ledger account(s).

Simple vs. Compound Entry: a Simple journal entry affects exactly two accounts — one debited, one credited (e.g. goods sold for cash: Cash A/c Dr., To Sales A/c). A Compound entry involves at least two debits and one credit, or one debit and two-or-more credits (e.g. goods sold partly for cash and partly on credit: both Cash A/c and Debtors A/c are debited, Sales A/c is credited with the full amount).

Types of Journal — Special Journal vs. General Journal

Books of original entry fall into two categories. (1) Special Journals (also called Subsidiary Books) — each records one specific transaction type, adopted once transaction volume makes a single journal unwieldy. (2) General Journal (Journal Proper) — records transactions for which no special journal exists.

Special JournalRecordsPosting to Ledger
Cash Journal / Cash BookAll transactions involving cash inflow or outflow (see 1.6).—
Purchase Journal (Purchase Day Book)Credit purchases of goods only — from Purchase (inward) invoices. Cash purchases, and credit purchase of any non-goods asset, are excluded.Total → Purchases A/c (General Ledger); each entry → the supplier's personal A/c (Suppliers' Ledger).
Sales Journal (Sales Day Book)Credit sales of goods only — from Sales (outward) invoices. Cash sales, and sale of any non-goods asset, are excluded.Total → Sales A/c (General Ledger); each entry → the customer's personal A/c (Debtors' Ledger).
Purchase Returns Journal (Returns Outward Book)Goods purchased on credit and returned to suppliers — from Debit Notes issued.Total → Purchase Returns A/c; each entry → the supplier's A/c (Creditors' Ledger).
Sales Returns Journal (Returns Inward Book)Goods sold on credit and returned by customers — from Credit Notes issued.Total → Returns Inward A/c; each entry → the customer's A/c (Debtors' Ledger).
Bills Receivable JournalBills of exchange received from customers on credit sales — date of drawing/acceptance/maturity, tenure, amount.Total → Bills Receivable A/c; each entry → the customer's A/c (Debtors' Ledger).
Bills Payable JournalBills of exchange accepted, owed to suppliers on credit purchases.Total → Bills Payable A/c; each entry → the supplier's A/c (Creditors' Ledger).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: NON-GOODS OR CASH ITEMS FORCED INTO A DAY BOOK

THE TRAP: a credit purchase of furniture, equipment or machinery gets entered in the Purchase Day Book; a cash purchase/sale of goods gets entered there too, since it “feels like” a purchase/sale transaction.

THE TWIST: the Purchase and Sales Day Books record CREDIT transactions in GOODS only. Cash purchases/sales of goods go to the Cash Book; credit purchase/sale of any non-goods (long-term) asset goes to the Journal Proper — regardless of how routine the item looks.

General Journal / Journal Proper — Types of Entries

The Journal Proper records: purchase/sale of a non-current asset on credit; rectification entries; adjustment entries; opening entries; and closing entries transferring Nominal Accounts to Trading & Profit and Loss Account.

  • Opening Entries — bring forward, as the first entry of a new period, the balances of Asset, Liability and Equity accounts appearing in the preceding period's Balance Sheet.
  • Transfer Entries — move an amount/balance from one account to another (e.g. correcting a wrong booking, or transferring Drawings to Capital).
  • Closing Entries — passed at year-end to close all Nominal (expense/income) accounts by transferring them to the profit-determining accounts: Trading A/c, Profit & Loss A/c, Consignment A/c, etc.
  • Adjustment Entries — passed at finalisation to honour the accounting concepts and conventions (detailed at 1.8.2).
  • Rectification Entries — correct errors committed while recording, posting, casting or balancing (detailed at 1.8.2).
  • Occasional/Miscellaneous Entries — any other transaction with no dedicated subsidiary book.

Rules of Journalising

Journalising follows the same rules as debiting/crediting an account, applied via two alternative, equivalent bases.

Account Type (Golden Rules)DebitCredit
Nominal AccountExpenses and LossesIncomes and Gains
Real AccountWhat comes inWhat goes out
Personal AccountThe receiverThe giver
Accounting-Equation ComponentDebitCredit
AssetsIncreaseDecrease
LiabilitiesDecreaseIncrease
CapitalDecreaseIncrease
DrawingsIncreaseDecrease
ExpensesIncreaseDecrease
RevenueDecreaseIncrease

Steps in Journalising: (1) identify the accounts involved; (2) classify each as Personal/Real/Nominal, or as Asset/Liability/Capital/Drawings/Expense/Revenue; (3) apply the debit/credit rule to find which account is debited and which credited; (4) record date, particulars and amount; (5) write the narration.

Functions: Historical (chronological record for reference), Recording (each entry narrated in plain language), Analytical (splits every transaction into its debit and credit aspect). Advantages: no transaction omitted; date/reason traceable via narration; eases ledger posting; shows the full story in one entry; is the basis for the ultimate Trial Balance; serves as court evidence. Limitations: unwieldy for a large transaction volume if only a single journal is kept; not a simple recording system; journalising is time-consuming.

1.5.2 Ledger

The Ledger is the book of account in which transactions are recorded, in classified and summarised form, after they have first been entered in the Journal — hence the “Book of Final Entry.” The process of recording in the ledger is called Posting. It forms the basis for preparing the Trial Balance.

Format of a Ledger Account
……………… Account
DateParticulars(₹)Date

Functions: a permanent store-house of all transactions, arranged for ready reference; summarises the effect of transactions account-wise so the status of each account can be read off at any date; acts like a “mirror” of the concern's operations for planning future action.

Subdivisions of Ledger (by nature of accounts maintained):

  • Personal Ledger — contains personal accounts of debtors and creditors, sub-divided into: (a) Debtors'/Customers'/Sales Ledger, and (b) Creditors'/Suppliers'/Purchase/Bought Ledger.
  • Impersonal (General) Ledger — contains every account NOT in the Personal Ledger, i.e. Real and Nominal accounts, and Personal accounts other than trade debtors/creditors.

Advantage of this sub-division: it provides complete, detailed information of all similar-nature accounts in one book, and discloses summarised information once the accounts are balanced.

Ledger Posting Rules — increases/decreases recorded by account category:

CategoryIncreases on…Decreases on…
AssetsDebit sideCredit side
Liabilities & CapitalCredit sideDebit side
Expenses/LossesDebit sideCredit side
Incomes/GainsCredit sideDebit side

Balancing an account: total both sides and find the difference. If the debit total exceeds the credit total, the account has a Debit Balance, written on the credit side as “By Balance c/d.” If the credit total exceeds the debit total, it has a Credit Balance, written on the debit side as “To Balance c/d.” Equal totals mean a Nil balance. The prior period's closing balance (c/d) becomes the new period's opening balance, shown as b/d (brought down).

CONCEPT

1.6 Cash Book, Bank Book, Bank Reconciliation Statement ★★★ HIGH

The Cash Book is the book of account that records all cash receipts and cash payments of an organisation — whether effected in liquid cash, cheque or online transfer. Receipts are entered on the debit side, payments on the credit side.

Features: records only cash-type transactions; proforma is like a ledger account (two sides); it is BOTH a book of primary entry and a book of final entry — hence called a “journalised ledger”; its balance reflects cash available.

Type of Cash BookColumns per SideNotes
Single ColumnCash onlyUsed by small organisations with no bank account (is, in effect, the entity's Cash Account); an entity with a bank account can still keep this and a separate Bank A/c in the ledger.
Double ColumnCash + BankAdds a Bank column instead of a separate ledger Bank A/c. Gives rise to the Contra Entry (below).
Triple ColumnCash + Bank + DiscountDebit-side Discount column = Discount Allowed; Credit-side Discount column = Discount Received. Discount columns are NOT balanced — their totals are transferred to the respective Discount Accounts in the General Ledger.
Multi-columnarCash/Bank + several fixed expense-head columnsUsed where large cash transactions recur under fixed heads (clubs, schools, colleges).

Contra Entry: in a Double/Triple Column Cash Book, a transaction moving money between Cash and Bank (deposit into bank, withdrawal from bank) is posted on BOTH sides of the same Cash Book — the letter “C” is written on both sides in the Ledger Folio (L.F.) column.

Trade DiscountCash Discount
Allowed by seller to buyer for bulk purchaseAllowed to encourage prompt payment

Petty Cash Book

Where cash transactions are too numerous for one person to record, handling splits: one group for petty (small, frequent) transactions, the rest for everything else — giving the Petty Cash Book, kept by the Petty Cashier. Its proforma mirrors a Single Column Cash Book, though it may also be kept in multi-columnar (Analytical) form with pre-specified expense-head columns on the credit side.

Ordinary SystemImprest System
Chief cashier hands the petty cashier a pre-decided lump sum; on exhausting it, the petty cashier submits expenditure details for review and reimbursement.A fixed periodic estimate (the Imprest Cash/Float) is advanced. At period-end the petty cashier submits a statement of petty expenses; the chief cashier reimburses exactly that amount, restoring the float to its original figure — so the cash held never exceeds the imprest amount.

Bank Book

Instead of an extra column in a Double/Triple Column Cash Book, an organisation with a high volume of bank transactions may keep a separate subsidiary book — similar to the Cash Book — recording all bank receipts and payments: the Bank Book or Bank Journal. Like a Single Column Cash Book it has two sides; receipts are debited, payments credited. Separate Bank Books can be kept for each bank account. A Bank Book is distinct from a Pass Book/Bank Statement, which is a copy of the CLIENT's account as it appears in the BANK's own ledger. Maintaining a Bank Book eases reconciliation and cuts the chance of missed entries.

Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS)

A statement prepared to reconcile the balance as per Cash Book (bank column) with the balance as per Pass Book, since the two rarely agree in practice due to a time gap or communication gap between entries made by the client and by the bank. The BRS is NOT part of the books of account, is prepared periodically to verify accuracy, and does NOT itself rectify any error in the books — it only identifies the causes of the discrepancy as on a date.

Common causes of disagreement: cheque issued but not presented at the bank; cheque deposited but not yet collected; amount deposited directly by other parties; incidental charges/overdraft interest debited by the bank; interest on deposit credited by the bank; dishonour of a cheque deposited; clerical errors by either side; payment made by the bank under standing instruction. (Digital transactions have eliminated many of these causes in practice.)

MethodHow It Proceeds
Without Amended Cash BookStart from EITHER available balance (Cash Book bank column, or Pass Book). Make logical additions/subtractions for every item of disagreement. Once every item is adjusted, the two balances tally.
Amended Cash Book MethodFirst correct the Cash Book itself for items that are correctly in the Pass Book but not yet in the Cash Book (and for any error made BY THE CLIENT). The BRS is then drafted to reconcile this corrected Cash Book balance with the Pass Book balance. Errors made BY THE BANK stay in the Reconciliation Statement, never in the amended Cash Book.
Item (starting from Cash Book, favourable/Dr. balance)Add or Less
Cheques issued/drawn but not yet presented for paymentAdd
Cheque wrongly credited by the bank / amount collected directly by the bank on the client's behalfAdd
Rebate on a retired bill, or any item correctly in the Pass Book but not yet entered in the Cash Book (in the client's favour)Add
Cheques deposited/paid into the bank but not yet collected/creditedLess
Cheque entered in the Cash Book but not yet actually bankedLess
A previously-discounted bill now dishonoured, not yet recorded in the Cash Book; bank charges/interest debited by the bank but not yet in the Cash BookLess
EXAM TRICK: every one of the above directions REVERSES on two independent switches — (1) starting from the Pass Book instead of the Cash Book, and (2) an overdraft/unfavourable balance instead of a favourable one. Illustration 5 below starts from an overdrawn Cash Book balance and shows the reversed logic directly.

CONCEPT

1.7 Trial Balance (Preparation and Scrutiny) ★★★ HIGH

The Trial Balance is a statement drawn up from ledger balances to test the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger accounts — a columnar statement of five columns: Serial Number, Name of Ledger Account, Ledger Folio, Debit Amount, Credit Amount. If the accounting is correct and complete, its two amount columns tally.

Proforma of a Trial Balance
Trial Balance of ……… as on ………
Sl. No.Ledger AccountL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)

Features: a Trial Balance is just a statement, NOT an account; it does not form part of the double-entry system; it does not appear in the actual books of account, being prepared as a separate document; it is drawn as on a particular DATE, not for a period; it may be prepared monthly/quarterly/half-yearly/annually, but MUST be drafted at the end of every accounting year, before the financial statements. If the books are arithmetically accurate, total Debit balances agree with total Credit balances.

Advantages, Limitations, and What a Trial Balance Does NOT Prove

Advantages: its agreement is a useful check on ledger postings, proving both aspects of every transaction were posted; it proves the accounts are arithmetically correct (correct amount against each account); it facilitates preparing financial statements by presenting ledger balances in summarised form.

Limitations: can be drafted only where books are kept under the double-entry system — smaller concerns not following double entry cannot draft one; its agreement is NOT conclusive proof of absolute accuracy — only a prima facie proof, since certain errors escape it entirely.

Errors NOT identified by a Trial Balance:

  • Error of Omission or Duplication — an entry completely omitted from (or duplicated in) the books.
  • Error of Commission — a wrong amount entered in the correct accounts, or the wrong account of the correct type used.
  • Errors of Principle — recording not in accordance with accounting principles, e.g. purchase of office furniture debited to Purchases A/c instead of Furniture and Fittings A/c.
  • Errors of Original Entry — the transaction amount itself entered incorrectly in a subsidiary book.
  • Compensating Errors — two or more mistakes that cancel each other out.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: “THE TRIAL BALANCE TALLIED, SO THE BOOKS ARE CORRECT”

THE TRAP: a tallied Trial Balance is read as proof the books contain no errors.

THE TWIST: agreement is only prima facie evidence of ARITHMETICAL accuracy — Errors of Omission, Commission (right accounts, wrong amount on both sides), Principle, Original Entry, and Compensating Errors all leave a Trial Balance perfectly tallied. Illustration 7 below shows exactly this: the intern's Trial Balance tallied at ₹13,50,000 yet still carried two classification errors.

Preparation of a Trial Balance

Total MethodBalance Method
The total of each ledger account's debit side AND credit side are both carried to the Trial Balance. Can be drafted even before the ledger accounts have been balanced.Only after every ledger account has been balanced. For each account, just ONE figure (the balance) is carried to the Trial Balance.

CONCEPT

1.8 Adjustments and Rectifications

1.8.1 Depreciation and Amortisation ★★★ HIGH

Depreciation is the gradual, permanent decline in the book value of a tangible fixed asset (except freehold land), arising from physical wear and tear, passage of time, or obsolescence. It is a part of the cost of a tangible fixed asset that has expired through usage or lapse of time, and is charged to write off that cost over the asset's estimated useful life.

Depreciation is charged on every fixed asset EXCEPT freehold land, since (unlike machinery or furniture) land's useful life is treated as infinite. Characteristics: it reduces book value; the reduction is permanent, gradual and continuing; it is provided every year, whether from use or the mere passage of time; it is usually gradual, barring sudden physical deterioration or technological obsolescence. (Depreciation for corporate entities is governed by Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013, effective 1.4.2014.)

DepreciationAmortisationDepletion
Wearing-out/loss of value of a depreciable TANGIBLE asset through use, time or technological/market obsolescence — allocated as expense over useful life.Gradual, systematic write-off of an INTANGIBLE asset (patents, purchased goodwill, copyrights) over its useful life.Reduction in a WASTING asset (quarry, mine) as extraction physically reduces the available quantity of material.

Methods of Recording Depreciation

(1) Charged to the Asset Account(2) Provision for Depreciation A/c Maintained
Depreciation is credited straight to the Asset A/c; the Asset is shown in the Balance Sheet at written-down value (cost less depreciation to date).Asset A/c stays at ORIGINAL COST; depreciation is credited to a Provision for Depreciation (Accumulated Depreciation) A/c instead, whose balance shows total depreciation to date. Balance Sheet shows Cost less Provision for Depreciation. Usable with either SLM or WDV.
Depreciation A/c    Dr.…
    To Asset A/c (Method 1) / To Provision for Depreciation A/c (Method 2)…

(Being depreciation on asset charged)

Profit and Loss A/c    Dr.…
    To Depreciation A/c…

(Being depreciation transferred to Profit and Loss A/c)

Under the Provision-for-Depreciation approach, on SALE of an asset its ACCUMULATED depreciation is transferred to the credit side of the Asset Account (or of a dedicated Asset Disposal A/c) so that the profit or loss on disposal is correctly measured: Cash/Bank A/c Dr. and Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr., To Asset Sales A/c (or vice-versa via an Asset Disposal A/c — see Illustration 13).

Methods of Calculating Depreciation — SLM and WDV

Straight Line Method (SLM) — Depreciation p.a. = (V − S) ÷ n

V = Cost of the asset (incl. capitalised expenses) · S = Residual/scrap value · n = Estimated useful life (years). A FIXED, equal amount is charged every period, on the ORIGINAL cost throughout — by the end of the asset's life, exactly V−S has been written off, leaving book value = S.

Reducing/Diminishing Balance (WDV) Method

For a newly acquired asset: Depreciation = Original Cost × Rate of Depreciation.
For an existing asset: Depreciation = Opening WDV × Rate of Depreciation.
The RATE is constant, but since it is applied to a shrinking base (the previous year's WDV) each year, the AMOUNT charged keeps falling.

Straight Line Method (SLM)Written Down Value (WDV) Method
Depreciation computed on ORIGINAL cost, every yearDepreciation computed on the WRITTEN-DOWN (book) value at the start of each year
Annual charge is EQUAL throughout the asset's lifeAnnual charge DECLINES every year, since the base itself shrinks
By the end of the estimated life, book value = scrap value exactly, since (V−S)/n charged for n years totals V−SBeing a fixed percentage of a continually-shrinking balance, book value falls toward — but mathematically never exactly reaches — zero or scrap value

ILLUSTRATION 9 — SLM: Proportionate Depreciation for a Part Year

A machine costs ₹7,00,000, plus ₹3,00,000 cartage/installation — Total Cost = ₹10,00,000. Depreciation @20% p.a. SLM for the year ending 31st March 2023, for four different purchase dates.

Depreciation = Total Cost × Rate × (months held ÷ 12).

(a) Purchased 1st April 2022 (12 months): ₹10,00,000 × 20% × 12/12 = ₹2,00,000.

(b) Purchased 1st July 2022 (9 months): ₹10,00,000 × 20% × 9/12 = ₹1,50,000.

(c) Purchased 1st October 2022 (6 months): ₹10,00,000 × 20% × 6/12 = ₹1,00,000.

(d) Purchased 1st January 2023 (3 months): ₹10,00,000 × 20% × 3/12 = ₹50,000.

Answer: total depreciation charged — ₹8,000 (2021), ₹9,200 (2022), ₹285 + ₹1,296 (part-year charges on the two lots sold in 2023 up to their sale dates) and ₹7,048 (year-end 2023 on the remaining/added machinery). Closing balance carried to 2024 = ₹78,432.

Profit or Loss on Sale of an Asset — the Two Accounting Approaches

When an asset is sold before its useful life ends and the sale price differs from its book value, the difference is a profit or loss on sale.

(a) No Provision for Depreciation A/c(b) Alternative — All Adjustments Through the Asset A/c Itself
WDV of the portion sold is transferred to an Asset Disposal A/c: (i) Asset Disposal A/c Dr., To Asset A/c; (ii) Cash/Bank A/c Dr., To Asset Disposal A/c (sale proceeds); (iii) Depreciation (P&L) A/c Dr., To Asset Disposal A/c (if any); (iv) Asset Disposal A/c Dr., To P&L A/c (profit) OR P&L A/c Dr., To Asset Disposal A/c (loss).(i) Cash/Bank A/c Dr., To Assets A/c (sale proceeds); (ii) Depreciation (P&L) A/c Dr., To Assets A/c; (iii) Assets A/c Dr., To P&L A/c (profit) OR P&L A/c Dr., To Assets A/c (loss).

Change of Method

The depreciation method used must reflect the pattern in which the asset's future economic benefits are expected to be consumed, and should be reviewed at least at every financial year-end. If the expected consumption pattern changes significantly, the method is changed to match — accounted for as a change in accounting estimate under AS 5 (depreciation is an accounting ESTIMATE, not an accounting POLICY). Once selected, the method should be applied consistently period to period.

CONCEPT

1.8.2 Adjustment Entries and Rectification of Errors ★★★ HIGH

Financial statements are prepared from ledger balances, but those balances are not always the true picture — adjustment entries correct them to reflect reality at period-end, updating the records for transactions not yet properly reflected. They are a fundamental, necessary part of the accounting cycle, are passed at PERIOD-END, reflect in BOTH the Income Statement and Balance Sheet, are NOT based on a source document (invoice/bill), and comply with accounting principles. Once complete, the ADJUSTED Trial Balance can be drafted.

Adjustment entries classify into three groups: Pre-payments and Pre-receipts (prepaid expenses; unearned/pre-received revenue — e.g. prepaid insurance, subscription received in advance); Accruals (accrued/outstanding expenses incurred but unpaid; accrued income earned but unrecorded — e.g. an outstanding electricity bill); and Non-cash expenses/estimates (below).

AdjustmentEntry
Closing StockStock-in-Trade A/c Dr., To Purchases/Trading A/c
Goods withdrawn by owner for personal useDrawings A/c Dr., To Purchases A/c
Goods distributed as free samples to the publicAdvertisement A/c Dr., To Purchases A/c
Goods distributed as free samples to employeesWages/Salaries A/c Dr., To Purchases A/c
Goods-in-TransitGoods-in-Transit A/c Dr., To Purchases/Trading A/c
Abnormal loss of stockAbnormal Loss A/c Dr., To Purchases/Trading A/c
Stock used as stationeryStationery A/c Dr., To Purchases/Stock A/c
Materials used to construct a Fixed AssetFixed Assets A/c Dr., To Purchases/Stock A/c
Goods sent on approval, pending decision at Balance Sheet dateSales A/c Dr., To Sale or Return Suspense A/c; and Stock on Sale or Return A/c Dr., To Trading A/c
Outstanding expensesExpenses A/c Dr., To Outstanding Expenses A/c
Prepaid expensesPrepaid Expenses A/c Dr., To Expenses A/c
Pre-received incomesIncome A/c Dr., To Pre-received Income A/c

Mutual set-off between debtors and creditorsCreditors A/c Dr., To Debtors A/c

Rectification Entries (Correction Entries)

Rectification entries correct errors discovered in the accounting records; like every other type in this section, they are passed in the Journal. When an error affecting the Trial Balance is found, the normal practice is to route the difference through a Suspense Account until the error is traced. On identification, one effect goes to the correct account head and the other to Suspense — this applies to ONE-SIDED errors only (e.g. the Sales Book total wrongly cast, but individual customer accounts correctly debited — only Sales A/c is affected). In every OTHER case, rectification is a straightforward debit/credit between the correct and the wrong account head — no Suspense A/c involved.

Type of ErrorRectification
Error of Principle — revenue item entered as capital or vice versaA journal entry giving the correct effect.
Error of Omission — transaction forgotten entirelySimply pass the correct entry.
Error of Commission — posted to the wrong account headDebit/credit the wrong head and post to the correct head.
Compensating Errors — two+ errors offsetting each otherPass a correcting entry for each.
Wrong totalling of a subsidiary bookAffects the Trial Balance — route through Suspense A/c.
Posting on the wrong side of an accountA DOUBLE-effect entry — one to cancel the wrong side, one to give the correct side.
Posting of the wrong amountAn entry for the DIFFERENTIAL amount only.

Timing of Detection — Before Trial Balance, After Trial Balance, After Final Accounts

Detected…Double-Sided ErrorsSingle-Sided Errors
Before Trial BalanceAsk (i) what was the correct entry? (ii) what entry was actually passed? Then pass the entry that converts (ii) into (i).No separate journal entry — simply correct the affected account by an appropriate posting.
After Trial BalanceSame method as “before”.Route through a Suspense Account.
After Final AccountsSame method, but every NOMINAL account in the entry is replaced by Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c (the P&L itself is already closed); the Suspense A/c balance is carried forward to the next year.Same Suspense-A/c method, with nominal accounts again replaced by Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c.
Building A/c    Dr.3,00,000
    To Purchase A/c3,00,000

Double-sided example: a Building costing ₹3,00,000 was wrongly passed through the Purchase A/c — rectification debits Building and credits Purchase, cancelling the wrong debit and giving the correct one.

Suspense A/c    Dr.1,000
    To Sales A/c1,000

Single-sided example (after Trial Balance): Sales Day Book was overcast by ₹1,000, so Sales A/c is credited and the excess is routed via Suspense A/c.

Suspense Account

Where the Trial Balance does not agree, the difference is temporarily parked in a Suspense Account so that Final Accounts can still be prepared. As errors are traced and rectified, the Suspense A/c is gradually squared off and eventually closed. Until then it appears in the Balance Sheet — on the ASSETS side if it carries a debit balance, on the LIABILITIES side if a credit balance.

Effect of Errors on Profit or Loss

The Profit & Loss A/c is built entirely from NOMINAL accounts (income, gain, expense, loss). An error that touches a nominal account changes profit or loss; an error confined to REAL or PERSONAL accounts does NOT.

16 EXAM FACTS — JOURNAL, LEDGER, CASH BOOK, TRIAL BALANCE & RECTIFICATION (Module 1)

① Journal is the book of ORIGINAL entry (Journalising, each entry followed by a Narration); Ledger is the book of FINAL entry (posting summarises transactions account-wise) and is itself the basis for the Trial Balance.

② Special Journals/Subsidiary Books (Cash Book, Purchase & Sales Day Books, Purchase & Sales Returns Books, Bills Receivable/Payable Journals) each record ONE transaction type; the Journal Proper (General Journal) catches everything else — non-current asset purchase/sale on credit, opening/transfer/closing entries, adjustment entries, rectification entries.

③ TRAP: the Purchase and Sales Day Books record CREDIT transactions in GOODS only — a cash purchase/sale of goods belongs in the Cash Book, and a credit purchase/sale of any non-goods (long-term) asset belongs in the Journal Proper, however routine it looks.

④ Golden Rules of journalising: Personal A/c — Dr. the receiver, Cr. the giver; Real A/c — Dr. what comes in, Cr. what goes out; Nominal A/c — Dr. expenses/losses, Cr. incomes/gains.

⑤ Cash Book variants: Single Column (cash only); Double Column (cash + bank, giving rise to the Contra Entry, marked “C” on both sides); Triple Column (adds a Discount column — Discount Allowed debited, Discount Received credited — never balanced, only totalled off to the ledger Discount A/cs).

⑥ Trade Discount is NEVER recorded in the books; Cash Discount IS recorded, in the Discount column of the Triple Column Cash Book.

⑦ Petty Cash Book, Imprest System: a fixed periodic float (the imprest) is advanced; at period-end the petty cashier is reimbursed EXACTLY the amount spent, restoring the float to its original figure — so cash held never exceeds the imprest.

⑧ A Bank Reconciliation Statement reconciles the Cash Book's bank-column balance with the Pass Book balance; it is NOT part of the double-entry books and does NOT itself rectify any error — it only identifies the causes of disagreement as on a date.

⑨ BRS add/less rule, starting from a FAVOURABLE Cash Book balance: cheques issued but not yet presented → ADD; cheques deposited but not yet collected/credited → LESS. Both directions REVERSE if starting from the Pass Book instead of the Cash Book, or if the balance is an OVERDRAFT instead of favourable.

⑩ Amended Cash Book Method: first correct the Cash Book for items correctly in the Pass Book but missing/wrong in the Cash Book (and for any client-side error); errors made BY THE BANK stay in the Reconciliation Statement and are never entered into the amended Cash Book.

⑪ A Trial Balance is a STATEMENT, not an account — it is not part of the double-entry system, is drawn AS ON a date (not for a period), and its agreement is only PRIMA FACIE proof of arithmetical accuracy, never conclusive proof the books are error-free.

⑫ Five error-types a perfectly tallied Trial Balance can NEVER catch: Error of Omission/Duplication, Error of Commission (right accounts, wrong amount on both sides), Error of Principle, Error of Original Entry, and Compensating Errors.

⑬ Depreciation is charged on every fixed asset EXCEPT freehold land. SLM charges a FIXED, equal amount every year — (Cost − Residual) ÷ Life; WDV applies a constant RATE to the shrinking prior-year book value, so the amount charged keeps falling while book value never mathematically reaches zero/scrap.

⑭ Rectification: a ONE-SIDED error (only one account/side affected, e.g. a subsidiary book wrongly cast) is routed through a Suspense A/c; a DOUBLE/TWO-SIDED error (wrong account head used for both legs, e.g. an asset debited to Purchase A/c) is corrected directly between the wrong and correct heads — no Suspense A/c involved.

⑮ Timing changes the rectification route: BEFORE the Trial Balance, a one-sided error needs no separate journal entry (just correct the posting); AFTER the Trial Balance it goes via Suspense A/c; AFTER Final Accounts, every NOMINAL account leg in the entry is replaced by “Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c” (the P&L itself is already closed), and any Suspense A/c balance carries forward to next year.

⑯ The Suspense A/c appears in the Balance Sheet — Assets side if it carries a debit balance, Liabilities side if a credit balance. An error confined to REAL or PERSONAL accounts never disturbs Profit; only an error touching a NOMINAL account changes it.
