Bills of Exchange,
Consignment, Joint Venture

Accounting for three special transaction types: Bills of Exchange under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — drawing, discounting, endorsement, dishonour, retirement and renewal; Consignment business, where a consignor sends goods to a consignee-agent for sale on commission; and Joint Venture, a temporary partnership dissolved once its one specific deal is complete.

MUST NOT SKIP: the full 18-row Journal-Entries-for-Trade-Bills reference (Books of Drawer vs. Books of Drawee) — every numerical illustration in this module is just one row of that table worked out in full.

2.1–2.3

Module Learning Objectives

This module builds detailed, application-oriented understanding of accounting for certain special transactions — used to determine surplus, ensure control on resources, and support divisional performance evaluation. After studying this module, you will be able to: understand the detailed process and accounting for Bills of Exchange — drawing, acceptance, discounting, endorsement, collection, dishonour, noting, retirement and renewal (2.1, covered here); account for Consignment business in the books of both consignor and consignee, including stock valuation and losses (2.2); and account for a Joint Venture business (2.3). 2.2 and 2.3 follow later in this module.

Glossary — Bills of Exchange, in Plain Words

The technical terms 2.1 introduces, explained simply. (Consignment and Joint Venture terms follow later in this module.)

Negotiable InstrumentA document entitling a person to a certain sum of money, transferable from person to person by delivery or by endorsement and delivery — a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque [Section 13(1), Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881].
Bill of ExchangeAn instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer [Section 5, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881].
Drawer / MakerThe party who issues (draws) the bill — the creditor, lender or seller.
DraweeThe party to whom the order to pay is sent — the debtor or purchaser. Becomes the "Acceptor" once he writes his acceptance on the bill.
PayeeThe party to whom the bill is payable — may be the drawer himself, or someone else.
AcceptanceThe drawee's written agreement, on the bill itself, to pay it — only after this does the drawee become the "acceptor".
EndorsementThe drawer/holder signing the bill over to a creditor (e.g. to settle his own debt) instead of collecting it or discounting it himself.
DiscountingSelling the bill to a bank before maturity for cash less a deduction ("discount") for the unexpired period.
Bills Receivable (B/R)A bill from the drawer's/holder's viewpoint — shown as an asset on his Balance Sheet.
Bills Payable (B/P)The same bill from the drawee's/acceptor's viewpoint — shown as a liability on his Balance Sheet.
Days of GraceThree extra days added to a time bill's stated period to arrive at the legal due date. Demand / at-sight / on-presentation bills get none.
DishonourFailure to honour a bill — by non-acceptance (drawee refuses to accept) or by non-payment (acceptor fails to pay on the due date).
Noting (of a Bill)A Notary Public's formal recording of the fact of dishonour, for a fee (the Noting Charge) — paid by the holder, but ultimately recoverable from the party responsible for the dishonour.
Retirement of a BillThe drawee paying the bill before its due date, by mutual understanding with the drawer/holder.
Rebate on BillThe allowance (interest for the unexpired period) the holder gives the drawee on early (retired) payment — an expense for the holder, income for the drawee.
Renewal of a BillCancelling a bill the drawee cannot pay on time and, by mutual agreement, drawing a fresh bill for the amount due (plus interest for the extended period).
Accommodation BillA bill drawn and accepted without any real trade consideration, purely to raise finance for one or more of the parties — also called a Kite Bill.
Deficiency AccountThe account in the drawee's/acceptor's books to which an unrecoverable shortfall is transferred on insolvency of the other party.

CONCEPT

2.1 Accounting for Bills of Exchange ★★★ HIGH

"Negotiable" means transferable from one person to another; "instrument" means a written document creating a right in favour of a person. A Negotiable Instrument is thus any document entitling a person to a certain sum of money, transferable by delivery or by endorsement and delivery, under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

Section 13(1), Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881: "A negotiable instrument means a promissory note or bill of exchange or cheque, payable either to order or to the bearer."

Section 5, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881: "A bill of exchange is an instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer of the instrument."

The order to pay is not "conditional" merely because payment is tied to the lapse of a period after an event that, in the ordinary course, is certain to happen (even if its exact timing is uncertain). The sum is still "certain" even if it includes future interest, or is payable at an indicated/market rate of exchange, or provides that on default of an instalment the whole unpaid balance becomes due.

Essential elements of a Bill of Exchange:

  1. Must be in writing, in any language or form.
  2. Must be drawn on a particular date.
  3. Has three parties — Drawer/Maker, Drawee and Payee.
  4. Must be signed by the Drawer/Maker.
  5. Must contain an unconditional and imperative order to pay.
  6. The order to pay must be directed to a certain person.
  7. The order must be to pay a certain sum of money only.
  8. Must be accompanied by proper stamp duty as required by law.

Parties to a Bill of Exchange:

  • Drawer — issues the bill; the creditor, lender or seller; the "maker" of the bill.
  • Drawee — the party the order to pay is sent to; the debtor or purchaser. Becomes the Acceptor on writing acceptance on the bill.
  • Payee — the party the bill is payable to; may be the drawer himself, or someone else.

Classification of Bills of Exchange

  • Documentary Bill — supported by relevant documents confirming the underlying transaction.
  • Demand Bill — payable whenever demanded; no fixed date of payment; cleared whenever presented.
  • Usance Bill — a time-bound bill; payment due within a given time period.
  • Inland Bill — payable only within one country, not abroad; opposite of a foreign bill.
  • Foreign Bill — can be paid outside India, e.g. an export bill or import bill.
  • Clean Bill — has no supporting documentary proof, so carries comparatively higher interest.
  • Trade Bill — specifically related to trade; drawn for genuine consideration.
  • Supply Bill — drawn by a supplier/contractor on a government department.
  • Accommodation Bill — drawn, sponsored and accepted without any real consideration — see the dedicated section later in this topic.
BasisTrade BillAccommodation Bill
ObjectiveDrawn to facilitate genuine trade transactions of sale and purchase of goods.Drawn to help someone in need of financial assistance.
ConsiderationThere is a definite consideration for which the bill is accepted.Drawn without any consideration.
Extension of creditA form of credit extension.Not a form of credit extension.
Proceeds on discountingProceeds belong wholly to the party discounting it.Proceeds are shared by the parties in an agreed ratio.
Recovery on dishonourAmount may be recovered easily through the court.The drawer cannot file a suit against the drawee.

Maturity / Due Date and Days of Grace

Bill TypeRule for Due Date
Demand Bill / At Sight Bill / On Presentation BillBecomes due for payment as soon as it is presented — no time for payment is mentioned. No Days of Grace.
After Date BillTime for payment is measured from the bill's own date. 3 Days of Grace allowed.
After Sight BillPayable a fixed period after "sight" — the period begins from the date of ACCEPTING the bill, not its date. 3 Days of Grace allowed.

Period given in MONTHS → count by calendar months (ignore the actual number of days in each month), then add 3 Days of Grace.

Example: bill dated 4th May 2022, payable 3 months after date → 4th May + 3 months = 4th August 2022, + 3 Days of Grace = 7th August 2022.

Period given in DAYS → count actual calendar days, EXCLUDING the date of the transaction but INCLUDING the date of payment, then add 3 Days of Grace.

Example: bill dated 5th June 2022, payable after 65 days → 25 remaining days of June + 31 days of July + 9 days of August = 65 days, + 3 Days of Grace = 12th August 2022.

National Holiday on the due date — due date moves to the day BEFORE (e.g. due date falling on 26th January or 15th August → the day before, 25th January / 14th August). Emergency Holiday declared on the due date — due date moves to the day AFTER.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: MIXING UP THE TWO HOLIDAY RULES

THE TRAP: students apply the same shift (always "day before" or always "day after") to every holiday-on-due-date situation, and forget the Days-of-Grace addition happens BEFORE the holiday check, not instead of it.

THE TWIST: a pre-known national holiday shifts the due date one day EARLIER; a due date that turns out to be an emergency (unforeseen) holiday shifts it one day LATER. Always add the 3 Days of Grace first to get the base due date, THEN apply the holiday rule — both are illustrated together for the same bill in Illustration 1 below.

Bills Receivable and Bills Payable

Bills Receivable (B/R) — for the person who draws the bill and is entitled to receive its payment; shown on the assets side of that person's (the drawer's) Balance Sheet.

Bills Payable (B/P) — for the person who accepts the bill and is liable to pay it; shown on the liabilities side of that person's (the drawee's) Balance Sheet.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Calculating the Due Date of a Bill

(1) Bill dated 1st January 2023, tenure 4 months. (2) Bill dated 23rd November 2023, tenure 2 months.

Solution — Calculation of Due Date
ParticularsBill (1)Bill (2)
Date of drawing01.01.202323.11.2023
+ Tenure4 months → 01.05.20232 months → 23.01.2024
+ Days of Grace3 days3 days
Due date before holiday check04.05.202326.01.2024
Holiday adjustment—26.01.2024 is Republic Day (national holiday) → shift to the day BEFORE

Answer: Bill (1) due date = 04.05.2023. Bill (2) due date = 25.01.2024.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — The Same Bill Under Four Different Endings

Y accepted and returned it to X, and met his acceptance on maturity (due date: 01.01 + 3 months = 01.04 + 3 Days of Grace = April 4, 2023). Record the journal entries under: (i) X retains the bill to maturity and collects directly; (ii) X discounts it @12% p.a. with his bank on January 01, 2023; (iii) X endorses it to his creditor Z on January 01, 2023; (iv) X retains it, sends it for collection to his bank on March 31, 2023, and receives bank advice on April 05, 2023.

Dishonour of Bills

ModeMeaning
Dishonour by non-acceptanceThe drawee (or one of several drawees, where they are not partners) fails/refuses to accept the bill when duly required, or presentment is excused and the bill is not accepted. No accounting entries are required for this event itself.
Dishonour by non-paymentPayment is not made by the drawee to the holder on the date of maturity. Accounting entries are required in the books of drawer, drawee, and endorsee (if any).
Noting of a BillThe Notary Public's formal recording of the fact of dishonour, for a fee (the Noting Fee/Charge). It is an expense for the bill's holder, and is recovered from the party responsible.
Dishonour due to insolvencyEither nothing, or only a partial amount (the "Final Dividend"), is recovered from the insolvent drawee/acceptor. In the drawer's books the shortfall is debited to Bad Debts A/c; in the drawee's books it is transferred to Deficiency A/c.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: WHO ULTIMATELY BEARS THE NOTING CHARGES?

THE TRAP: students expense the noting charges permanently to whoever physically paid the notary — the holder (X), the bank, or the endorsee (Z) — and stop there.

THE TWIST: whoever pays the notary pays it first, but it is always ultimately RECOVERABLE FROM THE DISHONOURING ACCEPTOR (Y). That is why, in every one of Illustration 3's three cases, Y's account is finally debited with ₹15,050 (bill value + ₹50 noting charges) — even though X, the bank, or Z each physically paid the ₹50 first.

Renewal of a Bill

When the drawee cannot meet a bill on its due date, he approaches the drawer requesting an extension of time. If the drawer agrees, the OLD bill is cancelled and a FRESH bill, with new terms of payment, is drawn, duly accepted and delivered — this is Renewal. The new bill is drawn for an extended period, so interest is charged for that extension.

ILLUSTRATION 4 — Renewal of a Bill with Interest and Part-Cash

On February 01, 2023, X sold goods to Y for ₹18,000; ₹3,000 was paid by Y immediately, and for the balance he accepted a three-month bill drawn on him by X (due date: Feb 01 + 3 months = May 01 + 3 Days of Grace = May 04, 2023). On the date of maturity, Y requested X to cancel the old bill and draw a new bill for a period of 2 months, agreeing to pay interest in cash @12% p.a. (new due date: May 04 + 2 months = Jul 04 + 3 Days of Grace = July 07, 2023). Interest on ₹15,000 @12% p.a. for 2 months = ₹300.

Retirement of a Bill

When the drawee pays the bill BEFORE its due date, by mutual understanding with the drawer, it is termed Retirement of a bill.

Rebate on Bill = interest, at an agreed rate, for the UNEXPIRED period of the bill (i.e. from the date of early payment to the original date of maturity), allowed by the holder to the drawee.

Rebate is an EXPENSE for the payee/holder and an INCOME for the drawee — the exact mirror-image of the discounting entries seen earlier.

X sold goods worth ₹10,000 to Y on January 01, 2023 and immediately drew a 3-month bill on Y for the same amount (due date April 04, 2023). Y accepted the bill and returned it to X. On March 04, 2023, Y retired her acceptance under a rebate of 6% per annum for the one-month unexpired period. Rebate = ₹10,000 × 6% × 1⁄12 = ₹50.

    To Bills Receivable A/c10,000

(Being Y retired her acceptance; rebate allowed to her)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DISCOUNT vs. REBATE — SAME FORMULA, OPPOSITE DIRECTION

THE TRAP: students treat "discounting a bill with a bank" and "retiring a bill under rebate" as the same transaction, or apply the discount/rebate to the FULL bill period instead of the correct time span.

THE TWIST: Discount (Illustration 2/3) is charged on the UNEXPIRED period from the date of DISCOUNTING to the bill's due date, and is an expense for the DRAWER (who is getting cash early from a bank). Rebate (Illustration 5) is charged on the UNEXPIRED period from the date of RETIREMENT to the bill's due date, but is an expense for the HOLDER/PAYEE and an INCOME for the DRAWEE (who is paying early). In Illustration 5, the unexpired period is exactly 1 month (March 04 to April 04) — using the full 3-month bill tenure instead is the single most common numerical error on this topic.

BasisRetirement of a BillRenewal of a Bill
What happensDrawee pays BEFORE the due date.Old bill is cancelled; a NEW bill is drawn for a LATER due date.
Cash movementCash/Bank actually changes hands early.No cash need change hands at once — the debt is simply carried forward on new terms.
Adjustment madeRebate (interest ALLOWED to the drawee for paying early) — reduces the amount received.Interest CHARGED to the drawee for the extension — increases the amount now owed.
Who gainsThe drawee gains (income); the holder loses (expense).The drawer gains (interest income); the drawee loses (interest expense).

Accommodation Bills

Ordinary bills drawn for genuine consideration are "Trade Bills". Accommodation Bills are drawn and accepted WITHOUT any consideration — when two or more persons, not standing in a debtor-creditor relationship (and with no value passing between them), draw bills on each other intending to discount the bill after acceptance, appropriate the proceeds in an agreed proportion, and provide money in the same proportion for honouring the bills at maturity. Also called a Kite Bill.

In case of Accommodation Bills, no Days of Grace is given, as it is not a trade bill and cannot be legally challenged in the same way.

ILLUSTRATION 6 — Mutual Accommodation, Shared 2:1

X drew a bill for ₹6,000 on Y for mutual accommodation. Y accepted the bill and returned it to X, who discounted it immediately @6% p.a. Discount = ₹6,000 × 6% × 3⁄12 = ₹90. Per agreement, X and Y shared the proceeds 2:1. On the date of maturity, X remitted his share to Y, who honoured the bill by payment.

Glossary — Consignment & Joint Venture, in Plain Words

Terms used through 2.2 and 2.3, explained simply.

ConsignmentSending your own goods to an agent in another place who sells them for you, on commission. Ownership stays with you until the agent actually sells.
ConsignorThe sender/owner of the goods. Bears the profit or loss of the whole consignment business.
ConsigneeThe agent who receives and sells the goods for a commission. Passes NO entry merely on receiving the goods — never becomes their owner.
Proforma InvoiceThe memorandum invoice the consignor sends with the goods, showing quantity and a price — a description, not a bill; it creates no debt.
Account SalesThe periodic statement the consignee sends back: sales made, expenses deducted, commission due, and the balance remitted.
Ordinary CommissionThe consignee's basic fee for selling, on gross sales — does NOT cover the risk of bad debts.
Del Credere CommissionAn extra commission for guaranteeing collection of credit sales. Computed on TOTAL (cash + credit) sales unless the problem says otherwise. The consignee then absorbs bad debts.
Over-riding / Special CommissionAn extra reward paid when the consignee sells above a pre-set price or beats a sales target.
Invoice Price (IP)Cost plus a hidden margin (the Load) — used so the consignee cannot work out the consignor's true cost or profit.
Load / LoadingThe artificial margin sitting inside the Invoice Price (IP − Cost). It must be cancelled out, via Stock Reserve, wherever it survives into year-end figures.
Consignment StockUnsold goods still with the consignee at period end — the consignor's own asset, valued at cost/IP plus a fair share of the "getting-there" expenses.
Stock ReserveThe account that cancels the Load hiding inside consignment stock valued at Invoice Price.
Goods-in-TransitGoods despatched by the consignor but not yet arrived at the consignee's premises at the year end — valued using the consignor's own expenses only.
Normal LossUnavoidable loss from the goods' own nature (evaporation, spillage). Gets no value of its own — it silently shrinks the quantity used to value the surviving stock.
Abnormal LossAvoidable loss (theft, fire, accident). Valued at cost/IP and pulled out via a separate Abnormal Loss A/c so it doesn't distort the consignment's profit.
Non-recurring ExpensesOne-time "getting-there" costs (freight, carriage, insurance-in-transit, clearing, customs, octroi) — these ARE added when valuing stock, goods-in-transit and abnormal loss.
Recurring ExpensesOngoing costs after the goods arrive (godown rent, insurance of godown, selling expenses, commission) — these are NEVER added to stock value.
Joint VentureA temporary business undertaking between two or more persons for one specific job/project, sharing profit as agreed, dissolved once the job is done. No firm name is used.
Co-venturerEach party to a joint venture — a co-owner of the venture, not an agent.
Joint Bank AccountUnder the separate-books method, the one common bank account holding contributions, sale proceeds and payments — settled last, so it tallies.
Memorandum Joint Venture AccountA profit-finding statement built by pooling each co-venturer's own transactions — "memorandum" because it sits OUTSIDE the double-entry system.
CONCEPT

2.2 Accounting for Consignment ★★★ HIGH

In a consignment business, goods are sent by the consignor to the consignee purely for the purpose of selling them. The transaction is recorded in the books of the consignor — but the consignee passes no entry at all on merely receiving the goods. Since the goods leave the consignor's regular stock, a corresponding adjustment is made against Purchases A/c or Trading A/c. Goods sent may be recorded by the consignor either at Cost Price (CP) or at Invoice Price (IP) — IP being cost plus a fixed margin (the Load), used when the consignor does not want the consignee to know the true cost.

Advance by consignee to consignor: the consignor usually sends goods only after receiving an adequate advance — by bank draft, or by the consignee accepting a bill of exchange in the consignor's favour. The advance is adjusted later against amounts actually due. By agreement, a security proportionate to any unsold stock may be retained by the consignor and carried forward to the next period.

Expenses on consignment may be incurred by either party, but are never simply "reimbursed" — the consignee's own expenses are adjusted against the sale proceeds otherwise due to the consignor, inside the Account Sales.

Recurring vs. Non-recurring Expenses

This split decides which expenses enter the valuation of unsold stock, goods-in-transit and abnormal loss — get it wrong and every downstream figure is wrong.

Non-recurring (one-time, "getting there")Recurring (ongoing, after arrival)
Freight & carriage to consignee, packing/loading charges, export duty, transit insurance (consignor); unloading, dock charges, clearing charges, import/customs duty, octroi, carriage to godown (consignee)Godown rent, insurance of godown, carriage outward, establishment charges, advertising & publicity, salesmen's salary, commission, other selling expenses
Only the NON-RECURRING expenses (consignor's in full, consignee's non-recurring portion only) enter the valuation of unsold stock, goods-in-transit and goods abnormally lost.

Commission — Three Kinds

Ordinary Commission = Gross Sales × agreed %

Due to the consignee simply for rendering the regular activities of the consignment business.

Del Credere Commission = Gross Sales × agreed % (unless the problem restricts it)

Payable for taking on the risk of credit sales — bad debts and collection responsibility. Calculated on gross (total) sales unless otherwise agreed.

Over-riding / Special Commission = extra reward for beating a target

Paid over and above ordinary commission when the consignee sells above a pre-determined price, or exceeds a sales target.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DEL CREDERE COMMISSION BASE

THE TRAP: assuming del credere commission is calculated only on the CREDIT portion of sales, since it exists to cover credit-sale risk.

THE TWIST: unless the problem says otherwise, it is calculated on TOTAL (cash + credit) sales — e.g. cash sales ₹25,000 + credit sales ₹75,000 at 10% del credere gives ₹10,000 (10% of ₹1,00,000, not just ₹75,000). Always re-read the wording though: some problems (as one illustration in this module does) explicitly restrict del credere to "credit sales made by him" only — in that case, and only then, apply the rate to credit sales alone.

Loss of Goods — Normal vs. Abnormal

Consignment involves considerable movement and handling of goods, so some loss is common. It falls into two categories.

Normal LossAbnormal Loss
NatureUnavoidable, inherent in the goods (evaporation, spillage)Avoidable (goods pilfered, stolen, lost by fire/calamity)
Part of cost of goods sold?Yes — silently absorbedNo — kept out of cost of goods sold
Value assignedNone — it only shrinks the unit denominator used to value surviving stockValued at cost/IP and pulled out via a separate Abnormal Loss A/c
Where it can occur—In transit (consignor's premises → consignee's warehouse) OR at the consignee's premises (fire, theft, bad handling)
Expenses considered when valuing it—Goods lost in transit: consignor's expenses only. Goods lost at consignee's premises: consignor's expenses + consignee's non-recurring expenses.

When normal loss and abnormal loss occur at the same point, normal loss is adjusted first (silently absorbed) and abnormal loss is valued afterward, at cost, on the reduced quantity.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE ORDER FLIPS WITH THE LOCATION

THE TRAP: mechanically applying "normal loss first, then abnormal" in every case.

THE TWIST: that rule applies only when BOTH losses occur at the SAME point — e.g. both discovered at the consignee's godown: deduct normal loss first (no value), then value the abnormal loss on the reduced quantity. But an abnormal loss occurring IN TRANSIT is valued straight off the quantity originally despatched — before any normal loss (which typically only becomes apparent later, at the godown) is even applied. Read carefully WHERE each loss happened before choosing the order.

Valuing Unsold Stock & Goods-in-Transit

Stock Value (at Cost) = [Cost of goods sent + Consignor's non-recurring exp. + Consignee's non-recurring exp.] × (Unsold units ÷ Total units received)

Never add the consignee's recurring expenses (godown rent, insurance of godown, selling expenses, commission).

Stock Value (at IP) = [IP of goods sent + Consignor's non-recurring exp. + Consignee's non-recurring exp.] × (Unsold units ÷ Total units received)

This still carries the hidden Load. A Stock Reserve = Load × (Unsold units ÷ Total units sent) is created — debited to Consignment A/c — so only the TRUE cost of the unsold stock survives as an asset.

Goods-in-Transit Value = [Cost/IP of goods despatched + Consignor's OWN expenses only] × relevant proportion

No expense of the consignee is ever added — the goods have not reached the consignee's premises yet.

Books Maintained — Consignor & Consignee

Books of Consignor:

  • Consignment A/c — the profit-determining account: expenses/losses matched against revenue; the balancing figure (profit or loss) is transferred to P/L A/c.
  • Goods Sent on Consignment A/c — records goods sent (and returns), finally transferred to Purchases/Trading A/c.
  • Consignee's A/c — a personal account; its closing balance is the amount still due from the consignee.
  • Consignment Stock A/c — the unsold stock lying with the consignee at period end.
  • Consignment Debtors A/c — maintained by the CONSIGNOR only when del credere commission is not paid, i.e. the consignor itself bears the credit-sale risk.

Books of Consignee:

  • Consignor's A/c — its closing balance is the amount still due FROM the consignee TO the consignor.
  • Commission A/c(s) — separate accounts for Ordinary, Del credere and Over-riding/Special commission.
  • Consignment Debtors A/c — maintained by the CONSIGNEE only when del credere commission IS paid, i.e. the consignee itself bears the credit-sale risk.

Some consignees additionally keep a Consignment Inward A/c to record the movement of goods received — but generally, no accounting at all is done in the consignee's books for the mere receipt of goods.

Journal Entries at a Glance — Part A: Goods, Advances & Expenses

EventBooks of ConsignorBooks of Consignee
Goods sent — at CostConsignment A/c Dr → To Goods Sent on Consignment A/cNo entry
Goods sent — at IPConsignment A/c Dr → To Goods Sent on Consignment A/c (at IP); then Goods Sent on Consignment A/c Dr → To Consignment A/c (load cancelled)No entry
Expenses incurred by consignorConsignment A/c Dr → To Bank/Cash A/cNo entry

Discounting the Bill ReceivableBank A/c Dr, Discount on Bill A/c Dr → To Bills Receivable A/cNo entry

Expenses paid by consigneeConsignment A/c Dr → To Consignee A/cConsignor A/c Dr → To Bank/Cash A/c

Journal Entries at a Glance — Part B: Sales, Commission, Debtors, Losses & Settlement

EventBooks of ConsignorBooks of Consignee
Sale — cashConsignee A/c Dr → To Consignment A/cBank A/c Dr → To Consignor A/c
Sale — credit, del credere PROVIDEDConsignee A/c Dr → To Consignment A/c (treated exactly like a cash sale)Consignment Debtors A/c Dr → To Consignor A/c
Sale — credit, del credere NOT providedConsignment Debtors A/c Dr → To Consignment A/cNo entry
Commission due to consigneeConsignment A/c Dr → To Consignee A/cConsignor A/c Dr → To Commission A/c
Collection from Consignment Debtors — del credere providedNo entryBank A/c Dr → To Consignment Debtors A/c
Collection from Consignment Debtors — del credere NOT providedConsignee A/c Dr → To Consignment Debtors A/cNo entry
Bad debt — del credere PROVIDED (loss falls on consignee)No entryBad Debt A/c Dr → To Consignment Debtors A/c; then Commission A/c Dr → To Bad Debt A/c
Bad debt — del credere NOT provided (loss falls on consignor)Consignment A/c Dr → To Consignment Debtors A/cNo entry
Abnormal loss (transit / consignee's place)Abnormal Loss A/c Dr → To Consignment A/c (load cancelled via Consignment A/c Dr → To Abnormal Loss A/c, if at IP)No entry
Insurance claim on abnormal lossBank A/c Dr (received) / Insurance Claim A/c Dr (admitted, unrealised) / Consignee A/c Dr (received by consignee); net loss: P/L A/c Dr → To Abnormal Loss A/cBank A/c Dr → To Consignor A/c (if received on consignor's behalf)
Closing (unsold) stockConsignment Stock A/c Dr → To Consignment A/c (load cancelled via Consignment A/c Dr → To Stock Reserve A/c, if at IP)No entry
Profit / Loss on consignmentProfit: Consignment A/c Dr → To P/L A/c  |  Loss: P/L A/c Dr → To Consignment A/cNo entry
Final remittanceBank A/c / Bills Receivable A/c Dr → To Consignee A/cConsignor A/c Dr → To Bank A/c / Bills Payable A/c
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: NO ENTRY ON RECEIPT, AND BAD DEBTS FOLLOW THE GUARANTEE

THE TRAP: (i) recording something in the consignee's books the moment goods arrive; (ii) always debiting bad debts to Consignment A/c.

THE TWIST: (i) the consignee passes NO entry merely on receiving consigned goods — only money and things it owns get recorded. (ii) bad debts are borne by whoever guaranteed collection: charged against the consignee's own Commission A/c when del credere IS paid (it reduces the consignee's earnings, not the consignment's profit), but charged to Consignment A/c when del credere is NOT paid.

ILLUSTRATION 10 — Baseline: ordinary + del credere commission, provision for collection charges

Agarwal of Agra sent goods valued ₹1,00,000 on consignment to Biyani of Bhagalpur on 1.3.2022; freight & insurance ₹12,000. By 31.12.2022 Biyani had sold ALL goods for ₹1,50,000, incurring ₹2,000 selling expenses; only ₹1,48,000 was realised, the rest considered irrecoverable. Agarwal received the cheque on 5.1.2023, incurring ₹260 bank charges (credited by the bank 9.1.2023).

ILLUSTRATION 11 — Normal loss + abnormal loss: transit (a) vs. godown (b), same numbers

Singha Traders consigned 5,000 litres of edible oil, cost ₹32/litre, to M Ltd. of Mumbai (1.2.2023); freight & insurance ₹5,000 paid by consignor. (a) During TRANSIT, 200 litres were destroyed; insurer paid ₹5,000 in full settlement. M Ltd. paid clearing charges ₹6,100, godown rent ₹300, salesman's salary ₹900; entitled to 6% ordinary + 4% del credere commission. By 30.6.2023, 4,000 litres sold for ₹1,65,000; 100 litres lost to evaporation (normal loss).

(a) Consignment to Mumbai Account — loss occurs IN TRANSIT
Dr.       Consignment to Mumbai Account      Cr.
Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Goods Sent on Consignment A/c [5,000 × ₹32]1,60,000By M. Ltd. A/c [Sale]1,65,000
To Bank A/c [Freight & Insurance]5,000By Goods Destroyed-in-Transit A/c [WN]6,600
To M. Ltd. A/c [Clearing 6,100 + Godown Rent 300 + Salary 900]7,300By Consignment Stock A/c [WN]24,500
To M. Ltd. A/c [Commission: Ordinary 9,900 + Del credere 6,600]16,500

WN — value of goods destroyed-in-transit & unsold stock (abnormal loss deducted FIRST, before normal loss): Cost of goods sent 5,000 litres/₹1,60,000; + consignor's expenses ₹5,000 ⇒ 5,000 litres/₹1,65,000. Less: destroyed-in-transit [1,65,000 × 200/5,000] = 200 litres/₹6,600 ⇒ 4,800 litres/₹1,58,400. Add: consignee's non-recurring exp. (clearing) ₹6,100 ⇒ 4,800 litres/₹1,64,500. Less: normal loss 100 litres (no value) ⇒ 4,700 litres/₹1,64,500. Unsold stock = 5,000−200−100−4,000 = 700 litres; value = 700/4,700 × ₹1,64,500 = ₹24,500.

(b) Variant — if the SAME 200 litres were instead destroyed by THEFT at the consignee's godown (both normal and abnormal loss now occur at the same point — normal loss adjusted FIRST): Goods received 5,000 litres/₹1,65,000; + consignee's non-recurring exp. ₹6,100 ⇒ 5,000 litres/₹1,71,100. Less: normal loss 100 litres (no value) ⇒ 4,900 litres/₹1,71,100. Less: goods destroyed-at-godown [1,71,100 × 200/4,900] = 200 litres/₹6,984 ⇒ 4,700 litres/₹1,64,116. Unsold stock = 4,900−4,000 = 700 litres (valued by the same 700/4,700 proportion of ₹1,64,116).

Answer: (a) Profit on consignment = ₹7,300, goods destroyed-in-transit valued at ₹6,600. (b) The abnormal-loss figure changes to ₹6,984 purely because of WHERE the loss occurred and hence which deduction (normal or abnormal) came first.

ILLUSTRATION 14 — Goods at Invoice Price: loading, Stock Reserve, bad debt

On 1.1.2022 Shri G of Chennai consigned goods costing ₹1,32,000 to Shri H of Amritsar at a proforma invoice price of 20% above cost (₹1,58,400). Shri G paid freight & forwarding ₹4,000. Shri H: ₹2,000 p.a. establishment allowance (₹500 for 3 months), 5% commission on gross sales, paid ₹1,000 godown rent & insurance. 3/4 of the goods sold at 33⅓% profit on cost, half of that on credit; balance stock valued at IP. A customer owing ₹10,000 proved untraceable (written off); all other debtors cleared their dues. Shri H remitted the balance by bank draft on 31.3.2023.

ILLUSTRATION 20 — Advance by draft on account, surplus-price commission, goods-in-transit

Ram of Patna consigns to Shyam of Delhi for sale at invoice price or over; Shyam gets 5% commission on invoice price PLUS 25% of any surplus realised above invoice price. Ram draws a 90-days-sight bill on Shyam for 80% of invoice price as security; Shyam remits the balance by sight draft after deducting commission. Goods costing ₹20,900 (incl. freight) invoiced at ₹28,400. Sales made ₹26,760; goods unsold at 31 Dec. represented IP ₹6,920 (original cost incl. freight ₹5,220). Sight drafts received by Ram up to 31 Dec. totalled ₹6,280; the rest was still in transit.

WN — commission: Invoice value of goods 28,400 − unsold stock 6,920 = invoice value of goods sold 21,480. Total sale proceeds 26,760 − 21,480 = surplus price 5,280. Commission = 5% on 21,480 (₹1,074) + 25% on 5,280 (₹1,320) = ₹2,394.

Since the advance was drawn as 80% of INVOICE PRICE, it is adjusted only when goods are actually sold — the advance relating to the unsold stock (IP ₹6,920 × 80% = ₹5,536) must be carried forward rather than treated as settled; the "draft-in-transit" figure then falls out as the balancing figure.

Answer: Profit on consignment = ₹8,686.

Reverse-engineering from the Account Sales — a distinct exam technique

Where an Account Sales gives only the FINAL remittance and the deductions (not the total sales), total sales can be found by treating it as an equation. One illustration in the source: an agent remitted ₹4,11,650 by bank draft after deducting 5% commission on gross sales, expenses ₹5,000, bad debts ₹850 and a bill of ₹10,000 accepted as advance.

Let total sales = X, so commission = 0.05X. Final remittance = (Collection from debtors − bad debts) − advance already received (B/R) − expenses − commission:
4,11,650 = (X − 850) − 10,000 − 5,000 − 0.05X
4,11,650 = 0.95X − 15,850 ⇒ 0.95X = 4,27,500 ⇒ X = ₹4,50,000

Answer: Total (gross) sales = ₹4,50,000; commission due = ₹22,500. The same trick works to split sales made at plain invoice price vs. sales made at invoice price plus a further margin, by setting up a second simultaneous equation.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: COMMISSION IS ON GROSS SALES — EVEN "WRITE-OFF" SALES COUNT

THE TRAP: assuming a consignee earns no commission on goods sold as damaged/scrap, since those aren't "real" sales.

THE TWIST: since commission is allowed on GROSS sales, the consignee is entitled to commission even on the small sale proceeds of damaged/abnormal-loss goods sold off cheaply — the source itself notes this explicitly in one illustration where a consignee earned 6% commission even on a ₹50 sale of a written-off unit.

Consignment vs. Ordinary Sale

AspectConsignmentOrdinary Sale
RelationshipPrincipal (consignor) and Agent (consignee)Seller and Buyer
OwnershipRemains with the consignor until the consignee actually sells to a third partyTransfers to the buyer immediately, at the point of sale
Entry on receipt of goodsThe consignee passes no entry merely on receiving the goodsThe buyer records the purchase immediately
Unsold goodsCan be returned by the consignee to the consignorCannot ordinarily be returned merely because unsold
What the recipient owesThe consignee's liability is only for money actually due (sale proceeds realised) — not for the value of goods merely receivedThe buyer is a debtor for the full invoice value from the moment of purchase
CONCEPT

2.3 Accounting for Joint Venture ★★ MEDIUM

A Joint Venture (JV) is a business arrangement in which two or more parties agree to pool their resources for a specific business plan or project. Salient features:

  • An agreement between two or more persons, for the specific execution of a business plan/project.
  • A temporary partnership without the use of a firm name.
  • Profit & loss are shared on whatever terms are agreed — if there is no agreement on the ratio, they are shared equally by all parties (exactly the partnership default rule).
  • Terms are usually set out in a written agreement (duration, mode of association, liabilities, etc.).
  • Of short duration — it comes to an end once the purpose of the agreement is served.

The parties are called Co-venturers or Joint venturers. A joint venture is treated, as a matter of law, much like a partnership — but is terminated once the venture period is over, which is why a firm name is not generally used.

Joint Venture vs. Partnership

AspectPartnershipJoint Venture
Firm's nameAlways carried on with a firm's nameNo firm's name required
What the parties are calledPartnersCo-venturers
DurationNormally long-term, spanning various projectsFormed to complete one specific job/project
Governing lawThe Partnership Act, 1932No dedicated statute — but treated in law as a partnership
Number of membersLimited to 10 (banking business) / 20 (any other business)No limit specified
LiabilityUnlimited — may extend to a partner's personal estateLimited to the particular assignment/project agreed upon

Joint Venture vs. Consignment

AspectJoint VentureConsignment
RelationshipCo-venturers are joint OWNERS of the ventureOwner (consignor) and Agent (consignee)
Sharing of profitsCo-venturers share profit in the agreed ratioNo profit distribution — the consignee earns only commission
Ownership of goodsEvery co-venturer is a co-owner of the goods/projectOwnership stays with the consignor; only possession passes to the consignee
Contribution of fundsFunds are contributed by all co-venturers, in an agreed proportionInvestment is made by the consignor only
ContinuityNo continuity — ends once the project is completeCan be a continuous, ongoing process

A quick "Statement" method — profit without a full ledger

A and B enter a joint venture, profit-sharing 3:2. A purchased goods costing ₹2,00,000. B sold 95% of the goods for ₹2,50,000. A gets 1% commission on purchases, B gets 5% commission on sales. A drew a bill on B for 80% of original cost and got it discounted at ₹1,50,000.

Statement Showing Calculation of Profit on Joint Venture
Particulars₹
Sales2,50,000
Add: Closing stock (5% of ₹2,00,000)10,000
Total2,60,000
Less: Purchases2,00,000
Less: A's commission (2,00,000 × 1%)2,000
Less: B's commission (2,50,000 × 5%)12,500
Less: Discount charges [(2,00,000 × 80%) − 1,50,000]10,000
Net Profit35,500

Answer: B's share of profit = ₹35,500 × 2/5 = ₹14,200.

Method I — When a Separate Set of Books IS Maintained

Since the venture is short-lived, the books kept are not comprehensive — the basic purpose is simply to ascertain profit or loss. Three accounts are opened:

  • Joint Venture A/c — debited with every expense (whether paid personally by a co-venturer or out of the Joint Bank, capital or revenue in nature); credited with all sales (to outsiders and to co-venturers alike). Its balance is the venture's profit or loss.
  • Joint Bank A/c — basically the cash book of the venture: records initial contributions, sale proceeds, expenses, and final settlement (settled last, so it tallies).
  • Co-venturers' A/c — like a capital account in partnership; its balance is a co-venturer's claim to/from the business, settled through the Joint Bank A/c.

Method I vs. Method II

AspectMethod I: Separate BooksMethod II: No Separate Books
Books keptFresh set: Joint Venture A/c + Joint Bank A/c + Co-venturers' personal A/csEach co-venturer records the venture inside their OWN regular books
Cash handlingAll contributions/receipts/payments routed through one common Joint Bank A/cNo common bank account — each co-venturer pays/collects independently
When usedVenture is substantial enough to justify a fresh set of booksVenture is small/short and co-venturers operate from distant places
Variants— single method(a) each keeps a FULL record of all transactions (own + the other's); or (b) each keeps a record of ONLY their own transactions, profit found via a Memorandum Joint Venture A/c

Method II(a) — Each Co-venturer Records ALL Transactions

No Joint Bank A/c is opened; each co-venturer takes into account transactions done by himself AND by the other co-venturer. In the books of co-venturer A (and mirrored, with names swapped, in B's books):

  • Goods supplied/expenses paid by A: Joint Venture A/c Dr → To Purchases A/c / Cash-Bank A/c.
  • Goods supplied/expenses paid by B: Joint Venture A/c Dr → To B's A/c.
  • Sale proceeds received by A: Cash/Bank A/c Dr → To Joint Venture A/c. Received by B: B's A/c Dr → To Joint Venture A/c.
  • Unsold goods taken over by A: Purchase A/c Dr → To Joint Venture A/c (treated like a sale).
  • Profit: Joint Venture A/c Dr → To B's A/c (other's share) and To P&L A/c (own share). Loss: reversed.

Method II(b) — Memorandum Method (Each Records Only Own Transactions)

Each co-venturer keeps a "Joint Venture with [other's name] A/c" recording ONLY what he himself did, and periodically exchanges a statement of his own transactions with the other. A combined Memorandum Joint Venture A/c is then built (outside the double-entry system) purely to find the profit/loss, which is then brought into each co-venturer's own personal record.

  • Goods supplied from own stock: Joint Venture with [X] A/c Dr → To Purchases A/c / Goods sent to JV A/c.
  • Sale of goods: Cash/Bank/JV Debtors A/c Dr → To Joint Venture with [X] A/c.
  • Taking away unsold goods: Purchases/Drawings A/c Dr → To Joint Venture with [X] A/c (Goods sent to JV A/c).
  • Share of profit: Joint Venture with [X] A/c Dr → To P/L A/c. Share of loss: reversed.

Not recorded in either co-venturer's own books: transactions effected by the OTHER co-venturer directly (they only appear via the periodic statement, pooled in the Memorandum A/c), and any transaction not involving actual cash receipt or payment.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: UNSOLD STOCK TAKEN OVER, AND WHO PAYS FOR EXPENSES

THE TRAP: (i) simply removing/ignoring stock a co-venturer keeps for personal use; (ii) leaving out expenses a co-venturer paid from their own pocket, on the theory that "no venture cash moved."

THE TWIST: (i) stock taken over by a co-venturer is treated as INCOME of the joint venture — credited to Joint Venture A/c and debited to that co-venturer's own account, at the agreed value, exactly like a sale (seen with Pakhi's unused materials and Mukesh's plant above). (ii) Joint Venture A/c is debited with EVERY expense of the venture — capital or revenue in nature — whether paid personally by a co-venturer or through the Joint Bank Account; nothing is left out merely because it didn't pass through the common account.

Multi-period Ventures, and Converting a Consignment into a Joint Venture

If a joint venture runs beyond one accounting period, the closing stock (valued at basic cost plus proportionate non-recurring expenses) is shown on the CREDIT side of that year's Memorandum Joint Venture A/c and brought down to the DEBIT side of next year's account — the other accounts continue as usual.

A variation covered in the source: an ongoing consignment arrangement can be converted into a joint venture mid-stream. Normal consignment accounting continues right up to the point of conversion; on conversion, the value of the unsold stock is transferred out of the Consignment A/c and into a new Joint Venture arrangement, on whatever profit-sharing basis is agreed from that point.

Self-Assessment — Multiple Choice Questions

1. Which class of account is Consignment Account?

(a) Personal Account(b) Real Account(c) Representative Personal Account(d) Nominal Account

2. The Memorandum Joint Venture Account is prepared —

(a) for determining the amount due to co-venturer(b) for determining the amount due from co-venturer(c) for ascertaining the profit/loss on venture(d) None of the above

3. On dishonour of a bill of exchange that has been discounted, noting charges are initially paid by ______.

(a) Bank(b) Drawer(c) Drawee(d) Acceptor

4. The share of profit of a co-venturer maintaining only her/his own transactions is ______. (options as extracted)

(b) Debited to other co-venturer's personal account(c) Debited to Profit & Loss Account(d) None of the above

5. If any stock is taken by a co-venturer, it will be treated as ______.

(a) an income of the joint venture(b) an expense of the joint venture(c) to be ignored from joint venture

6. The balance in Consignment Account shows ______.

(a) Amount receivable from consignee(b) Amount payable to consignee(c) Profit/loss on consignment(d) Closing stock with consignee

7. Shyam and Ramya enter the business of buying and selling food grain for a period of one year, sharing profit in the ratio 2:4 — this agreement is a:

(a) Partnership(b) Consignment(c) Joint Venture(d) Lease

9. Which commission is allowed by the consignor to encourage the consignee to put in hard work introducing a new product in the market?

(a) Del-credere Commission(b) Over-riding Commission(c) Hard Work Commission(d) Ordinary Commission

10. If Kaveri's acceptance, which was endorsed by us in favour of Saleem, is dishonoured, the amount will be debited in our books to:

(a) Saleem(b) Kaveri(c) Bills Receivable Account(d) None of the above

Answers (from the source): 1–d, 2–c, 3–a, 4–b, 5–a, 6–c, 7–c, 9–b, 10–b.

Self-Assessment — True/False and Fill in the Blanks

True or False (as extracted): 1. A joint venture has a definite life. — True. 4. Proforma Invoice is a document sent by the consignor to the consignee. — True.

Fill in the Blanks (with answers, as given by the source):

  • A bill of exchange drawn on April 12, 2022, payable 3 months after sight, accepted on April 13, 2022 — date of maturity: July 16, 2022.
  • Partners in a joint venture business are called co-venturers.
  • The party who sends the goods on a consignment basis is the consignor.
  • Commission due to the consignee for rendering the regular activities of consignment business is called ordinary commission.
  • If cash sales are ₹25,000, credit sales are ₹75,000, and del-credere commission is 10%, the commission is ₹10,000 — confirming del credere is computed on TOTAL sales (25,000 + 75,000), not credit sales alone.
  • Non-recurring expenses are included while computing the value of stock on consignment.
  • At the time goods are sent to the consignee, the proforma invoice is prepared by the consignor.
  • The relationship between consignee and consignor is that of agent and principal.

On the due date the bill was dishonoured; Y, having become insolvent, paid 80% of his acceptance as full and final dividend on 12.4.2023. Pass the journal entries.

On 1.9.2023 C purchased goods worth ₹1,90,000 from B, endorsed A's bill to B, and paid ₹9,000 in full settlement. On 1.10.2023 B purchased goods worth ₹1,00,000 from A and paid by cheque. Pass journal entries in the books of B.

Jamal is entitled to 5% ordinary + 2% del-credere commission, plus reimbursement of expenses. Prepare the Consignment Account in Hardik's books and pass journal entries in Jamal's books. Arjun incurs carriage/electricity expenses of ₹6,500 and receives cash sales of ₹30,000; Arjun takes over stock worth ₹10,000 for personal use. At the end, Azad takes over the remaining stock, valued at ₹11,000. Prepare the accounts in the books of Azad and Arjun.

A five-bigha plot is bought for ₹60 lakh, partly bank-financed at 16% p.a.; Regular/Deluxe/Executive units are to be built and sold at cost plus 50%/40%/25% premium respectively; the balance area is taken by the co-venturers equally at cost. Mr. Kapoor meets the development/administration expenses and is entitled to 8% of sale proceeds for handling sales. The case asks the reader to work out: the cost per kattha of land, the sale price of each building type, the interest due to each co-venturer, the profit earned by each, and the amount needed for final settlement.

15 EXAM FACTS — BILLS OF EXCHANGE, CONSIGNMENT & JOINT VENTURE (Module 2)

① Consignment goods remain the CONSIGNOR'S property until the consignee actually sells them; the consignee passes NO entry merely on receipt.

② Goods sent are recorded at Cost or at Invoice Price (Cost + Loading); wherever the Load survives into year-end figures (closing stock, goods-in-transit, abnormal loss), it must be cancelled — via Stock Reserve for closing stock.

③ Ordinary commission = % on gross sales; Del credere commission = extra % for guaranteeing collection, on TOTAL sales unless the problem restricts it to credit sales; Over-riding/Special commission = extra reward for beating a target.

④ Bad debts follow the guarantee: charged to the consignee's own Commission A/c when del credere IS paid; charged to Consignment A/c when it is NOT paid.

⑤ Normal loss (evaporation, spillage) gets NO value — it only shrinks the quantity denominator. Abnormal loss (theft, fire) IS valued and removed via a separate Abnormal Loss A/c.

⑥ When normal and abnormal loss occur at the SAME point, normal loss is adjusted first, then abnormal loss on the reduced base — but an abnormal loss occurring IN TRANSIT is valued straight off the quantity despatched, before normal loss (which shows up later, at the godown).

⑦ Only NON-RECURRING "getting-there" expenses (freight, carriage, clearing, customs, octroi) enter stock/goods-in-transit/abnormal-loss valuation; RECURRING expenses (godown rent, insurance of godown, selling expenses, commission) never do.

⑧ Goods-in-Transit at year-end is valued using ONLY the consignor's own expenses — no consignee expense is ever added, since the goods have not reached the consignee yet.

⑨ Commission is on GROSS sales — a consignee earns commission even on the small sale proceeds of damaged/write-off goods.

⑩ A joint venture has NO firm name, is temporary (ends once the job is done), and — absent any agreement — profit/loss is shared EQUALLY.

⑪ Joint Venture A/c is debited with EVERY expense of the venture — capital or revenue, whether paid personally by a co-venturer or through the Joint Bank Account.

⑫ Stock/an asset taken over by a co-venturer is CREDITED to Joint Venture A/c at the agreed value, exactly like a sale/income of the venture — never simply ignored.

⑬ Method I (separate books): Joint Venture A/c + Joint Bank A/c + Co-venturers' A/cs. Method II (no separate books, for small/short/distant ventures): (a) each records ALL transactions in own books, or (b) each records only OWN transactions, pooled via a Memorandum Joint Venture A/c that sits outside double entry.

⑭ An ongoing consignment can convert into a joint venture mid-stream — consignment accounting runs up to the conversion date, then the unsold stock is transferred into the new joint venture on the agreed profit-sharing basis.

⑮ Bills of Exchange: a written, unconditional, signed and dated order to pay a certain sum (Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 5); Days of Grace (3 days) fix a time bill's due date but demand bills get none, and noting charges, though paid by the holder first, are ultimately recoverable from the acceptor.

MODULE 2 CLOSING DRILL (retrieval practice — do not skip): put this document down and, on rough paper, write from memory: the three types of consignment commission and which one is computed on total sales by default; the two-step rule for valuing unsold consignment stock at Invoice Price (including where Stock Reserve fits in); which expenses enter stock/goods-in-transit valuation and which never do; the normal-vs-abnormal loss order-of-adjustment rule, and how it flips between transit and godown; who bears a consignment bad debt under each del-credere scenario; the three accounts kept under the separate-books (Joint Bank) method of joint venture accounting; and how a co-venturer taking over unsold stock gets treated in the Joint Venture A/c. The complete final-accounts chain for non-corporate entities: the Trading Account, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of a commercial proprietorship or partnership (3.1); the Receipts & Payments Account, Income & Expenditure Account and Balance Sheet of a Not-for-Profit Organisation (3.2); and deriving financial statements from single-entry, incomplete records (3.3).

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: understand the different components of the financial statements of commercial organisations, and thoroughly draft the Income Statement (Trading Account and Profit & Loss Account) and Balance Sheet of a proprietorship or partnership firm (3.1); prepare the financial statements of a not-for-profit organisation — specifically the Receipts and Payments Account, Income and Expenditure Account and Balance Sheet (3.2); and understand the process of preparing financial statements from incomplete records (3.3).

Glossary — Module 3, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across this module, explained simply. This part (3.1) uses the first block; later parts add their own vocabulary.

Income StatementThe generic term for the statements that determine the operating result — for a non-corporate trading entity this means the Trading A/c, Profit & Loss A/c, and (for a partnership) the Profit & Loss Appropriation A/c.
Trading AccountThe first income statement — matches the Cost of Goods Sold against Sales for the period, using only DIRECT costs and direct income, to find Gross Profit or Gross Loss. A nominal account, closed into the P&L A/c.
Gross Profit / Gross LossThe Trading Account's own balance — credit side greater than debit side gives Gross Profit; debit side greater than credit side gives Gross Loss.
Profit & Loss AccountThe second income statement — charges INDIRECT expenses and losses against Gross Profit and other indirect incomes, to arrive at Net Profit or Net Loss. Closed into the Capital Account(s).
Net Profit / Net LossThe Profit & Loss Account's own balance, transferred to the Capital Account of a proprietor (or, for a firm, into the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account first).
Profit & Loss Appropriation AccountPrepared only by partnership firms — distributes Net Profit among partners after interest on capital/drawings, salary and commission to partners, and any transfer to reserve.
Manufacturing AccountPrepared only by a proprietor/firm that manufactures (not merely trades) goods — an extension placed before the Trading A/c, collecting materials, wages and direct expenses to arrive at the Cost of Goods Manufactured.
Balance SheetThe financial statement showing the assets, liabilities and capital of the concern as at a specific date — a statement of financial position, not itself an account.
Direct ExpensesCosts incurred from the time of purchase up to making the goods saleable — e.g. carriage inward, freight, octroi, wages. Charged to the Trading Account.
Indirect ExpensesAdministrative, selling and distribution, and financial expenses not directly tied to bringing goods to a saleable state — e.g. office salaries, rent, advertising, carriage outward, interest, depreciation. Charged to the Profit & Loss Account.
Closing Stock ValuationValued at cost or net realisable value, WHICHEVER IS LOWER — the convention of conservatism.
Outstanding / Accrued ExpenseAn expense for the current period that remains UNPAID at year-end — added to the expense in the Income Statement, shown as a current liability in the Balance Sheet.
Prepaid ExpenseAn expense PAID in advance, relating to a future period — deducted from the expense in the Income Statement, shown as a current asset in the Balance Sheet.
Accrued IncomeIncome EARNED but not yet received — added to the income in the Income Statement, shown as a current asset in the Balance Sheet.
Income Received in AdvanceCash RECEIVED for a future period's income — deducted from the income in the Income Statement, shown as a current liability in the Balance Sheet.
MarshallingThe specific order in which assets and liabilities are arranged in the Balance Sheet.
Rigidity / Permanence OrderMarshalling with the most permanent assets at the top and current assets below; capital and long-term liabilities above short-term liabilities. The traditional non-corporate format.
Liquidity OrderThe reverse marshalling sequence — the most liquid (current) assets and liabilities placed first.
Provision for Doubtful DebtsA charge against profit for debts that MAY turn bad but are not yet confirmed lost — deducted from Sundry Debtors in the Balance Sheet.
Goods on Approval BasisGoods sent to a customer who has not yet accepted them — if wrongly recorded as an actual sale, must be reversed out of Sales (at selling price) and added back into Closing Stock (at cost).
Receipts & Payments Account(3.2) The summarised cash book of a not-for-profit organisation — every receipt and payment, capital or revenue, of any period.
Income & Expenditure Account(3.2) The not-for-profit organisation's own income statement — only revenue items, only the current period, on an accrual basis.

CONCEPT

3.1 Financial Statements of Commercial Organisations ★★★ HIGH

Besides record-keeping, a major objective of accounting is determining the operating result and disclosing the financial position. For a commercial (profit-seeking) organisation this means ascertaining the profit earned or loss suffered during a period — through the Financial Statements: the Income Statement and the Balance Sheet. (A Cash Flow Statement is also, strictly, a financial statement, but is outside the scope of this chapter.)

3.1.1 Income Statement is the generic term for the components that determine the operating result. For non-corporate commercial organisations the components differ by form of organisation:

Form of Non-Corporate Commercial OrganisationComponents of Income Statement
Proprietary organisationTrading A/c, P/L A/c
Partnership organisationTrading A/c, P/L A/c, P/L Appropriation A/c

Trading Account

The Trading Account is the first income statement prepared by a non-corporate trading entity, to determine the gross operating result (Gross Profit or Gross Loss). Its principle is matching the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) of the period against the corresponding Sales — it considers only DIRECT costs and direct income (i.e. Sales). It is a nominal account, closed by transferring the Gross Profit/Gross Loss to the Profit & Loss A/c.

Debit side:

  • Opening Stock — for a trading concern this means finished goods only, taken from the Trial Balance.
  • Purchases — cash as well as credit purchases. Deductions from Purchases include purchase returns, goods withdrawn by the proprietor, and goods distributed as free samples.
  • Other Direct Expenses — all expenses incurred from the time of purchase up to making the goods saleable: freight inward, octroi, wages, etc.
  • Gross Profit — arises when the credit side of the Trading A/c exceeds the debit side.

Credit side:

  • Sales Revenue — income from the main business activity, recognised (per the accrual concept) as soon as goods/services are sold; sales returns are deducted.
  • Closing Stock/Inventories — for a trading business, finished goods only; valued at cost or net realisable value, WHICHEVER IS LOWER (the convention of conservatism).
  • Gross Loss — arises when the debit side of the Trading A/c exceeds the credit side.
Proforma of Trading Account
Trading Account for the year ended ….
Particulars(₹)(₹)Particulars(₹)(₹)
To Opening StockBy Sales
To Purchases  Less: Sales Returns
  Less: Purchase returnsBy Closing Stock
To WagesBy Profit and Loss A/c
To Other Direct expenses  (Gross Loss transferred)
To Profit and Loss A/c
  (Gross Profit transferred)

Profit & Loss Account

The Profit & Loss Account is drafted after the gross operating result and determines Net Profit or Net Loss, by charging indirect expenses and losses against the Gross Profit and other indirect incomes. It is closed by transferring the Net Profit/Net Loss to the Capital Account(s) of the proprietor or partners.

Debit side:

  • Other Expenses — all expenses not directly related to the main business activity, mainly Administrative, Selling and Distribution expenses: salary to office staff, salesmen's commission, insurance, legal charges, audit fees, advertising, free samples, bad debts, etc. Also includes loss on sale of fixed assets, interest, and provisions — accrued expenses must be included too.
  • Abnormal Losses — e.g. stock destroyed by fire, goods lost in transit — all charged against the P&L A/c.

Credit side:

  • Revenue Incomes — arise in the ordinary course of business: commission received, discount received, etc.
  • Other Incomes — purely incidental to the main activity: interest received, dividend received, etc.

The end result flows down the chain — Trading A/c → P&L A/c → Balance Sheet (as an addition to owners' equity). The profit belongs to the owners of the business; in company organisations, where ownership is widely distributed, the profit figure is shown separately in the Balance Sheet.

Proforma of Profit & Loss Account
Profit & Loss Account for the year ended ….

To Trading A/cBy Trading A/c
  (Gross Loss transferred)  (Gross Profit transferred)
To Administrative expensesBy Other Income
To Office salariesBy Interest received
To CommunicationBy Commission received
To Travel & ConveyanceBy Profit on sale of assets
To Office rentBy Rent received

Profit & Loss Appropriation Account Partnership firms only

Shows the appropriation of Net Profit among the partners of a partnership business. Sole proprietorships are NOT required to prepare it. Before distribution, appropriation may be needed for interest on capital and drawings, commission and salary payable to a partner (as per the deed), and for any reserve to be created — the remaining surplus is distributed to partners and added to their capital.

Format of Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
Profit and Loss Appropriation Account for the year ended ….

To Commission to Partners A/cBy Interest on Drawing A/c
To Salary to Partners A/c
To Reserve A/c
To Partners' Capital A/c (Divisible Profit)

Manufacturing Account Manufacturers only

The above accounts serve a trading concern that purchases and sells goods. A proprietorship/partnership that PRODUCES goods and sells them additionally prepares a Manufacturing Account — an extension of the Trading Account.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "WAGES & SALARIES" vs "SALARIES & WAGES"

THE TRAP: treating both labels as the same expense and posting them to the same statement.

THE TWIST: a Trial Balance can carry BOTH labels as two separate figures — and the source's own worked solution (Illustration 4, M/s BJ & Sons) posts them to two different statements: "Wages & Salaries" ₹80,000 goes to the TRADING Account (a direct, factory-linked cost, first word "Wages"), while "Salaries & wages" ₹2,20,000 goes to the PROFIT & LOSS Account (an indirect, office-linked cost, first word "Salaries"). Reading the FIRST word tells you which statement it belongs to.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CARRIAGE INWARD vs CARRIAGE OUTWARD

THE TRAP: treating all carriage/freight as one "direct" figure.

THE TWIST: only the cost of BRINGING goods IN is direct. In the same Illustration 4 solution, Carriage Inwards ₹50,000 is posted to the Trading Account (a direct expense, alongside freight, octroi, wages), while Carriage Outwards ₹40,000 is posted to the Profit & Loss Account (a selling/distribution expense) — the cost of SENDING goods out to customers is never a Trading Account item.

3.1.2 Balance Sheet

The Balance Sheet is the financial statement prepared to show the financial position of the organisation on a specific date — the assets and liabilities of a concern at a particular point of time. It is prepared AFTER drafting the Income Statements (Trading A/c and P&L A/c).

The Balance Sheet may be drafted in horizontal or vertical form. In the traditional (horizontal) format followed by non-corporate organisations, Liabilities appear on the LEFT-hand side and Assets on the RIGHT-hand side — the format used throughout every worked illustration below.

Marshalling is the specific order in which items appear in the Balance Sheet:

OrderAssets sequenceLiabilities sequence
Rigidity / Permanence OrderMost permanent assets at the TOP, current assets belowCapital and long-term liabilities above short-term (current) liabilities
Liquidity OrderThe reverse sequence — most liquid (current) assets firstThe reverse sequence — current liabilities first
Balance Sheet — the layout used throughout the source's own worked illustrations (Rigidity/Permanence Order)
Balance Sheet as at ….
Liabilities(₹)Assets(₹)
Capital
  Add: Net Profit / Less: Net Loss
  Less: Drawings		Fixed Assets (Land & Building, Plant & Machinery, Furniture & Fixtures, Motor Car, Loose Tools … each less accumulated Depreciation)
Reserves (e.g. Reserve Fund, General Reserve)Investments
Long Term Liabilities (Loans)Current Assets: Closing Stock; Sundry Debtors (less Provision for Doubtful Debts); Bills Receivable; Prepaid expenses; Accrued/Receivable income; Cash at Bank; Cash in Hand
Current Liabilities: Sundry Creditors; Bills Payable; Outstanding expenses; Income received in advance; Bank Overdraft

Preparation of Final Accounts

Final accounts are prepared from the ledger balances. Each ledger account is posted to one of the income statements (Manufacturing A/c, Trading A/c or P&L A/c) or to the Balance Sheet, depending on its nature. In addition, some ADJUSTMENTS may be required — to honour the accounting principles, or to rectify existing errors — for which adjustment entries or rectification entries are passed. The effect of these adjustments/rectifications is always 'double,' reflected in the income statement(s) AND/OR the Balance Sheet.

Some of the important adjustments include:

  • Closing stock
  • Outstanding expenses or Accrued expenses
  • Prepaid expenses
  • Accrued income
  • Income received in advance
  • Goods sold on approval basis
  • Goods distributed as free samples
  • Goods withdrawn by proprietor/partner for personal use
  • Depreciation and Amortisation
  • Bad debts
  • Provision for doubtful debts
  • Provision for discount on debtors
  • Abnormal loss of stock
  • Interest on capital
  • Interest on drawings, etc.
  • Asset recorded as expense, or vice versa

Sequence: the Trading Account is prepared first and its balance (Gross Profit/Loss) is transferred to the Profit & Loss Account. The P&L Account is then prepared and its balance (Net Profit/Loss) transferred to the Capital Account (after drafting the P&L Appropriation Account, for partnership firms). Finally, the Balance Sheet is drafted from the ledger balances reflecting assets, liabilities and capital.

The Single-vs-Double Treatment Rule — The Double Effect of Every Adjustment

A ledger balance already sitting inside the Trial Balance has completed its double entry — it is posted to its natural home ONCE. An adjustment given OUTSIDE the Trial Balance (in the "Additional Information") still needs both legs of the entry — it is posted TWICE, and always in two different statements.

Adjustment (given outside the Trial Balance)Effect ① — Trading / Profit & Loss A/cEffect ② — Balance Sheet
Closing stockCredit side of Trading A/cCurrent asset
Outstanding / Accrued expenseAdded to the relevant expense (debit side)Current liability
Prepaid expenseDeducted from the relevant expense (debit side)Current asset
Accrued incomeAdded to the relevant income (credit side)Current asset
Income received in advanceDeducted from the relevant income (credit side)Current liability
Goods sold on approval, wrongly booked as an actual saleDeducted from Sales at selling price (Trading A/c)Added back into Closing Stock at cost (Trading A/c credit side, hence Balance Sheet asset)
Goods withdrawn by proprietor/partner for personal useDeducted from Purchases (Trading A/c)Added to Drawings, hence deducted from Capital
DepreciationDebited to P&L A/cDeducted from the concerned fixed asset
Further bad debts (given outside the TB)Added to Bad Debts, debited to P&L A/cDeducted from Sundry Debtors before computing the new provision
New Provision for Doubtful DebtsDebited (or, if smaller than the old provision, netted as a credit) to P&L A/cDeducted from Sundry Debtors
Provision for discount on debtorsDebited to P&L A/cDeducted from Sundry Debtors (after Provision for Doubtful Debts)
Stock destroyed by fire / abnormal lossValue of stock destroyed is added into Closing Stock on the credit side of the Trading A/c, alongside the actual closing stock — the insurance claim admitted and the net uninsured loss do NOT appear in the Trading A/cInsurance claim receivable is a current asset; the net uninsured loss is a P&L charge
Interest on capitalDebited to P&L (Appropriation) A/cAdded to Capital
Interest on drawingsCredited to P&L (Appropriation) A/cDeducted from Capital
Asset wrongly recorded as an expense (e.g. purchase of an asset debited to Purchases)Deducted from Purchases (Trading A/c)Recorded as a Fixed Asset; any resulting profit/loss on the correction is a P&L item
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ITEMS ALREADY INSIDE THE TRIAL BALANCE

THE TRAP: treating every item on the adjustments checklist as needing a fresh, separate posting — even when the figure is already sitting inside the given Trial Balance.

THE TWIST: a Trial Balance figure needs only ONE posting, to its natural statement — it has already completed its double entry. It is only the items given OUTSIDE the Trial Balance, in the "Additional Information," that need the double posting. In Illustration 4, "Bad debts ₹10,000" sits inside the Trial Balance and is posted to the P&L Account exactly once, with no further effect on Debtors. Contrast Illustration 5, where "further Bad Debts ₹6,000" is an OUTSIDE adjustment — it is both added to the Bad Debts charge in the P&L Account AND deducted from Debtors before the new Provision is computed, hitting the accounts twice.

Glossary Additions — 3.2, in Plain Words

Receipts & Payments AccountA summarised Cash Book of the NPO — every cash/bank receipt and payment, capital or revenue, of any period, recorded on pure cash basis. Starts with the opening Cash & Bank balance, ends with the closing Cash & Bank balance.
Income & Expenditure AccountThe NPO's own income statement, closely resembling a Profit & Loss Account — only revenue items of the CURRENT period, recognised on accrual basis. Balances to a Surplus (income > expenditure) or a Deficit (expenditure > income).
SubscriptionThe annual membership fee — a revenue receipt recognised on accrual basis, adjusted for amounts outstanding and received in advance at both the start and the end of the year.
Entrance FeesA one-time fee charged at admission. Non-recurring by nature, so often capitalised (added to Capital Fund) — but by the institution's own rules it may instead be credited straight to Income & Expenditure A/c as ordinary revenue.
Life Membership FeeA lump sum paid once, in place of yearly subscriptions, for lifetime membership. A capital receipt — credited straight to Capital Fund, OR held as a deferred receipt and released to Income & Expenditure A/c over a number of years.
LegacyMoney or property an NPO receives under the will of a deceased person, after his/her demise. A one-time capital receipt — added directly to Capital Fund, after tax if any.
Endowment FundA donation given with the donor's specific instructions on how it must be used or invested. Treated as a capital receipt, never as revenue.
Capital FundAlso called General Fund or Accumulated Fund — the NPO's "capital." Equals the excess of assets over liabilities; each year's Surplus is added to it (a Deficit deducted), and capitalised incomes — legacies, capitalised entrance/life-membership fees — are added too.
Special FundA fund created out of a donation/subscription earmarked for one purpose (e.g. a "Building Fund"), or set aside out of Surplus. Its own income and expenses adjust against the fund itself — they never pass through the Income & Expenditure Account.
CONCEPT

3.2 Financial Statements of Not-for-Profit Organisations ★★★ HIGH

Non-profit Organisations (NPOs) are formed primarily to render some specific service to society, not with a profit motive — educational institutions, public medical organisations, social/cultural clubs (Rotary, Lions), religious institutions, trade unions, charitable trusts. Their accounting follows the entity concept, the same as other organisations, but certain items of income and expenditure are unique to them and need special treatment.

Features: governed by an elected body or trustee board; operation is not driven by any profit motive unlike trading concerns; main purpose is to provide social service; main source of income is donation and membership subscription; the membership process is non-transferable.

Typical income itemsTypical expenditure items
DonationsUpkeep of grounds
Entrance feesTournament expenses
SubscriptionsPrizes
Grants receivedEvents

These organisations get their funds by way of entrance fees, life membership fees, annual subscriptions, donations, grants and legacies. An NPO prepares three financial statements: the Receipts & Payments Account, the Income & Expenditure Account, and the Balance Sheet.

Treatment of Special NPO Income Items

  • Entrance/Admission Fees: follow the institution's own by-laws first. If there is no rule, a one-time fee paid by members for acquiring membership is added to Capital Fund (a capital receipt) — there's also a view that admitting new members is an ongoing activity, so entrance fees may be taken as a normal revenue receipt every year. If the fee is a small amount covering only the cost of admission, it may be credited to Income & Expenditure A/c as revenue.
  • Donations: may meet capital or revenue expenses. A donation received for a special purpose is credited to a Special Fund (e.g. Building Fund) from which the amount is disbursed; the fund may be invested, and income from such investments is credited to the fund A/c only — never to Income & Expenditure A/c. Follow the institution's by-laws for other donations; failing a rule, non-recurring donations are credited to Capital Fund and recurring donations to Income & Expenditure A/c (small, unearmarked amounts may simply be treated as revenue receipts). Donations PAID BY the concern are debited to Income & Expenditure A/c.
  • Legacy: trusts are often formed in memory of a person by their will; after the person's demise the funds pass to the institution. One-time in nature — taken to Capital Fund.
  • Endowments: donations to be used strictly per the donor's instructions — treated as capital receipts.
  • Life Membership Fees: capital receipts. Either credited straight to Capital Fund, or treated as a deferred receipt in the Balance Sheet with a specific amount credited to Income & Expenditure A/c each year on some logical basis; the balance carries forward till a member's contribution is fully exhausted. If a life member dies beforehand, the balance of his contribution is transferred to Capital/General Fund.
  • Subscriptions: annual, recurring receipts, recognised as revenue on the accrual concept — credited to Income & Expenditure A/c (see the four-way adjustment below).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SUBSCRIPTION — A FOUR-WAY ADJUSTMENT, NOT A TWO-WAY ONE

THE TRAP: students adjust only for the amount outstanding or advance at YEAR-END and forget the OPENING position — or add where a "less" is needed.

THE TWIST: Subscription for the current year = Cash received during the year + Outstanding at the END of the year (this year's income, not yet received) − Outstanding at the START of the year (last year's income, now received, must be excluded) + Advance received at the START of the year (last year's advance is THIS year's income) − Advance received at the END of the year (this year's advance belongs to NEXT year, must be excluded). All four legs, every time.
