3.2.1 Preparation of Receipts and Payments Account

The Receipts and Payments Account is the summarised form of the Cash Book of a non-profit organisation. Entries are made on cash basis; items pertaining to the previous year, current year, or subsequent years are all recorded. It is a memorandum account, Real Account in nature, with receipts shown on the left side and payments on the right side. Capital as well as revenue items are entered. It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank and ends with the closing balance of cash and bank.

Proforma of Receipts and Payments Account
ReceiptsPayments
Starts with opening balance 
All receipts — capital or revenue; may be related to any period, previous, current or subsequentAll payments — capital or revenue; may be related to any period, previous, current or subsequent
 Ends with closing balance

Six features: (1) contains all Cash and Bank transactions of a particular financial period; (2) a memorandum account; (3) Real Account by nature; (4) starts with the opening balances of Cash and Bank; (5) is a summary of the Cash Book — all Cash Receipts, both capital and revenue, are debited to it, all Cash Payments, both capital and revenue, are credited to it, ending with the closing Cash and Bank balances; (6) every entry is made on Cash Basis — no provisions are recorded in this account.

3.2.2 Preparation of Income and Expenditure Account

The Income and Expenditure Account is the income statement of the non-profit organisation. Only revenue items — revenue incomes and revenue expenditures — are recorded, both taken on the basis of accrual concept, and this account should reflect only items pertaining to the current period. Incomes are recorded on the credit side, expenses on the debit side. The balance shows either a Surplus (excess of income over expenditure) or a Deficit (excess of expenditure over income).

Proforma of Income and Expenditure Account
ExpensesIncome
Only revenue expensesOnly revenue receipts
Only related to current periodOnly related to current period
Shows either Surplus…or Deficit

Eight features: (1) Nominal Account by nature; (2) all revenue expenditures of the period are debited on accrual basis; (3) all revenue incomes of the period are credited on accrual basis; (4) all capital incomes and expenditures are excluded; (5) only current year's incomes and expenses are recorded — amounts related to other periods are deducted, amounts outstanding for the current year are added; (6) Profit on Sale of Asset is credited, Loss on Sale of Asset is debited, annual Depreciation on Assets is also debited; (7) if income exceeds expenditure it is a Surplus, added to Capital/General Fund in the Balance Sheet; (8) if expenditure exceeds income it is a Deficit, deducted from Capital/General Fund in the Balance Sheet.

Receipts & Payments A/c vs. Income & Expenditure A/c

Receipts & Payments AccountIncome & Expenditure Account
A summarised Cash Book.Closely resembles the Profit & Loss Account of a trading concern.
Receipts are debited, Payments are credited.Incomes are credited, Expenditures are debited.
Transactions recorded on Cash basis.Transactions recorded on Accrual basis.
Amounts related to a previous or future period may remain included; only the CURRENT year's outstanding amount is excluded.All amounts not related to the current period are excluded; outstanding amounts of the CURRENT period are added.
Records both Capital and Revenue transactions.Serves the purpose of a Nominal Account — revenue transactions only.
Serves the purpose of a Real Account.Serves the purpose of a Nominal Account.
Starts with opening Cash and Bank balances, ends with closing Cash and Bank balances.Does not record such balances — its final balance shows a Surplus or a Deficit for the period.
Does not record notional loss or non-cash expenses like bad debts, depreciation, etc.Considers all such expenses, to match them against revenues.
Its closing balance is carried forward to the SAME account of the next accounting period.Its closing balance is transferred to Capital Fund/General Fund/Accumulated Fund in the SAME period's Balance Sheet.
It helps to prepare an Income & Expenditure A/c.It helps to prepare a Balance Sheet.
Exam habit: R&P wants CASH received/paid in ANY period; I&E wants ACCRUED income/expense of the CURRENT period only — every "convert R&P into I&E" question is just this filter applied line by line.

Fund Accounting — Capital Fund & Special Fund

  • Capital Fund (also called "General Fund" or "Accumulated Fund") is actually the Capital of a non-profit concern — found as the excess of assets over liabilities. Usually the "Surplus" or "Deficit" for the period is added with or deducted from it. A portion of capitalised incomes, like donations, may also be added to it.
  • Special Fund may be created out of a special donation or subscription, or out of a portion of the "Surplus." For example, a club may have a "Building Fund." It is used for meeting some specific expenses or for acquiring an asset. Any income derived from investments made against the fund, or any profit/loss on sale of such investments, is transferred to this fund — NOT to Income & Expenditure A/c. The balance of the Fund is shown as a liability in the Balance Sheet.
Special Fund A/c ………… Dr.(amt.)
  To Bank A/c(amt.)

(Being an expense of the fund's specific purpose met out of the Special Fund)

Asset A/c ………… Dr.(cost)
  To Bank A/c(cost)

(Being an asset purchased out of the Special Fund)

Special Fund A/c ………… Dr.(bal.)
  To Capital Fund A/c(bal.)

(Being balance of the Special Fund closed off — whether after meeting an expense, or after the asset purchase, or at the end of the fund's life)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SPECIAL FUND ITEMS BYPASS THE INCOME & EXPENDITURE ACCOUNT

THE TRAP: a donation earmarked for a purpose (e.g. ₹50,000 "for Building Fund") gets credited to Income & Expenditure A/c like an ordinary donation, or interest earned on the fund's investments gets credited as ordinary income.

THE TWIST: earmarked donations, and any income/profit/loss on investments made against that fund, stay INSIDE the Special Fund and are shown directly as a liability in the Balance Sheet — the Income & Expenditure Account never sees them. In the source's own Illustration 19 (RR Clinic), ₹50,000 of the ₹1,55,000 total donation received is "for Building Fund" — only ₹1,05,000 (the balance) is credited to Income & Expenditure A/c; the ₹50,000 appears directly as "Building Fund" on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ENTRANCE FEES HAVE NO SINGLE UNIVERSAL RULE

THE TRAP: assuming entrance fees are ALWAYS capitalised (or ALWAYS revenue) across every question.

THE TWIST: the by-laws of the institution govern — and the source's own illustrations show BOTH treatments used, purely as per the question's stated rule: fully capitalised (Illustration 17 — "Entrance fees to be treated as revenue income" is the STATED exception, so read the rule given); 75% capitalised, 25% revenue (Illustration 18); and fully revenue with no capitalisation at all (Illustration 20). Always apply the specific instruction given in the question — never a default assumption.

3.2.3 Preparation of Balance Sheet

The Balance Sheet of an NPO is prepared as on the last day of the accounting period, on the same accounting equation as any other entity — it has assets and liabilities. But there is no Capital Account; instead there is a Capital Fund. The Surplus or Deficit thrown up by the Income & Expenditure Account is carried into the Balance Sheet as an adjustment to the Capital Fund — a Surplus is ADDED to it, a Deficit is DEDUCTED from it.

Preparation of opening and closing Balance Sheet from a given Receipts & Payments A/c and Income & Expenditure A/c — while drafting:

(A) Opening Balance Sheet:

  • Take the opening balance of Cash and Bank given in the Receipts and Payments Account as "Balance b/d" — it appears on the assets side of the opening Balance Sheet.
  • All the opening assets and liabilities given as adjustments appear on the respective sides of the opening Balance Sheet.
  • The difference between the assets side and the liabilities side of the opening Balance Sheet is treated as "Capital Fund."

(B) Closing Balance Sheet:

  • Take the closing balance of Cash and Bank given in the Receipts and Payments Account as "Balance c/d" — it appears on the assets side of the closing Balance Sheet.
  • Fixed assets from the opening Balance Sheet carry forward, adjusted for additions/sales during the year (per the Receipts & Payments A/c) and for depreciation/loss on sale (per the Income & Expenditure A/c).
  • All closing current liabilities — including the Capital Fund adjusted for Surplus/Deficit, and any other funds (Donations, Entrance Fees, etc.) — appear on the liabilities side.
  • Every item on the credit (Receipts) side of the Receipts & Payments A/c must be cross-checked against the corresponding item on the debit (Expenditure) side of the Income & Expenditure A/c, and vice-versa, to find the adjustment needed.

Restaurant Trading and Bar Trading

Some clubs run a Restaurant or Bar for members and outsiders. ⚠ TRAP: RESTAURANT/BAR TRADING PROFIT IS ONE LINE IN THE I&E A/c, NOT A FULL RE-LISTING

Glossary Additions — 3.3, in Plain Words

Single Entry SystemNot really a "system" at all — a casual, unscientific way of recording where some transactions are fully recorded, some only half-recorded, and some skipped entirely. More accurately called Incomplete Records.
Statement of AffairsA list of estimated assets and liabilities, used to find Capital/Net Worth by balancing figure when no ledger exists to give a real Capital balance. Looks like a Balance Sheet, but isn't one.
Net Worth MethodAlso called the Balance Sheet Approach or Comparison Approach — finds profit by comparing Capital at two points in time, instead of matching incomes against expenses.
Conversion MethodRebuilding the missing double-entry ledger accounts (Debtors, Creditors, Cash/Bank, etc.) from whatever fragments of data exist, so that the "missing" figures pop out as balancing figures.
Missing/Balancing FigureThe one unknown amount in a reconstructed account — found by making both sides of that account tally. The entire technique the Conversion Method runs on.
DefalcationCash or goods misappropriated by an employee (e.g. a cashier). Under incomplete records, the shortfall itself is usually found as a balancing figure.
CONCEPT

3.3 Preparation of Financial Statements from Incomplete Records ★★★ HIGH

Recording transactions in a systematic, scientific manner means following the double entry system. However, many small entities — grocery stores, kirana shops, small-time traders, semi-skilled service providers — do not. They record transactions casually and sketchily, so some transactions are fully recorded, some partially, and some omitted altogether. This incomplete manner of recording is commonly called the Single Entry System — a misnomer, since it isn't really "one entry" per transaction so much as inconsistent, partial recording. It would be more accurate to call it Incomplete Records.

Features of Single Entry System:

  • It is an unscientific approach of recording transactions.
  • Usually followed by small businesses, semi-skilled service providers and workers who cannot maintain books under the double entry system.
  • There is no uniformity in recording of transactions.
  • Usually, only the cash and personal accounts are recorded.
  • The original vouchers of different transactions are kept for future reference, though the relevant accounts are not prepared.

Limitations/Defects:

  • As the principle of double entry is not followed, a Trial Balance cannot be prepared — hence arithmetical accuracy cannot be guaranteed.
  • Profit or loss can be found out only by estimates, as nominal accounts are not maintained.
  • It is not possible to make a Balance Sheet in the absence of real accounts.
  • It is very difficult to detect frauds or errors.
  • External agencies like banks cannot use the financial information — a bank cannot decide whether to lend money or not.
  • It is quite likely that the business and personal transactions of the proprietor get mixed up.

Single Entry vs. Double Entry System

Single Entry SystemDouble Entry System
A casual and unscientific approach of recording transactions.The scientific approach of record-keeping.
Some transactions are not recorded at all; some are recorded in only one of their two aspects.Both aspects (debit and credit) of every transaction are recorded.
No subsidiary books are maintained, except the Cash Book (itself treated as part of the ledger).Various subsidiary books — Sales Book, Purchases Book, etc. — are maintained.
Preparation of a Trial Balance is not possible — accuracy of work is uncertain.Preparation of a Trial Balance is possible.
Only a rough estimate of profit or loss is made, and a Statement of Affairs (resembling but not proving a Balance Sheet) is prepared.Trading A/c, Profit & Loss A/c and the Balance Sheet are prepared in a scientific manner.
The possibility of fraud and misappropriation is greater.The possibility of fraud and misappropriation is comparatively lower.
Followed by small businesses, sole traders, partnership firms and professionals who cannot afford formal books.Followed by most concerns.

Two Approaches to Preparing Final Accounts from Incomplete Records

Such smaller entities are still interested in knowing their operating results and financial position at the end of every accounting period, even though their partial records make this hard to determine directly. There are two recognised approaches:

  1. Balance Sheet Approach / Net Worth Approach / Comparison Approach — finds profit by comparing Capital/Net Worth at two points in time.
  2. Conversion Approach — reconstructs the missing double-entry accounts to fill in the missing information.

Approach 1: Balance Sheet / Net Worth / Comparison Approach

The operating result is found by comparing the entity's net worth (capital) at two different points in time. The capital balances are themselves determined by preparing a Statement of Affairs — a list of estimated assets and liabilities, with Capital taken as the balancing figure (excess of assets over liabilities).

Three statements are prepared under this approach:

  • Statement of Affairs (opening) — ascertains the capital/net worth at the BEGINNING of the period.
  • Statement of Profit & Loss — compares opening and closing capital/net worth to find trading profit/loss, then adjusts it to the net profit/loss for the period.
  • Final (Revised) Statement of Affairs — prepared at the END of the period with closing asset/liability balances, after providing for adjustments such as depreciation and provision for bad & doubtful debts.

Steps for preparing Final Accounts under this Approach:

  1. Prepare the Statement of Affairs as at the beginning and end of the accounting period, to determine opening and closing capital/net worth.
  2. Prepare the Statement of Profit & Loss to determine trading profit/loss, and thereafter the net profit/loss.
  3. Prepare the Final (Revised) Statement of Affairs as at the end of the period, disclosing the closing financial position after adjustments.

Care must be taken to see which adjustments have already been factored into the closing Statement of Affairs and which have not — an adjustment (e.g. depreciation, bad debts) should be taken account of in one place only: either the closing Statement of Affairs, or the Statement of Profit, never both.

Profit = (Closing Capital − Opening Capital) + Drawings − Additional Capital Introduced

Closing/Opening Capital: the balancing figures from the closing and opening Statements of Affairs. Drawings (cash or goods, by the proprietor/partners) must be ADDED BACK — they reduced capital for a reason unrelated to trading. Additional/Fresh Capital Introduced must be DEDUCTED — it increased capital for a reason unrelated to trading.

Then, to reach Net Profit / Divisible Profit: Less: adjustments not yet reflected (interest on capital, interest on drawings, depreciation, bad debts, etc.) → Net Profit/Loss for the Period → Less: appropriation items (interest on partners' capital, partners' salaries, etc., for a firm) → Divisible Profit.

Statement of Affairs vs. Balance Sheet

Statement of AffairsBalance Sheet
Prepared by an entity following the single entry system.Prepared by an entity following the double entry system.
Prepared for determining the Capital or Net Worth at two different points in time.Prepared for disclosing the financial position of the entity.
Reflects the estimated financial position.Reflects the true financial position.
The information contained is comparatively less reliable.The information contained is more reliable.
The balance of the Capital account is taken as the "excess of assets over liabilities" — i.e. a balancing figure.The balance of the Capital account is available from regular accounting records — i.e. an actual ledger balance.
It has no statutory format.The format is specified under various statutes, e.g. the Companies Act, Banking Regulation Act, etc.
A Statement of Affairs is NOT proof of arithmetical accuracy — unlike a Trial Balance-backed Balance Sheet, it is compiled on estimates and cannot itself be verified.

Statement of Profit & Loss vs. Profit & Loss Account

Statement of Profit & LossProfit & Loss Account
Prepared by an entity following the single entry system.Prepared by an entity following the double entry system.
Profit/loss is determined by comparing capital/net worth at two points in time.Profit/loss is determined by matching expenses/losses against incomes/gains.
All items of expenses, losses, incomes and gains do NOT get properly disclosed.All expenses, losses, incomes and gains get properly disclosed.
Information provided is comparatively less reliable.Information provided is reliable.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SIGN ERRORS IN THE NET WORTH FORMULA

THE TRAP: students subtract Drawings from the capital-increase (instead of adding it back), or add Additional/Fresh Capital Introduced (instead of deducting it) — flipping both signs the wrong way.

THE TWIST: Drawings pull money OUT of the business for reasons unconnected with trading, so they understate the capital-increase and must be ADDED BACK to recover true profit. Additional Capital Introduced puts money INTO the business for reasons unconnected with trading, so it overstates the capital-increase and must be DEDUCTED. See Illustration 23: Add Drawings ₹9,300, Less Fresh Capital Introduced ₹7,500.

Approach 2: Conversion Approach

Under the Conversion Approach, an organisation's financial statements are prepared from whatever transactions it did record, by entering them in the relevant accounts under the double entry system and thereafter determining the "missing information." Usually the regular accounts — Debtors A/c, Creditors A/c, Cash Book, Assets A/c, etc. — are prepared with the data available, and the relevant ledger balances are calculated. There is no fixed approach; the steps depend on the data available in each case. Since data kept under the single entry system are converted to the double entry system, it is called the Conversion Approach.

In practice: reconstruct a Total Debtors Account, Total Creditors Account, and Cash/Bank Account (and Bills Receivable/Payable Accounts, where bills are involved) from whatever opening balances, closing balances, and receipts/payments are known. Whichever single figure is NOT already given — credit sales, credit purchases, cash sales, cash missing, opening capital — is found as the balancing figure needed to make that account's two sides tally. The reconstructed data then feeds into a full Trading A/c, Profit & Loss A/c and Balance Sheet, exactly as under double entry.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ASSUMING THE BALANCING FIGURE IS ALWAYS "SALES" OR "PURCHASES"

THE TRAP: assuming a Total Debtors/Creditors Account always balances to give Credit Sales/Credit Purchases, and plugging the balancing figure into the wrong line.

THE TWIST: what's missing changes case to case — read what IS already given before you decide what to solve for. In Illustration 26, Credit Purchases (₹2,30,000) was GIVEN, so the Total Creditors A/c balancing figure is instead the CLOSING CREDITORS balance (₹70,000). Always check which figures are already stated in the question before assuming the identity of the balancing figure.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: WRITING OFF CASH DEFALCATION STRAIGHT TO P&L

THE TRAP: treating cash found missing/embezzled as an automatic Profit & Loss expense (a straight write-off).

THE TWIST: the source's own solved case (Illustration 27, Chirag — where a cashier absconded with the available cash after a riot) finds the shortfall as the balancing figure of the Cash Book (₹4,500) and then carries it to the BALANCE SHEET as an ASSET — "Amount Recoverable from Cashier" — not as a loss in the Trading and Profit & Loss Account, since recovery from the employee is treated as possible.

17 EXAM FACTS — FINAL ACCOUNTS (Module 3)

① Trading Account isolates Gross Profit (Sales − Cost of Goods Sold); Profit & Loss Account isolates Net Profit (Gross Profit ± indirect incomes/expenses) — never merged into one figure.

② Every adjustment given OUTSIDE the Trial Balance gets a DOUBLE effect (Trading/P&L AND Balance Sheet); an item already INSIDE the Trial Balance gets only ONE effect.

③ Closing Stock inside the Trial Balance goes to the Balance Sheet only; Closing Stock given as an adjustment goes to BOTH the credit of Trading A/c and the asset side of the Balance Sheet.

④ Direct/manufacturing expenses (carriage inward, wages, freight in) load into the Trading Account; indirect/office-and-selling expenses (carriage outward, salaries, rent) load into the Profit & Loss Account.

⑤ Provision for Discount on Debtors is computed on Debtors AFTER deducting further bad debts and the new Provision for Doubtful Debts — never on the gross Debtors figure.

⑥ Receipts and Payments Account is a summarised Cash Book — every cash/bank receipt and payment (capital or revenue) at its actual amount, with no accrual adjustment.

⑦ Income and Expenditure Account is the NPO's Profit & Loss Account — nominal in nature, prepared on the ACCRUAL basis, for the year revenue items relate to (not the year cash moved).

⑧ Every figure carried from Receipts & Payments into Income & Expenditure needs adjustment for opening/closing outstanding and prepaid/advance amounts.

⑨ Capital receipts of a non-profit body — life membership fees, specific donations, legacies — are credited to the Capital Fund or a special fund on the Balance Sheet, never through Income & Expenditure.

⑩ A special fund's own income and expenses (e.g. a Prize Fund's interest and prize payouts) stay ring-fenced inside that fund on the Balance Sheet — Income & Expenditure never sees them.

⑪ Single Entry System is incomplete double-entry recording, not a genuine alternative system — no Trial Balance can be drawn, so arithmetical accuracy can never be guaranteed and profit can only be estimated.

⑫ The Balance Sheet/Net Worth Approach finds profit by comparing Capital at two points in time — NOT by matching incomes against expenses like a real P&L Account.

⑬ Net Worth formula: Profit = (Closing Capital − Opening Capital) + Drawings − Additional Capital Introduced, then adjusted for interest on capital/drawings, depreciation and bad debts to reach Net Profit.

⑭ A Statement of Affairs LOOKS like a Balance Sheet but proves nothing — built on estimates, no statutory format, and its "Capital" is only ever a balancing figure, never a ledger balance.

⑮ Under the Conversion Approach, missing figures (credit sales, credit purchases, cash defalcated) are found by reconstructing the relevant account and treating the unknown as the balancing figure.

⑯ In a Total Debtors A/c, Credit Sales is the balancing figure only when opening/closing Debtors and collections are already known; if Credit Sales is itself given, the balancing figure becomes the closing Debtors balance instead.

⑰ Cash found missing while reconstructing the Cash Account is NOT written off straight to P&L — it is carried to the Balance Sheet as "Amount Recoverable from Cashier/Employee," an asset, since recovery is presumed possible.

Partnership
Accounting

The complete accounting cycle of a reconstituted partnership firm: admission, retirement and death of a partner, the treatment of a Joint Life Policy, dissolution of the firm (including piecemeal distribution), amalgamation of firms, conversion of a firm into a company (or sale to a company), and the accounting of a Limited Liability Partnership.

MUST NOT SKIP: goodwill is an internally-generated intangible asset and, per AS-26, is NEVER shown in the books unless purchased — every reconstitution event (admission, retirement, death) instead adjusts the PARTNERS' CAPITAL/CURRENT ACCOUNTS directly, in sacrificing or gaining ratio, and never creates a Goodwill account out of thin air.

4.1–4.8

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: understand the accounting for admission of a partner (4.1); know the process of accounting for retirement of a partner (4.2); do the accounting in the event of death of a partner (4.3); understand the treatment and accounting of Joint Life Policy taken on partners' lives (4.4); learn the accounting in the event of dissolution of a partnership, including the different methods of accounting for piecemeal distribution (4.5); understand the accounting for amalgamation of partnership firms (4.6); do the accounting in the event of conversion of a partnership firm into a company and sale of a partnership firm to a company (4.7); and understand the concept of a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) and its accounting (4.8).

Glossary — Module 4, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across this module, explained simply. This part (4.1) uses the first block; later parts add their own vocabulary.

PartnershipPer Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 — "the relation between two or more persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all." Those persons are Partners; together they are the Partnership Firm.
Partnership DeedThe (usually written) agreement between the partners governing the firm — capital ratios, profit-sharing, remuneration, and the terms on which settlements are made. In its absence, or its silence on a point, the matter is decided mutually by the partners.
Reconstitution of a FirmAny event that ends the existing partnership and begins a new one among a changed set of partners — admission, retirement, death, or a change in the profit-sharing ratio are all forms of reconstitution.
Capital Account — Fluctuating MethodONE account per partner. Every adjustment — interest on capital, salary, share of profit/loss, drawings, revaluation, goodwill, reserves — is posted straight into it, so its balance changes every year.
Capital Account — Fixed MethodTWO accounts per partner: a Capital Account that stays constant (touched only when capital is actually introduced or withdrawn) and a Current Account that absorbs every other adjustment.
Revaluation AccountA nominal account opened at every reconstitution to record increases/decreases in the book values of assets and liabilities, and to surface any "secret profit" or "secret loss" hidden in the old figures. Its balance (profit or loss) is shared among the OLD partners in the OLD profit-sharing ratio.
Memorandum Revaluation AccountUsed when the firm wants to record the EFFECT of revaluation without actually changing the asset/liability figures appearing in the Balance Sheet — the changes are recorded, shared among partners, then reversed out again.
Reserves / Accumulated ProfitsProfits earned in earlier periods but not yet distributed to the partners. Distributed among the OLD partners only, in the OLD profit-sharing ratio, at reconstitution — unless the firm decides to keep the reserve in the books.
General ReserveA specific, commonly-used reserve account holding undistributed past profits set aside for general purposes — treated exactly like any other reserve on reconstitution.
GoodwillThe firm's capacity to earn super-normal profit, built up by the existing partners. An internally-generated intangible asset — per AS-26 it fails the asset-recognition criteria (reliable cost measurement) and so is NEVER shown in the books unless it was actually purchased.
Premium for GoodwillThe extra amount (over and above capital) an incoming partner is expected to bring in, in return for the share of the firm's existing goodwill they will enjoy from the moment of admission.
Sacrificing Ratio(4.1) The ratio in which the EXISTING partners give up (sacrifice) a share of their future profit to the incoming partner — Old Ratio minus New Ratio.
Gaining RatioThe ratio in which the CONTINUING partners pick up the share given up by an outgoing (retiring/deceased) partner — New Ratio minus Old Ratio.
Average Profit Method(4.1) Values goodwill as an agreed number of years' purchase of the Adjusted Average Maintainable Profits — profits after removing exceptional items and adjusting for errors.
Super Profit(4.1) Future Maintainable Profit minus the Normal Return expected on Capital Employed — the "extra" profit the firm earns above what its capital alone would normally justify.
Capital Employed(4.1) Sundry trading assets (excluding non-purchased goodwill, non-trading and fictitious assets) minus current liabilities and provisions — the base on which "normal return" is judged.
Capitalisation Method(4.1) Values goodwill by capitalising either the maintainable profit or the super profit at the Normal Rate of Return, then comparing against actual capital employed.

CONCEPT

4.1 Admission of Partner ★★★ HIGH

Sometimes, for additional capital, technical support, or improved managerial efficiency, a continuing firm — with the consent of all partners — decides to admit a new partner. Section 31(1) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 provides that a person can be admitted as a new partner only with the consent of ALL existing partners, unless otherwise agreed. Admission is a form of reconstruction — the moment a new partner is admitted, the partnership among the existing partners ends and a new partnership begins.

Six accounting adjustments are usually required at the time of admission:

  1. Computation of the New Profit-Sharing Ratio.
  2. Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities.
  3. Memorandum Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities (to keep the Balance Sheet at old book values while still giving revaluation its effect).
  4. Distribution of Reserves, Accumulated Profits and Losses.
  5. Adjustment for Goodwill.
  6. Adjustment of the new partner's capital contribution and the capitals of the existing partners.

New Profit-Sharing Ratio & Sacrificing Ratio ★★★ HIGH

On admission, the existing partners usually sacrifice a portion of their future profit share, which the new partner becomes entitled to. The new profit-sharing ratio may be directly agreed upon by the partners, or worked out from what each existing partner gives up and what the new partner receives.

Sacrificing Ratio = Old Ratio − New Ratio

Computed separately for each existing (old) partner. A positive result is that partner's sacrifice; the goodwill premium the new partner brings in is shared among the old partners in exactly this ratio.

Illustration 1 — Computing the Sacrificing Ratio

A and B share profit/loss 4 : 3. New partner C is admitted; the new ratio among A, B and C becomes 5 : 3 : 2.

A's sacrifice = 4/7 − 5/10 = 40/70 − 35/70 = 5/70. B's sacrifice = 3/7 − 3/10 = 30/70 − 21/70 = 9/70.

Answer: Sacrificing Ratio of A and B = 5 : 9.

Illustration 2 — New Ratio when One Partner Retains His Original Share

X, Y and Z share profits 3 : 2 : 1. W is admitted with 1/6th share of future profits; Z retains his original share (1/6th) unchanged, so only X and Y sacrifice, proportionately, out of their old 3 : 2 relationship.

X's new share = 3/6 − (1/6 × 3/5) = 1/2 − 1/10 = 12/30. Y's new share = 2/6 − (1/6 × 2/5) = 1/3 − 2/30 = 8/30. Z's share = 1/6 = 5/30. W's share = 1/6 = 5/30.

Answer: New Profit-Sharing Ratio, X : Y : Z : W = 12 : 8 : 5 : 5.

Illustration 3 — New Ratio when the Incoming Partner Acquires from Named Partners

S and N share profit/loss 5 : 3. J is admitted for 3/10th share, acquiring 1/5th from S and 1/10th from N.

S's new share = 5/8 − 1/5 = 25/40 − 8/40 = 17/40. N's new share = 3/8 − 1/10 = 15/40 − 4/40 = 11/40. J's share = 1/5 + 1/10 = 3/10 = 12/40.

Answer: New Profit/Loss-Sharing Ratio = 17 : 11 : 12.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SACRIFICING RATIO COMPUTED THE WRONG WAY ROUND

THE TRAP: students subtract New Ratio − Old Ratio (the GAINING-ratio formula) when finding the sacrificing ratio on admission, or use the incoming partner's OWN share as the divisor for splitting the goodwill premium.

THE TWIST: Sacrificing Ratio is always Old Ratio − New Ratio (for each OLD partner only) — Gaining Ratio (New − Old) belongs to retirement/death, where the CONTINUING partners gain. The goodwill premium is shared strictly in the sacrificing ratio just computed, never in the old ratio and never in the new ratio.

Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities ★★★ HIGH

Revaluation is done at admission (or any other reconstruction) to unveil any "secret profit" or "secret loss" sitting in the books, so that assets and liabilities are brought to their fair values. A firm earns a profit when asset values rise and/or liability values fall; it suffers a loss when asset values fall and/or liability values rise. The effect is given through a Revaluation Account.

Journal Entries for Revaluation
ItemEventJournal Entry
AssetsUpward revaluationAsset A/c Dr. → To Revaluation A/c
Downward revaluationRevaluation A/c Dr. → To Asset A/c
Recording an unrecorded assetAsset A/c Dr. → To Revaluation A/c
LiabilitiesUpward revaluationRevaluation A/c Dr. → To Liability A/c
Downward revaluationLiability A/c Dr. → To Revaluation A/c
Recording an unrecorded liabilityRevaluation A/c Dr. → To Liability A/c
Revaluation ExpensesPaid by the firmRevaluation A/c Dr. → To Bank A/c
Paid by a partnerRevaluation A/c Dr. → To Partner's Capital A/c

The Revaluation Account's balance (profit or loss) is transferred to the CapitaI/Current Accounts of the OLD partners only, in their OLD profit-sharing ratio — the incoming partner has no stake in gains or losses that belong to the period before joining.

Proforma of Revaluation Account
Dr.     Revaluation Account    Cr.
To Assets (decrease in value)x xBy Assets (increase in value)x x
To Liabilities (increase in value)x xBy Liabilities (decrease in value)x x
To Partners' Capital/Current A/cs (profit, old p.s.r.)x xBy Partners' Capital/Current A/cs (loss, old p.s.r.)x x

Memorandum Revaluation Account ★★ MEDIUM

A firm may want to give the effect of revaluation WITHOUT actually changing the Balance Sheet figures of those assets and liabilities — in that case it opens a Memorandum Revaluation Account, prepared in two mirrored halves:

  1. Record the increase/decrease in the value of assets and liabilities, as usual.
  2. Share the resulting profit or loss among the OLD partners, in their OLD profit-sharing ratio.
  3. Reverse the increase/decrease in the value of assets and liabilities (bringing the Balance Sheet back to old book values).
  4. After the reversal, calculate the (opposite-sign) profit or loss this creates.
  5. Share this second profit/loss among ALL partners — including the new partner — in the NEW profit-sharing ratio.
Proforma of Memorandum Revaluation Account
First half — record & share in OLD ratio
To Assets (decrease)x xBy Assets (increase)x x
To Liabilities (increase)x xBy Liabilities (decrease)x x
To Partners' Capital A/cs (profit, OLD ratio)x xBy Partners' Capital A/cs (loss, OLD ratio)x x
Second half — reverse & share in NEW ratio
To Reversal of Items b/dx xBy Reversal of Items b/dx x
To Partners' Capital A/cs (profit, ALL partners, NEW ratio)x xBy Partners' Capital A/cs (loss, ALL partners, NEW ratio)x x
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: OLD-RATIO / NEW-RATIO CONFUSION ON REVALUATION

THE TRAP: students distribute the ordinary Revaluation Account's profit/loss in the NEW ratio (including the incoming partner), or — in a Memorandum Revaluation question — split BOTH halves in the same ratio.

THE TWIST: an ordinary Revaluation Account ALWAYS distributes to the old partners in the OLD ratio only. A Memorandum Revaluation Account is the one place the ratio deliberately flips mid-account: the first half (real profit/loss) goes to old partners in the OLD ratio; the second half (the reversal's mirror-image profit/loss) goes to ALL partners, including the new one, in the NEW ratio.

Distribution of Reserves, Accumulated Profits and Losses ★★ MEDIUM

Reserves and accumulated profits/losses are profits/losses earned in preceding periods but not yet distributed. For reserves and accumulated profits, partners' capital/current accounts are CREDITED; for accumulated losses they are DEBITED — in every case, among the OLD partners only, in the OLD profit-sharing ratio.

EventUnder Fluctuating Capital MethodUnder Fixed Capital Method
Reserves / Accumulated Profits (credit)Reserves A/c & P/L A/c Dr. → To Partners' Capital A/c (old partners, old p.s.r.)Reserves A/c & P/L A/c Dr. → To Partners' Current A/c (old partners, old p.s.r.)
Accumulated Loss (debit)Partners' Capital A/c Dr. → To P/L A/c (old partners, old p.s.r.)Partners' Current A/c Dr. → To P/L A/c (old partners, old p.s.r.)
Reserves and accumulated profits/losses always go to the OLD partners only, in the OLD ratio — the new partner has no claim on profits (or responsibility for losses) earned before joining.

If the firm instead decides to retain the reserve in the books rather than pay it out, the reserve is first credited to the old partners in the old ratio (as above) and then immediately debited back from ALL partners (including the new one) in the NEW ratio — reinstating the reserve figure on the Balance Sheet while still giving every partner the correct net effect. Illustrations 5 and 8 apply this exact two-step mechanic.

Adjustment for Goodwill ★★★ HIGH

Because of the goodwill generated by the OLD partners, the firm may earn super-normal profit — a share of which the new partner will enjoy from the moment of admission. For this reason an incoming partner is expected to bring in, over and above capital, a Premium for Goodwill.

AS-26 gives a clear rule: to be recorded in the books, ANY asset (tangible or intangible) must satisfy the asset-recognition criteria — (1) future economic benefits will flow to the firm, and (2) the cost can be reliably measured. Goodwill is usually internally generated and cannot satisfy criterion (2) with reliability. Goodwill is therefore not shown in the books of account — instead, its effect is routed entirely through the partners' Capital/Current Accounts.

Treatment of Goodwill on Admission — through the New Partner's Capital/Current A/c
SituationJournal Entry
(i) Premium paid by the new partnerBank/Cash A/c Dr. → To Old Partners' Capital/Current A/c (in sacrificing ratio)
(ii) New partner does NOT pay premiumNew Partner's Capital/Current A/c Dr. → To Old Partners' Capital/Current A/c (in sacrificing ratio)
(iii) New partner pays premium partlyNew Partner's Capital/Current A/c Dr. (extent not paid) & Bank/Cash A/c Dr. (extent paid) → To Old Partners' Capital/Current A/c (in sacrificing ratio)

If Goodwill is already appearing in the Balance Sheet before admission, it is left undisturbed — it is not known whether it is self-generated or purchased. When goodwill already sits in the books, the new partner will not separately pay premium for it, since that value already belongs to the old partners' capital. If the question specifically asks to write it off, do so among the OLD partners in the OLD ratio. When the incoming partner DOES bring in a share of premium for goodwill in cash, it is shared among the existing partners in the Sacrificing Ratio.

Illustration 4 — Goodwill Already in the Books, Premium Brought in Cash

X and Y share profit/loss 5 : 4. They admit Z for 1/5th share, given 2/15th by X and 1/15th by Y. A Goodwill account already appears in the books at ₹1,65,000 (assumed purchased goodwill, so it is left undisturbed). Z brings ₹2,10,000 in total — capital plus premium.

Bank A/c      Dr.2,10,000
    To Z's Capital A/c1,50,000
    To Premium for Goodwill A/c60,000

(Being amount brought in by Z as capital and premium for goodwill)

Premium for Goodwill A/c      Dr.60,000
    To X's Capital A/c40,000
    To Y's Capital A/c20,000

(Being transfer of premium brought by Z to X and Y's Capital A/cs in their Sacrificing Ratio)

New ratio: X's new share = 5/9 − 2/15 = 25/45 − 6/45 = 19/45. Y's new share = 4/9 − 1/15 = 20/45 − 3/45 = 17/45. Z's share = 1/5 = 9/45. Sacrificing ratio X : Y = 6/45 : 3/45 = 2 : 1 (which is exactly why the 60,000 premium splits 40,000 : 20,000).

Answer: New Profit-Sharing Ratio = 19 : 17 : 9.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PARTIAL GOODWILL IN CASH

THE TRAP: when the new partner brings in ONLY PART of the premium for goodwill in cash, students credit the old partners with only the cash portion and forget the balance entirely — or debit the shortfall to Bank instead of to the new partner's own Capital/Current A/c.

THE TWIST: the FULL premium must reach the old partners in the sacrificing ratio, regardless of how much cash actually came in — Bank/Cash A/c is debited only to the extent paid, and the New Partner's Capital/Current A/c is debited for the balance not yet paid (Situation (iii) above). The old partners are never shortchanged for a partner's inability to pay cash.

Valuation of Inherent (Non-Purchased) Goodwill ★★ MEDIUM

There are four recognised methods of valuing goodwill that has not been purchased.

(1) Average Profits Method: Value of Goodwill = Agreed Number of Years' Purchase × Average Maintainable Profit

Average Maintainable Profit is built up as: Average Annual Profits (simple average; if profits show an increasing trend, a weighted average may be used) − Exceptional/Casual Income + Abnormal Loss + Capital Expenditure wrongly charged against profits − Provision for Taxation (as required) = Adjusted Maintainable Profits. If profits are constantly decreasing, the lowest of the adjusted profits may be considered; more weightage is usually given to later years; adjustments for over/undercharged depreciation or over/under valuation of stock are also made where required.

(2) Super Profits Method: Super Profit = Future Maintainable Profit − Normal Return on Capital Employed; Goodwill = Super Profit × No. of Years' Purchase

Capital Employed = Sundry Assets (including goodwill AT COST paid, excluding non-purchased goodwill, non-trading assets and fictitious assets) − Current Liabilities & Provisions − Contingent/Probable Liabilities. Average Capital Employed = Capital Employed − ½ of the current year's trading profit after tax (if it remains undistributed). Trading profits exclude any non-trading income (e.g. interest on non-trading investments); provision for managerial remuneration must be adjusted; a change in the value of a fixed asset on revaluation does NOT affect Annual Trading Profit, though over/undercharged depreciation may need adjustment; an unadjusted decrease in a current asset (bad debts, reduced stock) must be corrected for; proposed dividend need not be deducted when calculating capital employed.

(3A) Capitalisation of Profits: Normal Capital Employed = (Maintainable Profit ÷ Normal Rate of Return) × 100; Goodwill = Normal Capital Employed − Actual Capital Employed

(3B) Capitalisation of Super Profits: Goodwill = (Super Profit ÷ Normal Rate of Return) × 100

Both variants require the same adjustments to profit (managerial remuneration, depreciation, etc.) as the Super Profits Method.

(4) Annuity Method: Goodwill = Annual Super Profit × Present Value of an Annuity of ₹1

A derivative of the super-profit concept — used when the super profit is expected to be earned uniformly over a number of years; the annuity factor is read off an Annuity Table for the relevant years and rate. Capital Employed / Average Capital Employed and Annual Average Profits are computed exactly as under the Super Profits Method.

Adjustment for Capital Contribution ★★ MEDIUM

At admission, the incoming partner brings capital into the firm — an amount mutually agreed, in cash or in the form of other assets. After passing entries for revaluation profit/loss, distribution of reserves, and goodwill, the ADJUSTED capital account balances stand. Partners may further decide to bring their closing capital balances into a pre-determined ratio — very often the new profit-sharing ratio, using either the new partner's capital or one partner's own capital as the "base" figure from which the total (and hence everyone else's) capital is derived.

Fluctuating Capital MethodFixed Capital Method
Accounts per partnerOne — the Capital Account only.Two — a fixed Capital Account, plus a Current Account.
Capital Account balanceChanges every year — absorbs interest on capital, share of profit/loss, drawings, revaluation and goodwill adjustments directly.Stays constant, at the agreed capital figure, unless capital is actually introduced or withdrawn.
Where adjustments are postedStraight into the Capital Account.Into the Current Account; the Capital Account is left undisturbed.
EXAM TRICK: when a question states "capitals are fixed" or "adjustments through Current Account," EVERY revaluation/reserve/goodwill entry that would normally hit the Capital Account must instead be redirected to the Current Account — Illustrations 5 and 9 test exactly this switch.

Illustration 5 — Admission with Fixed Capitals, All Adjustments through Current Accounts

X and Y share profit/loss 5 : 3. They admit Z with 1/5th share; Z pays ₹80,000 as capital but contributes nothing towards goodwill (valued at ₹60,000). Capitals are fixed; all adjustments are made through partners' current accounts.

Illustration 6 — Admission Combined with Rectification of Past Years' Errors

Sun and Moon share profit/loss 3 : 2. Balance Sheet as on 31.3.2023: Capital — Sun ₹50,000, Moon ₹41,000; Loan (Sun) ₹5,000; General Reserve ₹5,000; Sundry Creditors ₹15,000; Outstanding Expenses ₹1,500 (Total ₹1,17,500) against Property ₹35,000, Motor Car ₹7,500, Furniture ₹1,000, Debtors ₹25,000, Stock ₹45,000, Cash ₹4,000.

Pluto is admitted from 1.4.2023: (1) Property revalued to ₹45,000, Motor Car to ₹6,500, 5% provision created on Debtors. (2) Pluto pays premium for goodwill valued at 2 years' purchase of the last 3 years' AVERAGE profits, credited to old partners' LOAN accounts. (3) Pluto brings ₹37,500 capital. (4) New ratio 2 : 1 : 1. (5) Last 3 years' reported profits: ₹5,000, ₹6,000, ₹7,500 — subject to discrepancies discovered on verification.

Illustration 7 — Admission with a Guaranteed Minimum, Shortfall Borne by One Partner Only

P and Q (sharing 5 : 4) admit R for 1/5th share of profits. As Manager, R had been receiving a salary of ₹60,000 p.a. and a commission of 5% on net profit after charging such salary and commission; any excess R becomes entitled to as a partner (over the former remuneration) is to be borne by Q alone. Profit for the year ended 31.3.2023 = ₹4,27,500.

R's remuneration as Manager: Commission = (₹4,27,500 − ₹60,000) × 5/105 = ₹3,67,500 × 5/105 = ₹17,500. Total = ₹60,000 + ₹17,500 = ₹77,500.

R's share as partner = ₹4,27,500 × 1/5 = ₹85,500 — excess over ₹77,500 = ₹8,000, borne entirely by Q.

Residual profit after R's minimum = ₹4,27,500 − ₹77,500 = ₹3,50,000, split P : Q = 5 : 4 → P = ₹3,50,000 × 5/9 = ₹1,94,444; Q = ₹3,50,000 × 4/9 = ₹1,55,556, less the ₹8,000 borne for R = ₹1,47,556.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: A CURRENT-ACCOUNT BALANCE ASSUMED TO SIT ON THE "USUAL" SIDE

THE TRAP: students assume every partner's Current Account balance in the Balance Sheet is a CREDIT (liability) figure, since that is the more common case — and so misplace a partner's balance on the wrong side, throwing the Balance Sheet out of balance.

THE TWIST: a Current Account can carry EITHER balance for EITHER an old or a new partner — a gaining partner who must fund a goodwill/revaluation payment out of pocket, or one who transfers a large chunk of current balance into capital, can easily flip from credit to debit (as Bhusan, Charan and Dev all do in Illustration 9). Always total each partner's Current Account column individually before deciding which side of the Balance Sheet it belongs on — never assume.

CONCEPT

4.2 Retirement of Partner ★★★ HIGH

Retirement, like admission, is a reconstitution of the firm — the old partnership dissolves and a new one (of the continuing partners) takes over the same business. The mechanics largely mirror admission, run in reverse.

Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities: the logic is identical to admission — assets and liabilities are revalued, and the resulting profit or loss on revaluation is distributed among all partners (including the retiring partner) in the Old Profit-Sharing Ratio.

Reserves and accumulated profits: any Reserve or undistributed profit standing in the books at the date of retirement is transferred to all partners' Capital Accounts in the Old Ratio before the retiring partner's final dues are struck (see Illustration 11's Reserve entry below).

Adjustment for Goodwill — the Gaining Ratio

The firm's goodwill was built up by all the existing partners, including the one now retiring. So the continuing partners — who will enjoy a larger share of future profits — must compensate the retiring partner for his share of that goodwill, in their Gaining Ratio.

Gaining Ratio = Old Profit-Sharing Ratio − New Profit-Sharing Ratio

The ratio of the gain (increase) in profit share that each continuing partner makes on the outgoing partner's retirement.

Gaining Partners' Capital A/c  Dr. (in Gaining Ratio)
    To Outgoing Partner's Capital A/c

— with the outgoing partner's share of goodwill.

Sacrificing Ratio (Admission) vs. Gaining Ratio (Retirement)

Admission — Sacrificing RatioRetirement / Death — Gaining Ratio
What it measuresShare the OLD partners give up for the incoming partnerShare the CONTINUING partners take over from the outgoing partner
FormulaOld Ratio − New RatioOld Ratio − New Ratio
Who is compensated for goodwillThe sacrificing (old) partners, by the incoming partnerThe outgoing partner (or his estate), by the gaining partners
Capital A/c entryNew Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cGaining Partners' Capital A/c Dr. To Outgoing Partner's Capital A/c
EXAM TRICK: the subtraction "Old − New" is identical in both events — only the DIRECTION of who pays whom flips. Decide first whether a partner is joining or leaving before signing the goodwill entry.

Adjustment for Joint Life Policy (JLP)

A Joint Life Policy is a life-insurance policy covering the combined lives of all the partners, taken out precisely to fund a payout of this kind. Its value must be considered on every reconstitution (Admission, Retirement, or a change in profit-sharing ratio). Treatment: either (i) the surrender value is adjusted through the partners' Capital Accounts, or (ii) a Joint Life Policy Account is raised as an asset in the books of the firm.

Settlement of the Retiring Partner's Final Balance

After all the above adjustments (revaluation, goodwill, reserves, JLP), the amount due to the retiring partner is ascertained, then settled in the mode decided by the partnership deed — or, in its absence, as mutually agreed by the partners.

  • Lump Sum Payment: if the firm has sufficient liquid funds, the whole amount is paid off immediately from business funds (Cash/Bank).
  • Instalment / Loan Payment: if the firm has a paucity of liquid funds, the amount due is transferred to a Loan Account opened in the retiring partner's name, and paid off gradually in instalments, with interest on the unpaid balance.

Right of a Retiring Partner — Section 37, Indian Partnership Act, 1932

Where settlement is delayed, the retiring partner may claim the HIGHER of:

(a) Share in Profits — his profit share since the date of retirement, calculated in the ratio of the present adjusted capitals of the partners; OR

(b) Interest @ 6% p.a. — on the amount due to him, for the period from the date of retirement to the date of settlement.

Adjustment of capital accounts: where the deed requires the continuing partners' capitals to be realigned to the new profit-sharing ratio, the combined adjusted capital (after revaluation, goodwill and reserve adjustments, and any fresh cash brought in) is re-apportioned between them in the new ratio — worked out in Illustration 11 (Working Note 3) and fixed by agreement in Illustration 12 below.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SACRIFICING RATIO vs GAINING RATIO — WRONG DIRECTION

THE TRAP: a student applies "Old Ratio − New Ratio" correctly, but then debits/credits the wrong side of the goodwill entry — e.g. crediting the outgoing partner and debiting himself, or treating a retirement as if the outgoing partner must compensate the others.

THE TWIST: the subtraction is the same formula in both events, but the meaning flips. At ADMISSION it measures what the old partners GIVE UP — the new partner compensates THEM. At RETIREMENT/DEATH it measures what the continuing partners TAKE ON — THEY compensate the outgoing partner (or his estate). Always identify who is joining vs. leaving before signing the goodwill entry.

Memorandum Revaluation Account

Sometimes the partnership deed requires assets and liabilities to continue appearing in the Balance Sheet at their old (book) figures even though a revaluation is agreed for settlement purposes. In that case a real Revaluation Account cannot be used (it would permanently alter the book values). Instead, a Memorandum Revaluation Account is prepared in two parts:

  1. Part 1 records the actual gains/losses on revaluation exactly like an ordinary Revaluation A/c, and distributes the net profit/loss among all partners in the Old Ratio.
  2. Part 2 reverses every item of Part 1 (so the book values are restored to their old figures) and re-distributes the very same net amount among the continuing partners in the New Ratio — this is what lets the retiring partner's Capital A/c carry his old-ratio share while the continuing partners absorb the reversal in their new ratio.

ILLUSTRATION 12 — Memorandum Revaluation Account (Old Figures Retained in the Books)

GIVEN: A, B and C share profits in proportion to capital (A:B:C = 40,000:30,000:20,000 = 4:3:2). Balance Sheet 31.3.2023 — Capitals: A ₹40,000, B ₹30,000, C ₹20,000; Creditors ₹13,800 (Total ₹1,03,800). Assets: Land & Buildings ₹50,000, Plant & Machinery ₹17,000, Stock ₹16,000, Debtors (net) ₹9,800, Cash at Bank ₹11,000. B retires. Retirement-cum-Admission

In many cases, whenever an existing partner retires, another partner simultaneously joins the continuing partners. No separate treatment is needed — the same principles of Admission and Retirement are applied together, just as two sets of transactions on the same date. Illustration 15 below is one such case: X retires while R is admitted, on the same date.

4.2 in One Look

Revaluation profit/loss → ALL partners, OLD ratio. Reserves/accumulated profits → ALL partners, OLD ratio. Goodwill compensation → GAINING partners pay the retiring partner, in GAINING ratio. Settlement → lump sum now, OR a Loan A/c with instalments + interest (Section 37: higher of profit-share-on-adjusted-capitals, or 6% p.a. interest, if delayed beyond the deed's terms).

CONCEPT

4.3 Death of Partner ★★★ HIGH

If a continuing partner dies, the partnership firm is reconstituted, just as on retirement. If the other partners decide to continue the business, the books require the following adjustments:

  • Calculation of the new profit-sharing ratio and Gaining Ratio
  • Distribution of reserves and accumulated profits/losses
  • Revaluation of assets and liabilities
  • Adjustment for Goodwill
  • Adjustment for Joint Life Policy (JLP)
  • Adjustment for the interim period's profit/loss

Every one of these mirrors retirement exactly — except that "the retiring partner" becomes "the deceased partner," and settlement is made to his legal representative, the Executor, rather than to the partner himself. One genuinely new element appears: since death (unlike a pre-planned retirement date) can strike at ANY point in the accounting year, the deceased partner's share of profit has to be estimated for the part-year up to the date of death.

New PSR, Gaining Ratio, Reserves and Revaluation — Same as Retirement

New Profit Sharing Ratio & Gaining Ratio: as a consequence of death, the deceased partner's share of profit is distributed to the continuing partners, creating a gain in their share. Gaining Ratio is again calculated as Old Ratio − New Ratio.

Distribution of Reserves and Accumulated Profits/Losses: the balance of Reserves or undistributed profit (P&L A/c balance) is distributed among ALL partners — including the Executor of the deceased partner — in the Old Profit-Sharing Ratio.

Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities: the logic is the same as at admission; the revaluation profit or loss is distributed among all partners (including the Executor) in the Old Profit-Sharing Ratio.

Adjustment for Goodwill: the firm's goodwill was built by all the existing partners, including the deceased. So the continuing partners compensate the deceased partner (his Executor) in their Gaining Ratio — the same Capital-Account adjustment entry used for retirement.

Adjustment for Joint Life Policy (JLP): treatment again depends on the firm's accounting policy for the JLP. The surrender value plays no role here — only the maturity value of the Joint Life Policy is taken into consideration in the case of death (since the policy actually matures on a partner's death).

Adjustment for the Interim Period's Profit/Loss — the Genuine New Element

Unlike Admission and Retirement, whose dates are generally pre-planned, death can occur at any point during the accounting period. So the profit or loss for the "interim period" — from the start of the accounting year up to the date of death — must be estimated, and the deceased partner's share of it accounted for. A temporary account, generally called the Profit & Loss Suspense A/c, is opened in the books for this purpose.

(i) On Time Basis

The average profit of past period(s) is apportioned between the pre-death period and the post-death period, in the ratio of elapsed time — it assumes profit accrues evenly through the year.

(ii) On Sales (Turnover) Basis

The rate of profit on sales earned in the LAST year is computed, and applied to the ACTUAL sales achieved in the interim period — it tracks real performance rather than assuming a smooth spread.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TIME BASIS vs SALES BASIS — USING THE WRONG METHOD

THE TRAP: a question gives the interim period's actual sales figures (a Sales-Basis problem) but the student defaults to averaging last year's profit and splitting it by elapsed months — or the reverse, applying a smooth time-split when the question specifically hands over a profit-on-sales rate to apply to interim turnover.

THE TWIST: Time Basis apportions the AVERAGE of past profits pro-rata by elapsed months — it assumes profit is earned evenly across the year. Sales Basis instead computes last year's Profit ÷ Sales rate and multiplies it by the ACTUAL interim sales — it reflects real trading performance instead of a smooth assumption. Read which basis the question specifies before computing the deceased partner's share.

Settlement of the Deceased Partner's Final Balance — to His Executor

The amount payable on account of the deceased partner is made to his legal representative, commonly called the Executor — never to the deceased partner himself. Otherwise, the accounting procedure is identical to retirement, and the mode of payment depends on the partners' agreement:

  • Lump Sum Payment: if the firm has sufficient funds, the total amount payable is transferred to the deceased partner's Representative's (Executor's) Account, which is debited and Bank credited on payment of the dues.
  • Instalment Payment / Loan Payment: if the firm lacks funds for prompt payment, the total amount payable is transferred to a Loan Account in the name of the legal representative or Executor, and paid off gradually by instalments after considering interest on the unpaid balance. The word "Loan" may or may not be appended to the account name — but its gradual repayment will always resemble a loan.

4.3 in One Look

Everything is IDENTICAL to retirement — revaluation, reserves and goodwill all still move in Old Ratio (for the split) / Gaining Ratio (for compensation) — with two changes: (1) the deceased partner's profit share must be ESTIMATED for the part-year up to death, on a Time Basis or a Sales Basis; and (2) settlement (lump sum or an interest-bearing Loan A/c) is paid to the Executor, never to the deceased partner.

Settlement of the Deceased Partner's Dues ★★★ HIGH

Recall that because a partner's death rarely falls on the last day of the accounting year, the deceased's share of profit/loss for the broken period up to the date of death (the "interim period") is estimated — either on a Time Basis (last period's average profit apportioned pre-death/post-death) or a Sales Basis (last year's rate of profit on sales, applied to interim sales) — and routed through a temporary Profit & Loss Suspense A/c before being credited to the deceased partner's Capital A/c.

Once the deceased partner's final Capital A/c balance is arrived at (opening capital ± revaluation share ± reserves share + goodwill share + interim profit share − drawings), that balance is transferred out of the firm's books entirely — the accounting from this point mirrors retirement, except the payee is now the partner's legal representative, commonly called the Executor (or Heir).

The mode of payment depends on the partnership agreement:

ModeAccounting Treatment
(i) Lump Sum PaymentUsed when the firm has sufficient funds. The total amount payable is transferred to the deceased partner's Representative's/Executor's Account; on payment, Executor's A/c is debited and Bank A/c credited.
(ii) Instalment Payment / Loan PaymentUsed when the firm cannot pay promptly. The total amount payable is transferred to a Loan Account in the legal representative's name, paid off gradually by instalments together with interest on the unpaid balance. The word "Loan" may or may not be appended to the account's name — but gradual repayment with interest makes it function as one regardless.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: FORGETTING INTEREST ON THE EXECUTOR'S UNPAID BALANCE

THE TRAP: students transfer the deceased partner's final Capital A/c balance to the Executor's/Loan A/c and stop there, ignoring any gap between the date of death and the date(s) of actual payment.

THE TWIST: where settlement is deferred, interest runs on the unpaid balance from the date of death until the date it is actually paid (at the rate the deed specifies, or a rate given in the question) — this interest is a charge to the firm (Interest A/c Dr) and income to the Executor's A/c, and must be added before the final instalment is struck.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: WRITING OFF ALL OF AN OVER-STATED GOODWILL IN ONE RATIO

THE TRAP: when book goodwill (₹15,000) exceeds the freshly-valued goodwill (₹10,000), students write off the whole ₹15,000 in a single ratio.

THE TWIST: the over-valued slice (the ₹5,000 that was never real) belongs to whoever benefited from it originally — written off in the OLD profit-sharing ratio, including the deceased partner. Only the correctly-valued remaining goodwill (₹10,000, since the firm chooses not to carry goodwill going forward) is written off among the CONTINUING partners in their ratio.

CONCEPT

4.4 Treatment of Joint Life Policy ★★★ HIGH

When a partner dies, the amount due to them falls due for payment all at once — a sudden burden that can hurt the firm's financial position if it must be found from working capital. To guard against this, a firm commonly takes out a life insurance policy on the lives of its partners, paying the premium out of firm funds.

A Joint Life Policy (JLP) is a single life insurance policy taken out by a partnership firm covering the lives of all its partners together (as distinct from separate individual policies on each partner). It matures — and the insurer pays out — on the death of any one partner, or on expiry of the policy period, whichever occurs first.

The policy is an asset of the firm in which every partner has a proportionate stake, so it must be properly accounted for both on a change in the firm's constitution (admission, retirement, change in profit-sharing ratio) and on the death of a partner.

TermMeaning
Maturity Value / Sum AssuredThe amount receivable by the firm from the insurer on the death of a partner, or on expiry of the policy period — fixed at inception, does not change over the years.
Surrender ValueThe amount receivable if the firm terminates (surrenders) the policy before maturity. Unlike the maturity value, it is not constant — it gradually increases with time, and is treated as the policy's "fair value" for accounting.

Method A: JLP Not Treated as an Asset ★★★ HIGH

The premium paid is treated purely as an expense of the firm. It is debited straight to the Profit & Loss A/c; the JLP A/c does not appear in the Balance Sheet at all, and the policy's surrender value is never reflected in the books.

Joint Life Policy Premium A/c Dr.
To Bank A/c
(Being the annual premium paid on the JLP)
P & L A/c Dr.
To Joint Life Policy Premium A/c
(Being the premium charged off as an expense)

On change in constitution (admission, retirement, change in ratio): since nothing sits in the books, the surrender value as on that date is accounted for either by raising and immediately writing off a JLP A/c, or by adjusting the partners' capital accounts directly:

Raising and writing off JLP A/c — two-step:
(a) Joint Life Policy A/c Dr.
To Existing Partners' Capital A/cs (old profit-sharing ratio)
(Raising JLP A/c at surrender value)
(b) Continuing Partners' Capital A/cs Dr.
To Joint Life Policy A/c (new profit-sharing ratio)
(Writing off JLP A/c so nothing remains in the books)
OR — adjusting the capital accounts directly (net effect of the two entries above):
Gaining Partners' Capital A/c(s) Dr.
To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/c(s)

On the death of a partner: the JLP matures; the sum assured is received and distributed among all existing partners in the old profit-sharing ratio.

Joint Life Policy Receivable A/c Dr.
To Existing Partners' Capital A/cs (old p.s.r.)
(On maturity of the JLP)
Bank A/c Dr.
To Joint Life Policy Receivable A/c
(On receipt of the maturity value)

Method B: JLP Treated as an Asset (at Surrender Value) ★★★ HIGH

Premium paid is treated as an investment in an asset, shown in the Balance Sheet — but always at surrender value, which is lower than the cumulative premiums paid, so the excess must be written off each year. Two recognised approaches keep the JLP A/c pinned to surrender value.

Approach 1 — Surrender Value Method (single account):

Joint Life Policy A/c Dr.
To Bank A/c
(Premium paid, capitalised)
P & L A/c Dr.
To Joint Life Policy A/c
(Excess of premium paid over the year's increase in surrender value, written off — keeps JLP A/c at surrender value)

Approach 2 — Joint Life Policy Reserve Method (two accounts): the premium is treated as an "appropriation of profit" rather than a straight expense, funded through a dedicated JLP Reserve A/c. Both the JLP A/c and the JLP Reserve A/c appear in the Balance Sheet — JLP A/c on the assets side, JLP Reserve A/c on the liabilities side.

Joint Life Policy A/c Dr.
To Bank A/c
(Premium paid, capitalised)
P & L Appropriation A/c Dr.
To Joint Life Policy Reserve A/c
(An amount equal to the premium set aside as a reserve, out of profit)
Joint Life Policy Reserve A/c Dr.
To Joint Life Policy A/c
(Excess of premium paid over the year's increase in surrender value, adjusted between the two accounts — keeps BOTH JLP A/c and JLP Reserve A/c at surrender value)
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PREMIUM AS EXPENSE vs. PREMIUM AS ASSET

THE TRAP: treating every premium payment identically regardless of which method the firm follows — e.g. debiting P&L A/c under Method B, or capitalising to a JLP A/c under Method A.

THE TWIST: the SAME cash outflow gets opposite treatment. Method A: premium is a pure P&L expense, JLP never appears in the Balance Sheet. Method B: premium is capitalised to JLP A/c (an asset), with only the EXCESS over the year's rise in surrender value charged to P&L (Approach 1) or adjusted via the JLP Reserve A/c (Approach 2). Read the question's stated policy before passing a single premium entry.

Comparison — Surrender Value Method vs. JLP Reserve Method ★★★ HIGH

EventSurrender Value MethodJLP Reserve Method
On death of a partner (maturity of JLP)JLP Receivable A/c Dr.  To JLP A/cJLP Receivable A/c Dr.  To JLP A/c
On receipt of maturity valueBank A/c Dr.  To JLP Receivable A/cBank A/c Dr.  To JLP Receivable A/c
Closing of JLP Reserve A/cNot applicable — no such account existsJLP Reserve A/c Dr.  To JLP A/c (transferred at the last-recorded surrender value)
Closing of JLP A/c — profit on maturityJLP A/c Dr.  To All Partners' Capital A/cs (difference between the last recorded surrender value and the maturity value received)JLP A/c Dr.  To All Partners' Capital A/cs (difference between the current year's premium paid, if any, and the maturity value)
EXAM TRICK: under the Reserve Method, the JLP Reserve A/c must be closed out into JLP A/c FIRST (at its last surrender value) before the profit-on-maturity figure is struck — skip that step and the profit credited to partners' capital comes out wrong.

On change in constitution (admission, retirement, change in ratio), the JLP A/c already sits at surrender value under both approaches — no further adjustment is needed to the JLP A/c itself. Under the Reserve Method, a choice remains for the JLP Reserve A/c:

If partners decide…Treatment
…NOT to keep maintaining the JLP Reserve A/cJLP Reserve A/c is written back and distributed among the existing partners in their old profit-sharing ratio: JLP Reserve A/c Dr.  To Partners' Capital A/cs.
…TO keep maintaining the JLP Reserve A/cAdjustment made only through the Partners' Capital A/cs: Gaining Partners' Capital A/c(s) Dr.  To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/c(s).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING THE JLP RESERVE AS SPENDABLE PROFIT

THE TRAP: students see "Joint Life Policy RESERVE" and treat it like General Reserve — distributable cash-equivalent profit sitting on the liabilities side.

THE TWIST: the JLP Reserve A/c exists for one purpose only — to offset the JLP A/c on the assets side so the NET shown in the accounts equals surrender value. It is not free-standing distributable profit; on death or on a decision to stop maintaining it, it must first be transferred against the JLP A/c (or written back to partners) before any "profit on maturity" is worked out, otherwise the same value gets counted twice.

Each year, the excess of premium paid over the RISE in surrender value is written off to P&L A/c (e.g. Year 2020-21: premium 10,000 − rise in surrender value 2,000 = 8,000 written off), keeping the JLP A/c pinned to that year's surrender value. CONCEPT

4.5 Dissolution of Partnership Firms Including Piecemeal Distribution ★★★ HIGH

Whenever a reconstitution takes place — admission, retirement or death of a partner — the existing partnership stands dissolved, but the firm may continue if the remaining partners so desire. If instead the firm's business itself is discontinued for any reason, that is Dissolution of the Firm — all economic relations between the firm and outsiders end, and the books are finally closed.

AspectDissolution of PartnershipDissolution of the Firm
What endsThe relation between the outgoing partner(s) and the othersThe relation between ALL partners and between the firm and third parties
BusinessContinues, under the remaining partnersDiscontinued
Books of accountContinue (revalued/reconstituted)Finally closed

Modes of Dissolution of a Firm (Indian Partnership Act, 1932)

  1. By mutual consent [Sec. 40] — all partners agree, or as per a contract already made between them.
  2. By notice [Sec. 43] — where the partnership is "at will," any partner may dissolve it by giving written notice to all other partners.
  3. On the happening of a contingency [Sec. 42] — (i) expiry of a fixed term for which the firm was constituted; (ii) completion of the adventure for which the firm was formed; (iii) death of a partner; (iv) adjudication of a partner as insolvent.
  4. Compulsory dissolution [Sec. 41] — (i) all partners, or all but one, are adjudged insolvent; (ii) an event occurs making it unlawful to carry on the firm's business.
  5. By the Court [Sec. 44] — at the suit of a partner, on any of: insanity; permanent incapacity to perform duties; misconduct prejudicial to the business; wilful or persistent breach of agreement; a partner transferring his whole share to a third party / allowing it to be charged under Rule 49, Order XXI, First Schedule, CPC 1908; the business being workable only at a loss; or any other ground the Court considers just and equitable.

Settlement of Accounts on Dissolution — Section 48

Section 48 lays down the default rules, applicable "subject to agreement by the partners" — i.e. the Partnership Deed can override them.

Sec. 48(1) — Losses: Profits → then Capital → then Partners individually (in PSR)

"Losses, including deficiencies of capital, shall be paid first out of profits, next out of capital, and lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in the proportions in which they are entitled to share profits."

Sec. 48(2) — Assets, applied strictly in this order:

(i) Firm's debts to third parties → (ii) Each partner ratably for advances as distinguished from capital (i.e. partners' loans) → (iii) Each partner ratably for capital → (iv) Residue, if any, divided among partners in profit-sharing ratio.

Two separate accounting exercises follow from this: [A] Realisation of assets and payment of liabilities (through the Realisation Account), and [B] Settlement of partners' dues (through the Partners' Capital Accounts).

[A] The Realisation Account

Format of the Realisation Account
Dr.   Realisation Account   Cr.
Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Sundry Assets (book value, incl. Goodwill if shown)xxxBy Provision A/cs (Bad Debts / Depreciation, written back at gross)xxx
To Bank/Cash A/c (liabilities paid off)xxxBy Sundry Liabilities (book value)xxx
To Bank/Cash A/c (realisation expenses)xxxBy Bank/Cash A/c (assets realised)xxx
To Partners' Capital A/c (Profit on realisation, in PSR)xxxBy Partners' Capital A/c (assets taken over, at agreed value)xxx
By Partners' Capital A/c (liabilities taken over)xxx
By Partners' Capital A/c (Loss on realisation, in PSR)xxx

Cash/Bank and fictitious assets are NOT transferred to Realisation A/c (unless the whole firm is sold as a going concern) — nor is a debit balance of Capital A/c or of P&L A/c. If the question is silent about realised value, assume tangible assets realise at book value and intangible assets realise at Nil.

EventEntryNote
Assets transferredRealisation A/c Dr  To Sundry Assets A/cAt book value; gross debtors/gross assets if a Provision exists — the Provision is separately reversed: Provision A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c.
Liabilities transferredSundry Liabilities A/c Dr  To Realisation A/cAt book value.
Asset realised for cashBank A/c Dr  To Realisation A/c—
Asset taken over by a partnerPartner's Capital A/c Dr  To Realisation A/cAt the agreed value.
Liability paid offRealisation A/c Dr  To Bank A/cActual amount paid (may differ from book value — any discount is a realisation gain).
Liability taken over by a partnerRealisation A/c Dr  To Partner's Capital A/cAt agreed value. How the partner personally then settles it is his own affair — a discount he negotiates does NOT benefit the firm.
Unrecorded asset sold / taken overCash/Bank or Partner's Capital A/c Dr  To Realisation A/cAn asset that was never in the books enters the Realisation A/c only when it is realised or taken over — not merely because it is "discovered."
Unrecorded liability paidRealisation A/c Dr  To Cash/Bank A/cActual amount paid.
Realisation expensesRealisation A/c Dr  To Cash/Bank A/c (or To Partner's Capital A/c, if a partner pays)If a partner bears expenses personally under a separate agreement, NO ENTRY is required at all.
Balance of Realisation A/cProfit: Realisation A/c Dr, To Partners' Capital A/c (PSR)
Loss: Partners' Capital A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c (PSR)		—

[B] Settlement of Partners' Dues — Capital Accounts

  1. Open Capital Accounts with balances as per the Balance Sheet before dissolution; transfer any Current A/c balance into Capital A/c.
  2. Transfer undistributed Reserves / P&L (Cr.) / JLP Reserve / Investment Fluctuation Fund etc. to Capital A/cs in PSR.
  3. Transfer undistributed losses and fictitious/unrealisable assets (e.g. Advertisement Suspense A/c) to Capital A/cs in PSR.
  4. Repay a partner's loan before touching capital — "u/s 48, repayment of loan should enjoy priority over repayment of capital."
  5. A debit balance remaining in a partner's Capital A/c (after all transfers) must be brought in by that partner in cash — unless he is insolvent (treated separately below).

ILLUSTRATION 22 — Realisation Account, Capital Accounts & Bank Account (assets taken over by every partner)

A, B and C share profits 3:1:1 and dissolve. Balance Sheet: Creditors ₹6,000, Loan ₹1,500, Capitals A ₹27,500 / B ₹10,000 / C ₹7,000; Cash at Bank ₹3,200, Sundry Assets ₹17,000, Debtors ₹24,200 (less Bad Debts Provision ₹1,200) = ₹23,000, Stock ₹7,800, Furniture ₹1,000. Goodwill is ignored. A takes Furniture at ₹800 and Debtors of ₹20,000 at ₹17,200, and assumes the ₹6,000 creditors. B takes all the stock at ₹7,000 and other sundry assets of ₹7,200 (book value less 10%). C takes the remaining sundry assets at 90% of book value less a ₹100 allowance, and assumes the loan together with unrecorded accrued interest of ₹30. Dissolution expenses ₹270. The remaining debtors were sold to a collecting agency for 50% of book value.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING AN "UNRECORDED" ITEM AS ALREADY IN THE BOOKS

THE TRAP: a student sees "unrecorded asset" or "unrecorded liability" in the problem and immediately debits/credits Realisation A/c for it, the same way a recorded asset/liability is transferred.

THE TWIST: since it was never in the books, there is nothing to "transfer." An unrecorded asset enters the Realisation A/c only at the point it is sold or taken over by a partner; an unrecorded liability enters only when it is paid or taken over. If a part of an unrecorded asset is used to settle part of an unrecorded liability directly (a private set-off between the two), and any discount arises on that settlement, both are simply ignored in the firm's books — they never touched the Realisation Account at all.
