Retiring Partner / Deceased Partner's Estate — Liability for Firm's Debts

  • Debts due on the date of retirement/death: the retiring partner (or the deceased's estate) remains liable, to the extent of his share, for the whole of the debts due by the firm as on that date.
  • Debts incurred afterwards: if notice of retirement was not published as required by law, the retiring partner remains liable even for post-retirement debts.
  • A deceased or (already) insolvent partner's estate is never liable for debts contracted after that event.

Section 37 — if the amount due to a retired partner (or a deceased partner's executor) is left unsettled while the continuing partners keep carrying on the business with no final settlement, and the deed says nothing to the contrary, the outgoing party is entitled to the maximum of:

Interest @ 6% p.a. on the unsettled amount  OR  Profit × (Unsettled Dues ÷ Total Capital of the firm incl. the unsettled dues)

Example: C's unsettled capital ₹52,000 (retired 30.09.22); firm's net profit after retirement ₹25,000; other capitals A ₹57,000, B ₹76,000.
(i) Interest = 52,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,560.   (ii) Profit share = 25,000 × 52,000 / (52,000+57,000+76,000) = ₹7,027.
C is entitled to the higher of the two — ₹7,027.

Insolvency of a Partner — Garner vs. Murray

If a partner becomes insolvent and cannot pay the debit balance on his Capital A/c, that shortfall is a loss the solvent partners must bear. Before Garner vs. Murray, this was simply shared in the profit-sharing ratio, like an ordinary loss.

Justice Joyee held in Garner vs. Murray that a loss arising from a partner's insolvency must be distinguished from an ordinary (including realisation) loss. Unless otherwise agreed: (i) solvent partners must bring in cash equal to their own share of the realisation loss; and (ii) the solvent partners bear the insolvent partner's deficiency in the ratio of their Last Agreed Capitals — not the profit-sharing ratio.

Under fixed capital, the last-agreed capitals are simply the Balance Sheet capitals. Under fluctuating capital, they must first be adjusted for reserves, undrawn profit/loss, drawings, and undisclosed assets/liabilities (but not for realisation profit/loss) to arrive at the equivalent "last agreed capital." A partner with a nil or negative capital balance before dissolution bears none of the deficiency.

AspectOrdinary Realisation LossLoss from a Partner's Insolvency
Ratio usedProfit-sharing ratio (PSR)Last agreed Capital ratio (Garner vs. Murray)
Fixed vs. fluctuating capitalNo adjustment neededFluctuating capitals must first be adjusted for reserves/undrawn P&L/drawings (never for realisation profit/loss) before the ratio is struck
Partner with a debit Capital balanceStill shares the loss in PSRBears NONE of the other insolvent partner's deficiency (criticism of the rule, but this is the position)
Position in India—Sec. 48(b)(ii), Indian Partnership Act reaches the same result: available assets, after each solvent partner makes good his own share of the capital deficiency, are shared ratably in capital ratio — effectively identical to Garner vs. Murray unless the deed provides otherwise
Criticised for: (i) a solvent partner with a debit Capital balance bears nothing, however unfair; (ii) inapplicable with only two partners; (iii) a solvent partner with credit capital must still bring in cash for his OWN realisation-loss share, which can be pointless; (iv) a partner with large private wealth but small firm-capital ends up bearing LESS of the deficiency than one with more capital but fewer private assets.

If ALL Partners Are Insolvent — the Deficiency Account

Creditors here cannot be paid in full, so Sundry Creditors are not transferred to the Realisation Account. Cash in hand, sale proceeds of assets, and any surplus from partners' private estates (private assets exceeding private liabilities — a partner whose private liabilities exceed private assets contributes nothing at all), less expenses, are applied to the creditors. The unpaid balance of Creditors A/c is the firm's overall shortfall, transferred to a Deficiency Account; Capital A/c balances are also closed off to the same account.

(i) Creditors A/c Dr (total)  To Bank A/c (amount paid)  To Deficiency A/c (amount unpaid)

(ii) Deficiency A/c Dr  To Partners' Capital A/c — each insolvent partner's unrecoverable debit balance is written off through the Deficiency A/c, and the firm's total shortfall is finally shared amongst the outside liabilities in proportion to the amounts they were owed.

Return of Premium to a Partner on Dissolution Before Expiry of Term

Applies only when: (i) a partner was admitted for a fixed term; (ii) he paid a premium for goodwill on admission; (iii) the firm is dissolved before that term expires. No claim arises if: dissolution is due to that partner's own death; dissolution is due to his own misconduct; or the dissolution agreement contains no provision for any refund. The refund is borne by the other partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

Refund = Total Premium Paid × (Unexpired Term ÷ Total Term)

ILLUSTRATION 30: X admitted for 5 years (60 months), paid premium ₹1,20,000. Dissolved after 39 months — unexpired = 21 months. PSR Y:Z:X = 5:3:2.
Refund = 1,20,000 × 21/60 = ₹42,000, borne by Y and Z in 3:2 — Y's Capital A/c Dr ₹25,200, Z's Capital A/c Dr ₹16,800, To X's Capital A/c ₹42,000.

CONCEPT

Piecemeal Distribution ★★★ HIGH

So far the assumption was that all assets are realised, and all parties settled, on one date. In practice, dissolution assets are often realised gradually over time. Rather than wait for the final realisation to pay anyone, it can be agreed that different parties are paid, in order of preference, as and when cash comes in.

Order of Payment as Cash Is Realised:

(i) Realisation expenses → (ii) Provision for expenses yet to be incurred → (iii) Preferential creditors (Income Tax / Government dues) → (iv) Secured creditors — up to the amount realised from the asset securing them, balance (if any) ranks as unsecured → (v) Unsecured creditors — pro-rata if more than one → (vi) Partners' Loan — pro-rata if more than one partner has lent → (vii) Partners' Capital — by either the Surplus Capital (Highest Relative Capital) Method or the Maximum Loss Method.

Method 1 — Surplus Capital / Highest Relative Capital Method

Applicable only when all partners are solvent. Actual capital on the date of dissolution is compared with a notional "proportionate capital" (based on the minimum capital per unit of profit share) to find each partner's surplus. The partner(s) with surplus capital are paid FIRST; once capitals are proportionate to PSR, any further cash is shared in PSR — so a partner's final balance always equals his true share of realisation profit/loss with no later adjustment needed.

Step 1: Adjusted Capital = Capital balance ± undistributed profit/loss, reserves, drawings

Step 2: Base Capital = MINIMUM of (Adjusted Capital ÷ that partner's unit profit share), across all partners.

Step 3: Proportionate Capital = Base Capital × that partner's unit profit share

Step 4: Surplus Capital = Adjusted Capital − Proportionate Capital. Repeat the process among the partners still showing a surplus until an "absolute surplus" is isolated for the partner with the single highest relative capital — he is paid first.

Example — Computation of Surplus Capital (X, Y, Z; Capitals 35,000 / 33,000 / 18,000; Reserves split 5:3:2)

Method 2 — Maximum Loss Method

Maximum Loss = Total Amount Due to Partners − Cash Available for Distribution to Partners

Steps: (1) Prepare a statement showing distribution of cash. (2) Pay off external liabilities and partners' loans FIRST, in full, before touching capital. (3)–(4) At every instalment, assume NO further realisation will occur — compute the "maximum possible loss" on that assumption and charge it to all partners in PSR, as a notional debit against their capital, before paying anything. (5)–(6) If this notional charge exceeds a partner's capital, that partner's deficiency is reallocated to the other partners with positive balances, in their capital contribution ratio (Garner vs. Murray). (7) Repeat steps (3)–(6) at every instalment until final realisation.

AspectSurplus Capital / Highest Relative Capital MethodMaximum Loss Method
Core ideaFind each partner's capital IN EXCESS of what is proportionate to his PSR; pay the excess firstAt every instalment, assume the WORST CASE — nothing more will ever be realised — and charge that assumed loss in PSR before paying anyone
Ratio for the "extra" payoutSurplus paid in a sequence derived from capital differences, converging to PSRPSR used for the notional loss charge; any resulting DEFICIENCY of a partner is reallocated in CAPITAL ratio (Garner vs. Murray)
Number of computationsOne Highest-Relative-Capital working note calculated ONCE up front, then applied to every instalmentThe maximum-loss computation is repeated AT EVERY SINGLE INSTALMENT
Result if the final instalment matches the last assumed loss exactlyFinal balances already equal true realisation profit/loss shares — by designSame end result, reached via repeated worst-case charges instead of a single upfront ranking
Both methods must reach the IDENTICAL final answer for the total realisation loss borne by each partner — they are two different roads to the same destination, so a mismatch in a final answer signals an arithmetic slip, not a real difference in the methods.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PAYING PARTNERS' CAPITAL BEFORE A PARTNER'S LOAN

THE TRAP: once external creditors are cleared, students jump straight to distributing cash among partners' Capital Accounts.

THE TWIST: Sec. 48(2) inserts Partners' Loan (advances "as distinguished from capital") between creditors and capital. A loan from a partner ranks strictly ahead of that same partner's (or any partner's) capital — confirmed explicitly in the source: "repayment of loan should enjoy priority over repayment of capital."

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PSR INSTEAD OF CAPITAL RATIO FOR AN INSOLVENT PARTNER'S DEFICIENCY

THE TRAP: an insolvent partner's unrecoverable Capital A/c debit balance is shared among the solvent partners in their PROFIT-SHARING ratio, as if it were an ordinary realisation loss.

THE TWIST: Garner vs. Murray (and Sec. 48(b)(ii) of the Indian Partnership Act, which reaches the same result) requires this specific deficiency to be shared in the Last Agreed CAPITAL ratio — only the ordinary realisation profit/loss itself is shared in PSR. A partner already showing a debit Capital balance bears none of this deficiency at all.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING ONE MAXIMUM-LOSS INSTALMENT AS FINAL

THE TRAP: having computed the maximum possible loss and paid out one instalment, a student stops re-computing and simply distributes the next cash receipt in the final profit-sharing ratio.

THE TWIST: the maximum-loss assumption ("nothing more will ever be realised") must be re-applied FRESH at every single instalment, because the amount still unrealised keeps shrinking. Only once ALL assets are exhausted does the running "maximum loss" become the actual, final realisation loss.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DIVIDING SURPLUS CAPITAL IN PROFIT RATIO

THE TRAP: under the Highest Relative Capital method, once a partner's "surplus" is identified, students split it (or the next tranche) directly in the profit-sharing ratio.

THE TWIST: the base/proportionate capital calculation itself USES the profit-sharing ratio only as a divisor to find "capital per unit of profit share" — the actual surplus payouts are then made strictly by rank (highest relative capital paid first, in isolation, before the next-highest joins in), converging to the PSR split only at the very end, once every partner's capital has become exactly proportionate to his profit share.

CONCEPT

4.6 Amalgamation of Partnership Firms ★★★ HIGH

Amalgamation means two or more independent business entities join to run one combined business going forward. Whichever entities merge, every one of the merging entities' books is CLOSED — assets, liabilities and partners' capital are transferred out through a Realisation Account opened in each old entity's own books — and the new/absorbing entity opens fresh books, recording the assets and liabilities taken over at the AGREED (revalued) values, not at the old book values.

Four situations are tested, and the closing-the-old-books mechanics are identical across all four — only who is closing books, and what extra step (revaluation/goodwill of the CONTINUING firm) applies, changes:

Sit.Who MergesExtra Step Beyond Closing the Absorbed Entity's Books
(A)Two or more Sole Proprietors → new Partnership FirmNone — a brand-new firm opens fresh books at agreed values.
(B)Sole Proprietorship absorbed by an EXISTING FirmThe existing firm FIRST revalues its own assets/liabilities and adjusts its own goodwill, crediting its OLD partners in the OLD profit-sharing ratio, before recording the incoming proprietor's net assets.
(C)One Firm takes over Another FirmSame as (B) — the absorbing firm revalues/regoodwills itself first.
(D)Two or more Firms → a brand-new FirmNone — like (A), a fresh set of books opens; each old firm still closes via its own Realisation A/c.

(A) Closing the Books of an Amalgamating Sole Proprietor / Old Firm — the 18-Entry Pattern

Every merging entity's books close through this same sequence, entity by entity:

  1. Assets out: Realisation A/c Dr.  To Sundry Assets A/c (individually, at book values — Cash/Bank excluded if not taken over).
  2. Liabilities out: Liabilities A/c Dr.  To Realisation A/c (individually, at book values).
  3. PC recorded as due: New Firm/Purchasing Co. A/c Dr.  To Realisation A/c.
  4. Assets taken over by the proprietor personally: Capital A/c Dr.  To Realisation A/c.
  5. Assets not taken over, realised for cash: Bank A/c Dr.  To Realisation A/c.
  6. Unrecorded assets found → recorded (Assets A/c Dr. To Capital A/c), then realised (Bank A/c Dr. To Assets A/c) — or, if the new entity takes them over, routed through Realisation A/c like any other asset.
  7. Liabilities not taken over, paid off: Realisation A/c Dr.  To Bank A/c.
  8. Unrecorded liabilities → recorded (Capital A/c Dr. To Liabilities A/c), then paid (Liabilities A/c Dr. To Bank A/c).
  9. Liabilities taken over by the proprietor personally: Realisation A/c Dr.  To Capital A/c.
  10. Realisation expenses: Realisation A/c Dr.  To Bank A/c.
  11. Profit/Loss on Realisation (the balancing figure) → Partners' Capital A/cs, in the OLD profit-sharing ratio.
  12. Reserves/undrawn P&L → Reserves A/c & P&L A/c Dr.  To Capital A/c (reverse if a debit balance).
  13. PC settlement: Capital in New Firm A/c Dr.  To New Firm A/c.
  14. Final close: Capital A/c Dr.  To Capital in New Firm A/c  To Bank A/c (if any balancing cash movement remains).

In the New/Absorbing Entity's Books: Assets A/c [Acquired Value] + Goodwill A/c (if needed, balancing)  =  Liabilities A/c [Assumed Value] + Partners' Capital A/c [Purchase Consideration] + Capital Reserve A/c (if needed, balancing)

Net Assets Acquired = Purchase Consideration → no Goodwill, no Capital Reserve.
Net Assets Acquired < Purchase Consideration → the shortfall is Goodwill (debited).
Net Assets Acquired > Purchase Consideration → the excess is Capital Reserve (credited).

(B) An Existing Firm Absorbs a Sole Proprietorship

The absorbed proprietor's assets/liabilities are ADDED to the existing firm's own; the proprietor's capital in the new set-up equals the agreed Purchase Consideration; goodwill/Capital Reserve treatment mirrors situation (A). Additionally: (iv) before absorption, the EXISTING firm may revalue its own assets/liabilities — profit/loss on this revaluation is credited/debited to its OWN partners' Capital A/cs in their OLD profit-sharing ratio; (v) the existing firm's own goodwill (if raised) is credited to its partners in the OLD ratio; (vi) the existing firm's own Reserves & Surplus is likewise credited in the OLD ratio.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING EVERY AMALGAMATION ILLUSTRATION AS IDENTICAL

THE TRAP: assuming (a) goodwill is always raised on amalgamation, and (b) a partner's excess capital is always written off or refunded in cash.

THE TWIST: goodwill treatment is a TERM OF THE SCHEME — Illustration 40/41 raise goodwill (recorded, credited to old partners in old ratio); Illustration 42 explicitly says "goodwill is to be ignored," so W & Co.'s existing goodwill is simply written off through Realisation A/c, and none is raised for either firm. And a partner's credit balance in excess of his AGREED fixed capital in the new entity is settled in cash ONLY IF cash is available (as with C, paid ₹6,250) — if not, per Illustration 42, it becomes a LOAN from that partner to the new firm (as with B's ₹36,000), never a forced write-off.

CONCEPT

4.7 Conversion of a Partnership Firm into a Company and Sale of a Partnership Firm to a Company ★★★ HIGH

For various reasons, an existing partnership may sell its entire business to an existing Joint Stock Company (absorption by a company) or convert itself into a Joint Stock Company (flotation of a NEW company to take over the business). Either way, the firm is DISSOLVED and all its books are closed — the procedure is broadly the same as Amalgamation of Partnership.

  • The Purchase Consideration is satisfied by the company in cash, shares (equity or preference, at par or premium), debentures, or a combination of these. For the partnership, the ISSUE PRICE of the shares is what's relevant — that value forms part of the purchase consideration.
  • In the absence of any agreement, shares received from the purchasing company are distributed among the partners in the same ratio as they share profits and losses.

Purchase Consideration = Total Assets Taken Over (at agreed values) − Total Liabilities Taken Over (at agreed values)

Net Assets Taken Over < Purchase Consideration → difference is Goodwill (debited, balancing figure) in the purchasing company's books.
Net Assets Taken Over > Purchase Consideration → difference is Capital Reserve (credited, balancing figure).

Discharge in the selling firm's books: Shares in Purchasing Co. A/c + Debentures in Purchasing Co. A/c + Cash A/c  =  Purchasing Co. A/c (the amount receivable).
In the purchasing company's books: Purchasing Co.'s liability = Firm A/c  =  Share Capital A/c [face value] + Securities Premium A/c [if shares issued above face value] + Debentures A/c + Bank A/c.

Accounting Entries in the Books of the Selling Firm

Follow the SAME 14-step pattern as Situation (A) of Amalgamation (assets/liabilities out to Realisation A/c → PC due from "Purchasing Co. A/c" → realisation profit/loss → reserves/P&L to Capital → final close), with two points special to this topic:

  • Current Accounts close into Capital first: Partners' Current A/cs (credit balances) Dr.  To Partners' Capital A/cs — reversed if a Current A/c carries a debit balance — done BEFORE the final settlement, since only the Capital A/c is closed against the company's consideration.
  • Discharge of PC: Shares in Purchasing Co. A/c + Debentures in Purchasing Co. A/c + Cash A/c  Dr.  To Purchasing Co. A/c — then the shares/debentures/cash so received are distributed to close each partner's Capital A/c: Partners' Capital A/cs Dr.  To Shares in Purchasing Co. A/c  To Debentures in Purchasing Co. A/c  To Cash A/c.

ILLUSTRATION 45 — Suchandra, Ashmita & Kasturi Convert into TT (P) Ltd. (Goodwill by Super Profit Method)

Ashmita & Kasturi acquire interest in the new company in the ratio 3:2. PC is payable partly in shares, partly in cash to pay off Suchandra (who retires). Realisation expenses ₹1,17,300.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: FORGETTING SECURITIES PREMIUM ON THE SHARE COMPONENT OF PC

THE TRAP: valuing all shares received as part of PC at their FACE value, ignoring that PC is a fixed total amount to be split across cash/debentures/shares.

THE TWIST: in Illustration 44, total PC was ₹7,20,000; cash + debentures used up ₹5,40,000; the remaining ₹1,80,000 had to be covered by 12,000 shares of ₹10 face value — meaning each share was effectively issued at ₹15, not ₹10, giving the purchasing company a Securities Premium of ₹60,000 (12,000 × ₹5). Work the share value as a BALANCING figure of the total PC, never assume face value.

CONCEPT

4.8 Accounting of Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) ★★ MEDIUM

A Limited Liability Partnership is a specific form of business organisation consisting of partners whose liability is limited to the capital contribution made by them — a combination of both partnership and company, carrying the characteristics of both. Unlike a traditional partnership, an LLP partner's personal assets cannot be used to pay off the organisation's debts.

In India, LLPs are governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 (effective 1 April 2009) — the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does NOT apply to an LLP.

  • Nature: a body corporate formed/incorporated under a statute; has a legal entity SEPARATE from its partners; a change in partners does not affect the LLP's existence, rights or liabilities.
  • Features: any individual or body corporate may be a partner; minimum two partners; minimum two designated partners (individuals), at least one resident in India; the name must end in "Limited Liability Partnership" or "LLP."

Books of Account — Statutory Requirements (Sec. 34, LLP Act, 2008)

An LLP must maintain proper books of account relating to its affairs, on a cash or accrual basis, under the DOUBLE ENTRY system, at its registered office. Rule 24(1) requires the books to disclose, with reasonable accuracy at any time, the LLP's financial position, and to support the Statement of Account and Solvency. The books must contain:

  1. Particulars of all money received and expended, and the matters they relate to.
  2. A record of the LLP's assets and liabilities.
  3. Statements of goods purchased, inventories, work-in-progress, finished goods and cost of goods sold.
  4. Any other particulars the partners decide to include.

Rule 24(3): books of account must be preserved for EIGHT YEARS from the date they are made.

Statement of Account and Solvency

Within SIX MONTHS of the end of each financial year, every LLP must prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency, signed by its designated partners (Sec. 35). It must be filed in LLP Form 8 with the Registrar within THIRTY DAYS of the end of those six months. Under Sec. 36, this Statement (and the Annual Return) is open to public inspection on payment of the prescribed fee. Part B of Form 8 prescribes two statements:

  1. Statement of Assets and Liabilities.
  2. Statement of Income and Expenditure.

Non-compliance with Sec. 34: fine of ₹25,000 to ₹5,00,000 on the LLP, and ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 on every designated partner. Annual Return (Sec. 35): every LLP must file it within SIXTY DAYS of closure of its financial year — non-compliance carries the same fine slabs; a knowingly false statement in a return is punishable with imprisonment up to two years plus a fine of ₹1,00,000 to ₹5,00,000. Audit: the LLP's accounts must be audited per the prescribed rules; an auditor must be a Chartered Accountant in practice.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: MAPPING LLP FORMATS ONTO ORDINARY PARTNERSHIP FORMATS

THE TRAP: calling the partners' capital contribution a "Capital Account" and closing profit straight into it, as with an ordinary firm.

THE TWIST: the prescribed LLP formats keep "Contribution Received" (Partners' Funds) and "Reserves and Surplus" (which absorbs the year's profit/loss) as SEPARATE lines under Partners' Funds — profit for the year is shown as "Profit transferred to Reserves and Surplus," not merged into the Contribution figure. And the whole exercise runs off TWO prescribed statements (Assets & Liabilities; Income & Expenditure) filed in Form 8 — an LLP has no statutory requirement to prepare a Trading/P&L A/c and Balance Sheet in the traditional partnership format.

State True or False (from the source)

#StatementAnswer
1In absence of a partnership deed, profit or loss should be distributed among partners in their capital ratio.False
2In absence of a partnership deed, partners are entitled to interest on capital @ 6% p.a.False
3A new partner pays a premium for goodwill, shared by old partners in their new profit-sharing ratio.False
4Under the capitalisation-of-profits method, goodwill on future maintainable profits is more than goodwill on super profits.False
6After the death of a partner, the combined shares of the continuing partners decrease.False
8Loss on Realisation should be distributed according to capital ratio.False
9The surrender value of a Joint Life Policy is distributed among all partners in their old ratio upon retirement.True
10Adjustments are recorded in the Partner's Current Account under the Fixed Capital Method.True

Where a statement reads False, the correct rule is the opposite of what's stated — e.g. #1: profits/losses ARE shared EQUALLY (not in capital ratio) absent a deed; #3: premium is shared in the SACRIFICING ratio (not new ratio); #6: the continuing partners' combined share actually INCREASES on a partner's death.

20 EXAM FACTS — PARTNERSHIP ACCOUNTING (Module 4)

① In the absence of a Partnership Deed: profits/losses are shared EQUALLY, and NO interest is allowed on capital.

② Sacrificing Ratio (admission) = Old Profit-Sharing Ratio − New Profit-Sharing Ratio.

③ A new partner's premium for goodwill is credited to the OLD partners in their SACRIFICING ratio — not the new ratio, not equally.

④ At admission, existing General Reserve/accumulated profit is distributed to the OLD partners in the OLD ratio, before the new partner is admitted.

⑤ Gaining Ratio (retirement) is the ratio in which the continuing partners acquire the retiring/deceased partner's share of profit — used to adjust goodwill on exit, the mirror image of sacrificing ratio on entry.

⑥ On the death of a partner, the combined profit share of the CONTINUING partners INCREASES, not decreases.

⑦ The Joint Life Policy's surrender value is distributed among ALL partners in their OLD profit-sharing ratio on retirement/death, whether or not the policy is actually encashed.

⑧ The amount due to a deceased partner is payable to his/her EXECUTORS, credited via a Deceased Partner's Executor's A/c until settled.

⑨ A Realisation Account is opened ONLY at dissolution of the firm — a Revaluation Account is used instead at admission/retirement/death, where the firm continues.

⑩ Loss (or profit) on Realisation is always distributed in the PROFIT-SHARING ratio, never the capital ratio.

⑪ A Memorandum Revaluation Account is used when the BOOK VALUES of assets/liabilities are deliberately left unaltered but partners still need adjusting for a revaluation gain/loss.

⑫ The Surplus Capital Method (piecemeal distribution) applies only when ALL partners are solvent; where a partner may be insolvent, the Maximum Loss Method / Highest Relative Capital Method governs cash distribution instead.

⑬ Amalgamation (4.6): EVERY merging entity closes its OWN books through its OWN Realisation Account; the new/absorbing entity records assets and liabilities at AGREED (revalued) values, never at old book values.

⑭ When an EXISTING firm absorbs another business, it must FIRST revalue its own assets/liabilities and adjust its own goodwill — credited to its own partners in their OLD ratio — separately from the incoming entity's net-asset entry.

⑮ If a partner's credit balance exceeds the fixed capital agreed for the new/merged entity and there's no cash to pay the excess, it is carried forward as a LOAN from that partner — never written off or forced into capital.

⑯ Purchase Consideration = Total Assets taken over (agreed values) − Total Liabilities taken over (agreed values). PC > Net Assets → Goodwill; PC < Net Assets → Capital Reserve, in the purchasing entity's books.

⑰ When shares are part of the discharge of Purchase Consideration, their effective cost is the BALANCING figure of PC after cash/debentures — not automatically face value; any excess over face value is Securities Premium in the purchasing company's books.

⑱ In the absence of an agreement, shares received from a purchasing company are distributed among the selling firm's partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

⑲ The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does NOT apply to a Limited Liability Partnership — LLPs are governed solely by the LLP Act, 2008, and every LLP must file a Statement of Account and Solvency (Form 8, within 30 days of the close of six months from year-end) comprising a Statement of Assets & Liabilities and a Statement of Income & Expenditure.

⑳ An LLP's books of account must be preserved for EIGHT years (Rule 24(3)); its prescribed statements keep "Contribution Received" and "Reserves and Surplus" (which absorbs the year's profit) as separate lines — profit is never merged straight into the Contribution figure.

MODULE 4 CLOSING DRILL (retrieval practice — do not skip): put this document down and, on rough paper, write from memory: the sacrificing-ratio and gaining-ratio formulas, and which one applies at admission versus at retirement/death; how a JLP's surrender value is treated on retirement/death; the profit-till-death apportionment logic (time basis vs turnover basis, whichever the deceased partner's share is computed on); the Realisation Account format and the four-step order in which a dissolution closes (assets/liabilities transferred, assets realised/liabilities paid, expenses met, profit or loss split in the profit ratio); the difference between the Maximum Loss Method and the Highest Relative Capital Method for piecemeal distribution, and when Garner v. Murray-style capital-ratio deficiency-sharing applies versus when partners share an insolvent co-partner's deficiency in their OWN profit ratio; the four situations of Amalgamation and which one requires the absorbing entity to revalue itself first; the Purchase-Consideration formula for conversion/sale to a company and how the share component's effective cost is found as a balancing figure; and the LLP's two prescribed statements plus its filing deadlines (Form 8 in 30 days of the six-month mark; Annual Return in 60 days of year-end). Check every answer against the notes only after finishing — anything you could not retrieve cold, star it and redo it tomorrow morning. Given this is the largest and most heavily-weighted module (20%) in the paper, budget roughly ten minutes for this drill and do not compress it.

MODULE 5 OF 9 · SECTION E · SHARED 15% WEIGHT (MODULES 5–8) · ~16 PAGES

Lease
Accounting

Lease is an arrangement by which the lessor gives the right to use an asset for a certain period of time to the lessee on rent, in return for periodic rent payments — accounted for in India under Accounting Standard (AS) 19. The module covers the two lease types (Finance Lease and Operating Lease), the tests that classify a lease into one or the other, the accounting and disclosure of each in the books of both lessor and lessee, and Sale and Leaseback transactions.

MUST NOT SKIP: in a Finance Lease, the lessee recognises BOTH the leased asset AND a matching liability at the LOWER of (a) the asset's fair value at inception, or (b) the present value of minimum lease payments — after which every lease payment is split between a finance charge (a constant rate of return on the outstanding, reducing liability) and principal repayment.

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, per ICMAI's own SLOB mapping (equipping the student to determine surplus, ensure control on resources, evaluate divisional performance, or account for acquisition of assets through deferred payments), the student will be able to: identify the types of lease; gain detailed knowledge of the accounting and reporting of lease transactions as per AS 19; and gain knowledge of the comparative provisions under Ind AS.

Glossary — Module 5, in Plain Words

The technical terms used throughout this module, explained simply — all definitions per AS 19.

LeaseAn agreement whereby the lessor conveys to the lessee, in return for a payment or series of payments, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time.
LessorThe owner of the asset, who allows the lessee to use it for a specified period in return for periodic rent.
LesseeThe party who gets the right to use the asset for the lease period, in return for periodic rent payments.
Finance LeaseA lease that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards incident to ownership of an asset. Title may or may not eventually transfer.
Operating LeaseSimply "a lease other than a finance lease" — one that does NOT transfer substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership.
Lease TermThe non-cancellable period the lessee has agreed to take the asset on lease, plus any further option period the lessee is, at inception, reasonably certain to exercise.
Residual ValueThe estimated fair value of the leased asset at the end of the lease term.
Guaranteed Residual ValueThe part of the residual value guaranteed by the lessee (or a party on the lessee's behalf) — or, from the lessor's side, the part guaranteed by or on behalf of the lessee.
Unguaranteed Residual ValueThe difference between the asset's total residual value and its guaranteed residual value — the part nobody has promised to make good.
Fair ValueThe amount for which an asset could be exchanged (or a liability settled) between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm's-length transaction.
Minimum Lease Payments (MLP)For the lessee: total lease rent payable over the lease term + any guaranteed residual value. For the lessor: total lease rent receivable + any guaranteed residual value − contingent rent − service/tax costs reimbursable to the lessor.
Interest Rate Implicit in the LeaseThe rate at which the interest component inside the lessor's total receipts (principal + interest) is calculated — the discount rate that equates MLP + unguaranteed residual value to the asset's fair value plus the lessor's initial direct costs.
Gross InvestmentMinimum lease payments (from the lessor's standpoint) + any unguaranteed residual value accruing to the lessor.
Unearned Finance IncomeGross Investment in the lease MINUS the present value of (i) MLP under a finance lease, from the lessor's standpoint, and (ii) any unguaranteed residual value accruing to the lessor — both discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease.
Net Investment in the LeaseGross Investment minus Unearned Finance Income — the figure the lessor actually recognises as a receivable.
Incremental Borrowing RateThe rate of interest the lessee would pay on a similar lease or, if not determinable, the rate the lessee would incur at inception to borrow, over a similar term and security, the funds to purchase the asset.
Contingent RentThe portion of lease payments not fixed in amount, but based on a factor other than the mere passage of time — e.g. a percentage of sales, amount of usage, or a price index.
Sale and LeasebackA transaction where an asset's owner sells it, then immediately leases the same asset back from the buyer — the sale price and lease terms are usually negotiated together as one package.

CONCEPT

Lease Accounting — Meaning and Scope of AS 19 ★★ MEDIUM

A lease involves two parties — a lessor and a lessee — and an asset to be leased. The lessor, who owns the asset, agrees to let the lessee use it for a specified period in return for periodic rent payments. Lease transactions derive their accounting complexity from the number of alternatives available to the parties: a lease can be structured for tax benefit, to transfer ownership of the leased asset, or to transfer the risk of ownership. In India, accounting for leases is covered under Accounting Standard (AS) 19 — Leases.

Objective of AS 19: to prescribe the appropriate accounting policies and disclosures in relation to finance leases and operating leases, for both lessees and lessors.

Applicability — AS 19 applies to accounting for ALL leases, EXCEPT:

  • (a) lease agreements to explore for or use natural resources, such as oil, gas, timber, metals and other mineral rights;
  • (b) licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights; and
  • (c) lease agreements to use lands.

Key Definitions

Residual value of a leased asset is the estimated fair value of the asset at the end of the lease term. Economic life is either the period over which an asset is expected to be economically usable by one or more users, or the number of production/similar units expected to be obtained from it by one or more users. Useful life of a leased asset is either the period over which the leased asset is expected to be used BY THE LESSEE, or the number of production/similar units expected to be obtained from the lessee's use of it.

Minimum Lease Payments (Lessee) = Total lease rent payable over the lease term + any guaranteed residual value (by/on behalf of the lessee).

Minimum Lease Payments (Lessor) = Total lease rent receivable over the lease term + any guaranteed residual value (by/on behalf of the lessee) − contingent rent − cost for services and tax to be paid by, and reimbursed to, the lessor.

Gross Investment = Minimum Lease Payments (lessor's standpoint) + any unguaranteed residual value accruing to the lessor.

Unearned Finance Income = Gross Investment − Present Value of [MLP (lessor) + unguaranteed residual value], both at the interest rate implicit in the lease.

Net Investment in the Lease = Gross Investment − Unearned Finance Income.

CONCEPT

Classification of Leases — Finance Lease vs Operating Lease ★★★ HIGH

Classification is based on the extent to which the RISKS and REWARDS incident to ownership of a leased asset lie with the lessor or the lessee. Risks include the possibilities of losses from idle capacity or technological obsolescence, and of variations in return due to changing economic conditions. Rewards may be represented by the expectation of profitable operation over the asset's economic life, and of gain from appreciation in value or realisation of residual value.

Whether a lease is a finance lease or an operating lease depends on the SUBSTANCE of the transaction rather than its FORM.

Finance LeaseOperating Lease
Transfers substantially all the risks and rewards incident to ownership of the asset. Title may or may not eventually be transferred.Simply defined as "a lease other than a finance lease" — does NOT transfer substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership.
Lessee recognises BOTH the leased asset AND a lease liability, at the lower of fair value or PV of minimum lease payments.Lessee recognises NEITHER an asset NOR a liability — only a periodic rent expense.
Lessee charges depreciation on the leased asset, per AS-10.Lessor (who retains the asset) charges depreciation, per AS-10.
Each lease payment is apportioned between a finance charge (P&L) and a principal repayment (reduces the liability).The entire lease payment is charged to the P&L as rent, ordinarily on a straight-line basis over the lease term.
Substance of the transaction is that the lessor effectively SELLS the asset to the lessee — lessor recognises a receivable (net investment), not the asset itself.Lessor keeps the asset as a fixed asset on its own Balance Sheet and recognises rent as income, ordinarily straight-line.
Lessor recognises finance income as a constant periodic return on the net investment outstanding.Lessor's other operating-lease costs are recognised in the year incurred; initial direct cost may be expensed immediately or deferred.

The Classification Tests

A lease is a Finance Lease if ANY ONE of the following situations is present at inception:

  1. the lease transfers ownership of the asset to the lessee by the end of the lease term;
  2. the lessee has an option to purchase the asset at a price expected to be sufficiently lower than its fair value at the date the option becomes exercisable, such that, at inception, it is reasonably certain the option will be exercised (a "bargain purchase option");
  3. the lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset, even if title is not transferred;
  4. at inception, the present value of the minimum lease payments amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the leased asset; and
  5. the leased asset is of a specialised nature such that only the lessee can use it without major modifications.

Indicators of situations that could ALSO lead to a finance-lease classification (supporting evidence, not stand-alone tests):

  • if the lessee can cancel the lease, the lessor's cancellation losses are borne by the lessee;
  • gains or losses from fluctuation in the fair value of the residual fall to the lessee (e.g. a rent rebate equalling most of the sale proceeds at the end of the lease); and
  • the lessee can continue the lease for a secondary period at a rent substantially lower than market rent.

When classification is (and is not) revisited: classification is made ONLY at the inception of the lease. If the lessee and lessor later agree to change the lease's provisions, other than by renewing it, in a way that would have produced a DIFFERENT classification had those terms applied from the start, the revised agreement is treated as a NEW lease over its revised term. However, changes in ESTIMATES (e.g. of the asset's economic life or residual value) or changes in CIRCUMSTANCES (e.g. default by the lessee) do NOT give rise to a new classification for accounting purposes.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: MISCLASSIFYING A LEASE BY LOOKING AT TITLE ALONE, OR DEMANDING ALL FIVE TESTS

THE TRAP: a student sees no ownership-transfer clause and calls the lease "operating"; or a student thinks ALL FIVE situations (a)–(e) must be satisfied together before a lease counts as a finance lease.

THE TWIST: classification runs on substance, not legal form — ANY ONE of the five situations is sufficient on its own to make it a Finance Lease. A lease with no title-transfer clause can still be a finance lease purely because the PV of minimum lease payments is substantially all of fair value (the test most often used in the source's own illustrations), or because the lease term covers the major part of the asset's economic life.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: RECLASSIFYING A LEASE MID-TERM FOR THE WRONG REASON

THE TRAP: a change in the estimated USEFUL LIFE of the asset, or the lessee DEFAULTING on payments, is treated as a reason to reclassify the lease.

THE TWIST: AS 19 reclassifies a lease only when lessor and lessee mutually agree to change its PROVISIONS (other than a renewal) in a way that would have altered the original classification — treated then as a brand-new lease over the revised term. Mere changes in ESTIMATES or CIRCUMSTANCES never trigger reclassification.

CONCEPT

Accounting for a Finance Lease — In the Books of the Lessee ★★★ HIGH

Legally, ownership of the leased asset remains with the lessor — but since the risks and rewards of the asset stand transferred to the lessee, the SUBSTANCE of the transaction is that the lessee becomes the owner, and the transactions are recorded by substance, not by legal form.

Leased asset AND lease liability are BOTH recognised, at the LOWER of:

(a) the fair value of the leased asset at the inception of the lease; OR
(b) the present value of the minimum lease payments.

  • Apportionment of lease payment: each lease payment is split between finance charge and principal amount. The principal amount reduces the outstanding liability; the finance charge is allocated over the lease term so as to produce a CONSTANT rate of return on the REMAINING (reducing) principal balance.
  • Depreciation: the lessee charges depreciation on the finance-lease asset as per AS-10, exactly as for an owned asset.
  • Initial direct cost: for a finance lease, initial direct cost is included in the cost of the asset under lease.

Disclosure by the Lessee (Finance Lease)

In addition to the requirements of AS 10, Property, Plant & Equipment, the lessee discloses:

  • (a) assets acquired under finance lease, segregated from owned assets;
  • (b) for each class of asset, the net carrying amount at the Balance Sheet date;
  • (c) a reconciliation between the total of minimum lease payments at the Balance Sheet date and their present value, split into: not later than 1 year; later than 1 year and not later than 5 years; later than 5 years;
  • (d) contingent rents recognised as expense in the Statement of Profit & Loss for the period;
  • (e) the total of future minimum SUBLEASE payments expected to be received under non-cancellable subleases at the Balance Sheet date; and
  • (f) a general description of the lessee's significant leasing arrangements — including the basis for contingent rent, the existence/terms of renewal or purchase options and escalation clauses, and restrictions imposed by lease arrangements (e.g. on dividends, additional debt, further leasing).

A Small and Medium Sized Company (as defined in the Notification) need not comply with sub-paragraphs (c), (e) and (f).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: APPLYING THE INTEREST RATE TO THE ORIGINAL PRINCIPAL EVERY YEAR

THE TRAP: a student applies 14.97% to the original ₹14,85,590 in EVERY year of Illustration 4, instead of to the reducing balance — overstating every year's finance charge after Year 1.

THE TWIST: the finance charge is a constant RATE of return applied to the OUTSTANDING (reducing) liability, recomputed every year — exactly like a reducing-balance loan. The RATE stays 14.97% throughout, but the ₹ finance charge keeps falling (₹2,22,393 → ₹1,80,835 → ₹1,33,056 → ₹78,125) precisely because the balance it's applied to keeps shrinking.

CONCEPT

Accounting for a Finance Lease — In the Books of the Lessor ★★ MEDIUM

The substance of a finance lease is that the lessor SELLS the leased asset to the lessee. The lessor therefore recognises the asset given under finance lease as a RECEIVABLE at an amount equal to the Net Investment in the lease, with a corresponding credit to "Sale of Asset."

Net Investment = Gross Investment − Unearned Finance Income

Gross Investment = Minimum Lease Payment (lessor's standpoint) + Unguaranteed Residual Value

Unearned Finance Income = Gross Investment − Present Value of Gross Investment

Recognition of Finance Income: the lessor recognises finance income based on a pattern reflecting a CONSTANT periodic return on the net investment outstanding — i.e. interest/finance income is recognised in proportion to the outstanding balance receivable from the lease over the lease period.

Disclosure by the Lessor (Finance Lease)

  • (a) a reconciliation between total gross investment in the lease at the Balance Sheet date, and the present value of MLP receivable at that date, split into: not later than 1 year; later than 1 year and not later than 5 years; later than 5 years;
  • (b) unearned finance income;
  • (c) the unguaranteed residual values accruing to the benefit of the lessor;
  • (d) the accumulated provision for uncollectible MLP receivable;
  • (e) contingent rents recognised in the Statement of Profit & Loss for the period;
  • (f) a general description of the lessor's significant leasing arrangements; and
  • (g) the accounting policy adopted for initial direct costs.

A Small and Medium Sized Company (as defined in the Notification) need not comply with sub-paragraphs (a) and (f).

CONCEPT

Operating Lease — Accounting Treatment ★★ MEDIUM

An operating lease is a lease other than a finance lease.

In the Books of the Lessor:

  • records the leased-out asset as its own fixed asset in the Balance Sheet;
  • charges depreciation as per AS-10;
  • recognises lease income in the Profit & Loss Account using the STRAIGHT-LINE method — unless another method more systematically reflects the earning pattern derived from the diminishing value of the leased-out asset;
  • recognises other operating-lease costs in the year they are incurred; and
  • may expense initial direct cost of the lease immediately, or defer it.

In the Books of the Lessee: lease payments are recognised as an expense in the Profit & Loss Account on a STRAIGHT-LINE basis over the lease term — unless another method is more representative of the time pattern of the lessee's benefit.

Disclosure by the Lessee (Operating Lease)

  • (a) total future MLP under non-cancellable operating leases, split into: not later than 1 year; later than 1 year and not later than 5 years; later than 5 years;
  • (b) total future minimum SUBLEASE payments expected to be received under non-cancellable subleases at the Balance Sheet date;
  • (c) lease payments recognised in the Statement of Profit & Loss for the period, with minimum lease payments and contingent rents shown separately;
  • (d) sub-lease payments received (or receivable) recognised in the Statement of Profit & Loss for the period; and
  • (e) a general description of the lessee's significant leasing arrangements — the basis for contingent rent, renewal/purchase options and escalation clauses, and restrictions imposed by lease arrangements.

A Small and Medium Sized Company (as defined in the Notification) need not comply with sub-paragraphs (a), (b) and (e).

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Operating Lease: Uneven Rentals Spread on a Straight-Line Basis (Arun Ltd.)

Arun Ltd. has taken an equipment on operating lease for 5 years. Per the agreement, NO payment is due for the first 2 years; ₹21,00,000 is payable in EACH of the following 3 years. Advise Arun Ltd. on accounting for the lease rentals.

As per AS-19, lease payments under an operating lease are recognised as an expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit. The pattern of payment here does NOT follow a straight-line basis — it arises towards the end of the lease period — so this effect must be neutralised for accounting purposes: the total payment of ₹63,00,000 in the last 3 years (₹21,00,000 × 3) is spread over the ENTIRE lease period of 5 years.

Answer: ₹63,00,000 ÷ 5 years = ₹12,60,000 charged to the Profit & Loss Account as lease rent expense in EACH of the 5 years, regardless of the actual cash payment pattern.

CONCEPT

Sale and Leaseback Transactions ★★ MEDIUM

A sale and leaseback transaction involves the sale of an asset by the vendor, and the leasing of that same asset back to the vendor. The lease payments and the sale price are usually interdependent, as they are negotiated together as a package.

The accounting treatment depends on the TYPE of lease the leaseback results in.

Leaseback results in a FINANCE LEASE:

Any excess or deficiency of sale proceeds over the carrying amount is NOT recognised immediately as income or loss — it is DEFERRED and amortised over the lease term, in proportion to the depreciation of the leased asset. (No exceptions, unless there has been an impairment in value — the carrying amount is then reduced to recoverable amount per the impairment Accounting Standard.)

Leaseback results in an OPERATING LEASE:

If the transaction is established at fair value, any profit or loss is recognised IMMEDIATELY. If the sale price is BELOW fair value, profit/loss is recognised immediately EXCEPT where the loss is compensated by future lease payments at below-market price — then it is deferred and amortised in proportion to those lease payments. If the sale price is ABOVE fair value, the excess over fair value is deferred and amortised over the period the asset is expected to be used. Separately: if fair value at the time of the transaction is LESS than the asset's carrying amount, a loss equal to that difference is recognised immediately.

ILLUSTRATION 3 — Sale and Leaseback Resulting in an Operating Lease (PQ Ltd. / BR Ltd.)

PQ Ltd. sold machinery with WDV of ₹80 lakhs to BR Ltd. for ₹100 lakhs, and the same machinery was leased back by BR Ltd. to PQ Ltd. as an OPERATING lease. Comment on the treatment under each scenario below.

CaseFair Value (₹ lakhs)Sale Price (₹ lakhs)Treatment (WDV = ₹80 lakhs)
(a)100100 (= fair value)Profit of ₹20 lakhs (100−80) recognised IMMEDIATELY.
(b)120100Profit of ₹20 lakhs still recognised IMMEDIATELY.
(c)9076Loss of ₹4 lakhs (80−76) recognised IMMEDIATELY — UNLESS the loss is compensated by future lease payments, in which case it is deferred and amortised.
(d)80 (= carrying amount)100Profit of ₹20 lakhs is DEFERRED and amortised over the lease period.
(e)92100Profit of ₹12 lakhs (92−80) recognised IMMEDIATELY; balance profit of ₹8 lakhs (100−92) DEFERRED/amortised over the lease period.
(f)7078Loss of ₹10 lakhs (80−70) recognised IMMEDIATELY; profit of ₹8 lakhs (78−70) DEFERRED/amortised over the lease period.
EXAM TRICK: the split point is always the CARRYING AMOUNT vs FAIR VALUE. The slice of profit up to (Fair Value − Carrying Amount) is recognised NOW; only the slice above Fair Value gets deferred and amortised.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING ALL SALE-AND-LEASEBACK PROFIT/LOSS THE SAME WAY

THE TRAP: a student assumes ANY profit on a sale-and-leaseback must be deferred, or ANY loss recognised immediately, regardless of which lease type the leaseback results in.

THE TWIST: a FINANCE-lease leaseback ALWAYS defers profit/loss (amortised in proportion to depreciation) — no exceptions bar impairment. An OPERATING-lease leaseback instead runs on the fair-value test in Illustration 3 above: at/above fair value → immediate; below fair value → immediate UNLESS the shortfall is compensated by future below-market rentals, in which case it is deferred.

Applying the Classification Test — Two Worked Illustrations

Both illustrations below use the SAME method: find the present value of the lease payments (and any unguaranteed residual value), compare that to fair value, and — if it is "substantially all" of fair value — classify the lease as a Finance Lease before computing the unearned finance income.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — Classification Test + Unearned Finance Income (Vishnu Ltd. / Garur Ltd.)

Vishnu Ltd. leased a printing machine from Garur Ltd. for 3 years (useful life of the machine: 5 years); Garur Ltd. takes the machine back at lease termination. Cost of the machine = ₹15,00,000; Unguaranteed residual value at lease end = ₹2,00,000; Fair value = ₹15,00,000; IRR = 10%. Given: PVF10%,3 = 0.7513; PVAF10%,3 = 2.4868. Required: (a) is this a finance or operating lease? (b) the unearned finance income.

(a) PV of unguaranteed residual value = 2,00,000 × 0.7513 = ₹1,50,260. PV of lease payments = 15,00,000 − 1,50,260 = ₹13,49,740, i.e. 90% (approx.) of fair value. As the PV of lease payments makes a substantial portion of fair value, this is a FINANCE lease.

(b) Annual lease payment = PV of lease payments ÷ PVAF = 13,49,740 ÷ 2.4868 = ₹5,42,762 (approx.). Gross investment = (5,42,762 × 3) + 2,00,000 = ₹18,28,286.

Answer: Unearned finance income = Gross investment − Cost of machine = 18,28,286 − 15,00,000 = ₹3,28,286.

ILLUSTRATION 6 — Classification Test + Unearned Finance Income (VHR Ltd. / Alpha Ltd.)

VHR Ltd. leased equipment from Alpha Ltd. for 3 years from the beginning of 2021; equipment cost = fair value = ₹6,00,000; useful life = 5 years; property reverts to the lessor at lease termination; unguaranteed residual value = ₹75,000 at end of 2023; IRR = 10%. Given: PVF10%,3 = 0.7513; PVAF10%,3 = 2.4868. Required: (i) state, with reason, whether this is a finance lease; (ii) the unearned finance income.

(i) PV of residual value = 75,000 × 0.7513 = ₹56,348. PV of lease payments = 6,00,000 − 56,348 = ₹5,43,652. Annual payment = 5,43,652 ÷ 2.4868 = ₹2,18,615. PV of lease payments (₹5,43,652) equals 90.60% of fair value (₹6,00,000) — a substantial portion of fair value — so it constitutes a FINANCE lease.

(ii) Gross investment = (3 × 2,18,615) + 75,000 = ₹7,30,845. Cost of leased property = ₹6,00,000.

Answer: Unearned finance income = 7,30,845 − 6,00,000 = ₹1,30,845.

10 EXAM FACTS — LEASE ACCOUNTING (Module 5)

① AS 19 governs lease accounting in India; it excludes natural-resource exploration/use leases, film/patent/manuscript licensing agreements, and land leases.

② A Finance Lease transfers substantially all risks & rewards of ownership (title may or may not transfer); an Operating Lease is any lease that is NOT a finance lease.

③ Classification is decided ONLY at inception. A later change in ESTIMATES (economic life, residual value) or CIRCUMSTANCES (lessee default) never triggers reclassification — only a mutually-agreed change in provisions (other than renewal) that would have altered the original classification does.

④ Five situations classify a lease as Finance Lease — ownership transfer at term-end, bargain purchase option, lease term = major part of economic life, PV of MLP ≈ substantially all of fair value, or a specialised asset usable only by the lessee — ANY ONE is sufficient.

⑤ Lessee recognises the leased asset AND a matching liability at the LOWER of fair value at inception or PV of minimum lease payments; each payment then splits into finance charge (constant rate on the reducing liability) and principal repayment.

⑥ The lessee depreciates a finance-leased asset under AS-10 — exactly as if it were owned outright.

⑦ The lessor recognises the finance-leased asset as a RECEIVABLE at Net Investment = Gross Investment − Unearned Finance Income, and books finance income as a constant periodic return on the outstanding net investment — never depreciates the asset itself.

⑧ Under an Operating Lease: lessor keeps the asset (depreciates it per AS-10) and recognises rent income straight-line; lessee expenses rent straight-line — neither side puts an asset/liability on the lessee's Balance Sheet.

⑨ Sale-and-leaseback resulting in a Finance Lease: profit/loss on sale is ALWAYS deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to depreciation — no exceptions bar impairment.

⑩ Sale-and-leaseback resulting in an Operating Lease: recognition follows the fair-value test — at/above fair value, recognise now; below fair value, recognise now UNLESS the shortfall is compensated by future below-market rentals, in which case defer.

MODULE 5 CLOSING DRILL (retrieval practice — do not skip): put this document down and, on rough paper, write from memory: the five situations (a)–(e) that classify a lease as a Finance Lease and the three supporting indicators; the lower-of rule for initial recognition in the lessee's books, plus how a constant-rate finance charge is applied to a REDUCING balance; the Gross Investment → Unearned Finance Income → Net Investment formula chain from the lessor's side; the straight-line treatment of an Operating Lease on both sides; and the full sale-and-leaseback rule (finance lease → always defer; operating lease at/above fair value → recognise now; operating lease below fair value → recognise now unless compensated by future rent). Branch (including Foreign Branch)
and Departmental Accounts

A Branch is an extended location of an organisation, other than its head office, conducting business similar or related to the organisation's own — not a separate legal entity, and completely dependent on the head office for its operations, administration and (usually) its accounts. A Department, by contrast, is a segment into which a single entity's own operations are rationally split for better responsibility accounting and performance evaluation. This module covers the accounting methods for domestic dependent branches (Debtors System, Stock and Debtors System, Final Accounts Method), the fuller books kept by an independent branch and their incorporation into the H.O.'s own accounts, translation of a foreign branch's trial balance into home currency, and the columnar preparation of Departmental Final Accounts.

MUST NOT SKIP: whenever goods move at a built-in profit margin — Invoice Price at a branch, or inter-departmental transfer price between departments — that margin ("loading") sitting inside EVERY stock figure (opening stock, goods sent, goods returned, closing stock) must be stripped out through a Stock Reserve / Branch Adjustment entry before the true Gross Profit can be measured; forgetting just one of those four loading entries is the single most common numerical slip this module tests.

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, per ICMAI's own SLOB mapping (equipping the student with a detailed understanding of accounting for certain special transactions to determine surplus, ensure control on resources, evaluate divisional performance, or account for acquisition of assets through deferred payments), the student will be able to: do the accounting of domestic branches; understand the accounting of foreign branches; and gain the knowledge required for preparation of a Departmental Income Statement.

Glossary — Branch Accounting, in Plain Words

The technical terms used throughout Branch Accounting, explained simply.

BranchAn extended location of an organisation, other than its head office, conducting business similar or related to the organisation's own. Not a separate legal entity — fully controlled by, and dependent on, its H.O.
Domestic BranchA branch opened and operated in the same country where the organisation is registered and has its head office. Example from the source: State Bank of India's branches all over India.
Foreign BranchA branch opened and operated in a country OTHER than the country of its H.O. Example from the source: the Dubai branch of State Bank of India. Always independent — never dependent.
Dependent BranchA branch completely dependent on its H.O. for operation, administration, AND maintenance of its accounts — the H.O. keeps the branch's books.
Independent BranchA branch that maintains its own complete set of books, purchases and sells independently, and prepares its own Trial Balance, Trading & P&L Account and Balance Sheet at year-end.
Debtors Method / Synthetic MethodH.O. maintains one Branch Account per branch, treating the branch as a "debtor." A nominal account by nature — it ascertains only the branch's Net Profit/Loss, in one shot.
Stock and Debtors Method / Analytical MethodH.O. maintains separate Branch Stock A/c, Branch Debtors A/c and Branch Adjustment A/c, giving BOTH Gross Profit (via the Adjustment A/c) and Net Profit (via the Branch P&L A/c) in full detail.
Final Accounts MethodA Branch Trading & P&L Account plus a separate (personal-nature) Branch Account are prepared — applicable to every branch, goods-dealing or service-dealing.
Goods at CostGoods sent by H.O. to branch valued at the price H.O. itself paid — no loading to cancel.
Goods at Invoice Price (I.P.)Goods sent by H.O. to branch marked up above cost, so that the branch (and any thief) cannot see the true margin. The built-in margin must be cancelled to find true profit.
Loading / LoadThe margin sitting inside the Invoice Price (I.P. minus Cost). Must be cancelled out of opening stock, goods sent, goods returned AND closing stock before true profit is known.
Stock ReserveThe account that cancels the load hiding inside branch stock (opening or closing) valued at Invoice Price — shown in the H.O. Balance Sheet as a deduction from branch stock.
Branch Adjustment AccountThe Stock and Debtors Method's engine account — collects all the loading entries and reveals the branch's Gross Profit/Loss as its balancing figure.
Wholesale PriceSame as Invoice Price — the price at which H.O. sends goods to its branch. Wholesale Profit = Wholesale Price less Cost.
Retail Price / List PriceThe price at which goods are finally sold to the customer, by H.O. or by branch. Retail Profit = Retail Price less Cost (for H.O.) or Retail Price less Wholesale Price (for branch).
Goods-in-Transit / Cash-in-TransitGoods dispatched/cash remitted by one side but not yet received by the other as at the balance sheet date — the reconciling items between the H.O.'s Branch A/c balance and the branch's own H.O. A/c balance.
Incorporation of Branch Trial BalanceThe process by which H.O. merges an independent branch's own year-end Trial Balance into its own books, to prepare one consolidated Balance Sheet.
Net Investment MethodA foreign-branch translation method: every Trial Balance item EXCEPT the H.O. Account is converted at the CLOSING rate; the H.O. Account is carried at the figure at which the Branch Account already appears in the H.O.'s own books.
Current and Non-current MethodA foreign-branch translation method: current assets/liabilities are converted at the CLOSING rate; fixed assets and long-term liabilities are converted at HISTORICAL rates.
Difference in ExchangeThe balancing figure that makes a translated foreign-branch Trial Balance tally, arising because different items are translated at different rates — taken to the Branch P&L Account.
Branch Petty Cash (Imprest System)A fixed float H.O. sends the branch at the start of a period; the branch spends out of it, and H.O. reimburses only the amount spent, restoring the original balance.

CONCEPT

6.1 Branch Accounting — Meaning and Classification of Branches ★★★ HIGH

A branch is an extended location of an organisation, other than its head office, where businesses of similar or related nature to the organisation are conducted. A branch is NOT a separate legal entity, but rather an extended unit of the organisation — completely dependent on its head office for its operation and decision-making.

Organisations open branches to offer visibility and brand exposure that positively influences profits (profit-making organisations), or to satisfy a large number of stakeholders' needs by increasing outreach (non-profit organisations, e.g. charitable institutions).

Classification by geographical area of operation:

  • Domestic Branch — opened and operated in the same country as the H.O. Example: State Bank of India's branches all over India.
  • Foreign Branch — opened and operated in a country OTHER than the H.O.'s country. Example: the Dubai branch of State Bank of India.

A domestic branch is further classified by level of control:

  • Dependent Branch — completely dependent on H.O. for operation, administration and maintenance of its accounts. For a dependent branch, accounting is done BY THE H.O.
  • Independent Branch — maintains its own complete set of books. For an independent branch, accounting is done AT THE BRANCH ITSELF.

Branch accounting rests on the Responsibility Accounting system — a branch acts as a "Revenue Centre" in addition to being a "Cost Centre." At the end of each financial period it ascertains the financial result (profit or loss) of each branch. Common branch transactions: goods sent by H.O. (and returns), assets sent by H.O., cash remitted by H.O. for branch expenses, sales effected by the branch, branch proceeds sent to H.O., and goods sent by H.O. either at cost price or at invoice price.

Methods of Branch Accounting for a Dependent Branch

Recording takes place at the branch, but maintenance of accounts is done by the H.O. A dependent branch follows any ONE of four methods:

  1. Debtors Method / Synthetic Method — one Branch Account per branch, treated as a "Debtor."
  2. Stock-Debtors Method / Analytical Method — Branch Stock, Branch Debtors and Branch Adjustment Accounts kept in full detail.
  3. Final Accounts Method (Cost Basis) — a Branch Trading & P&L A/c plus a separate Branch Account.
  4. Final Accounts Method (on Wholesale Price Basis) — used where BOTH H.O. and branch sell to customers, and both contribute to organisational profit.

Debtors Method or Synthetic Method ★★★ HIGH

H.O. maintains a separate Branch Account for each branch, which appears as a "Debtor" in the H.O.'s books — giving H.O. the right to claim the money arising from the branch's operations after meeting its expenses. Primarily used for dependent branches that are generally small in scale and size. Also called the Synthetic Method.

  • Two ledger accounts are maintained: Branch Account and Goods Sent to Branch Account.
  • In the Branch Account, only transactions BETWEEN the H.O. and branch are recorded.
  • The Branch Account is, by nature, a nominal account which ascertains the branch's Net Profit or Loss.
  • Goods sent at "Cost" are accounted at cost price; goods sent at "Invoice Price" are accounted at invoice price, and the load thereon must be cancelled to find the true result.

Journal Entries under the Debtors Method

The source splits these into entries common to either cost or invoice price, and additional entries needed only when goods move at Invoice Price (to cancel the loading).

Transactions which do NOT appear in the Branch Account (because their effect is already absorbed into an adjusted closing figure): (a) branch expenses paid out of branch cash — reduces closing cash/increases closing liabilities; (b) purchase of goods/fixed assets by branch — increases closing book value; (c) sale of goods/fixed assets by branch — decreases closing book value; (d) bad debts, discount allowed, sales returns, cash received from branch debtors — closing debtors appear at the adjusted figure; (e) depreciation and profit/loss on sale of fixed assets — closing fixed assets appear at the adjusted figure; (f) abnormal losses — closing stock appears at the adjusted figure.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DEBTORS/CREDITORS-SIDE ITEMS SNEAKING INTO THE BRANCH ACCOUNT

THE TRAP: a candidate sees "Bad Debts ₹2,000," "Discount Allowed," or "Returns Inwards" listed among the given data and posts them as separate lines inside the Branch Account (as in Illustration 3 above).

THE TWIST: the source is explicit — bad debts, discount allowed and sales returns by customers never appear in the Branch Account, because the CLOSING DEBTORS figure given in the question is already net of them. Posting them separately double-counts the adjustment and unbalances the account.

Stock-Debtors Method or Analytical Method ★★★ HIGH

The two primary branch assets — Stock and Debtors — are accounted for in full detail through separate accounts, hence "Analytical Method." Ledger accounts maintained: Branch Stock A/c, Branch Debtors A/c, Goods Sent to Branch A/c, Branch Adjustment A/c, Branch Cash A/c, Branch Expenses A/c, Branch Profit & Loss A/c, and Branch Fixed Assets A/c. The Branch Adjustment Account reflects the branch's Gross Profit/Loss — so this method determines BOTH Gross Profit/Loss and Net Profit/Loss. Adopted by branches with large-scale operations needing detailed recording.

Debtors System vs Stock and Debtors System

BasisDebtors Method (Synthetic)Stock and Debtors Method (Analytical)
Ledger accountsBranch A/c + Goods Sent to Branch A/c onlyBranch Stock A/c, Branch Debtors A/c, Branch Adjustment A/c, Goods Sent to Branch A/c, Branch Cash A/c, Branch Expenses A/c, Branch P&L A/c, Branch Fixed Assets A/c
Nature of Branch A/cNominal account — ascertains Net Profit/Loss onlyBranch Stock A/c (Real), Branch Debtors A/c (Personal); Branch Adjustment A/c reveals Gross Profit/Loss
Profit ascertainedNet Profit/Loss only, in one stepBOTH Gross Profit/Loss (via Branch Adjustment A/c) AND Net Profit/Loss (via Branch P&L A/c)
SuitabilitySmall branches, fewer transactionsLarge-scale branches needing detailed control over stock & debtors

Loading (as a fraction of Invoice Price) = (Invoice Price − Cost Price) ÷ Invoice Price

If goods are invoiced at "Cost plus X%," then IP = 100 + X (taking CP = 100), and Loading÷IP = X ÷ (100 + X). Applied consistently in the source to opening stock, goods sent, goods returned, abnormal/normal loss AND closing stock — every one of these four-to-five figures carries the SAME fraction.

Excess Contribution to Gross Profit (when credit sales are at List Price but stock is carried at Invoice Price) = Credit Sales × (List Price − Invoice Price) ÷ List Price

Final Accounts Method ★★ MEDIUM

Applicable for EVERY branch, whether dealing in goods or in services. A Branch Trading & P&L Account AND a separate Branch Account (a personal account, following double entry) are prepared and maintained. The Branch Trading & P&L Account determines BOTH Gross Profit/Loss and Net Profit/Loss.

Final Accounts Method (on Wholesale Price Basis) ★★ MEDIUM

Adopted where BOTH H.O. and Branch sell goods to customers, so both contribute to the organisation's total profit; H.O. gets due credit for profit arising both on "Goods sent to Branch" and on goods it sells itself.

  • At Cost: the price at which H.O. purchased the goods.
  • At Retail Price (List/Catalogue Price): the value at which H.O. and Branch sell to customers. H.O.'s Retail Profit = Retail Price − Cost. Branch's Retail Profit = Retail Price − Wholesale Price.
  • At Wholesale Price (= Invoice Price): the price at which H.O. sends goods to Branch. H.O.'s Wholesale Profit = Wholesale Price − Cost.

Goods sent to BranchAt Wholesale Price

Goods lost abnormallyAt Cost
Closing stock of goodsAt Cost

Opening stock of goodsAt Wholesale Price

Goods-in-transitAt Wholesale Price
Sales by Branch to customersAt Wholesale Price basis / Retail Price to customer
Goods lost abnormallyAt Wholesale Price
Closing stock of goodsAt Wholesale Price

Branch Petty Cash under Imprest System

  • H.O. allows branches to maintain petty cash for small expenses, reimbursed by H.O. from time to time.
  • The Imprest balance is determined by H.O. and sent to the branch at the start of the period.
  • Branch petty expenses are incurred out of this Imprest balance.
  • This ensures the ORIGINAL Imprest balance of Branch Petty Cash is always maintained (H.O. reimburses exactly what was spent).
CONCEPT

Accounting for Independent Branch ★★★ HIGH

Where a branch has voluminous transactions, it prepares its accounts independently — purchasing and selling on its own, as well as selling goods sent by H.O. As the branch is owned by H.O., its profit or loss ultimately belongs to H.O. An independent branch maintains a complete set of books, and prepares its own Trial Balance, Trading & P&L Account and Balance Sheet at year-end. The branch maintains a Head Office Account; H.O., in turn, maintains a Branch Account. All remittances of cash, transfers of goods, etc. pass through these two accounts.

When H.O. receives the branch's accounts, it incorporates the branch's profit as: Branch A/c Dr.  To Profit & Loss A/c. Sometimes the balance of Branch A/c (in H.O. books) and H.O. A/c (in branch books) do not agree — the difference must be adjusted via Goods-in-Transit or Cash-in-Transit. Finally, the Branch Balance Sheet is amalgamated with the H.O. Balance Sheet, eliminating inter-branch/H.O. balances under the respective heads of assets and liabilities.

At branch level, all transactions are recorded in the branch's own Cash Book, Subsidiary Books, ledger accounts and Trial Balance. At H.O., transactions between branch and H.O. are also recorded in H.O.'s own books, which maintain a separate "Goods Sent to Branch Account" and "Branch Account" for each independent branch.

CONCEPT

Incorporation of Branch Trial Balance in H.O. Books ★★★ HIGH

An independent branch prepares its own Trial Balance and sends it to H.O. H.O. incorporates the branch's accounts with its own to ascertain the net financial result of the whole concern. Two methods exist.

(a) First Method: all revenue items pass through a Branch Trading and P&L Account, and the resulting profit/loss (together with branch assets and liabilities) passes through the Branch Account, to prepare a consolidated Balance Sheet.

ItemEntry
(a) Revenue expenses related to Trading A/c (Opening stock, Purchase, Returns Inwards, Wages, etc.)Branch Trading A/c Dr.  To Branch A/c
(b) Revenue incomes related to Trading A/c (Sales, Closing Stock, Returns Outwards, etc.)Branch A/c Dr.  To Branch Trading A/c
(c) Gross Profit of the branchBranch Trading A/c Dr.  To Branch P&L A/c  (reverse if gross loss)
(d) Revenue expenses related to P&L A/cBranch P&L A/c Dr.  To Branch (all revenue expenses) A/c
(e) Revenue incomes related to P&L A/cBranch (all revenue incomes) A/c Dr.  To Branch P&L A/c
(f) Net Profit of the branchBranch P&L A/c Dr.  To General P&L A/c  (reverse if net loss)
(g) Branch assetsBranch Asset A/c Dr.  To Branch A/c
(h) Branch liabilitiesBranch A/c Dr.  To Branch Liabilities A/c

(b) Second Method / Abridged Method: used when only net profit/loss is given (not detailed revenue items). Only net profit/loss is transferred to Branch Account; branch assets and liabilities do NOT separately appear, and the Branch Account shows a balance equal to net worth (Assets minus Liabilities) of the branch.

Closing of Branch Books ★★ MEDIUM

The branch closes its own accounts at year-end through two methods.

Method 1 — all revenue items pass through H.O. Account:

CONCEPT

Foreign Branch ★★★ HIGH

A foreign branch is opened and operated in a country other than the country where the organisation is registered and has its head office. Example: the Dubai branch of State Bank of India.

A foreign branch maintains its own books of accounts and drafts its Trial Balance in FOREIGN currency, sending it to H.O. The H.O. converts every item of the Trial Balance into its own domestic currency, and thereafter drafts the final accounts.

Method 1 — Net Investment Method: ALL items of the Trial Balance EXCEPT the H.O. Account are converted at the CLOSING rate.

The H.O. Account is represented at the figure at which the Branch Account already appears in the H.O.'s own books — subject to adjustment for goods-in-transit and cash-in-transit.

Method 2 — Current and Non-current Method: different rates apply to current items and to fixed/long-term items.

Current assets and current liabilities → CLOSING rate. Fixed assets and long-term liabilities → HISTORICAL rates (the rate ruling when the asset was acquired / the liability was created).

Domestic Branch vs Foreign Branch

Point of DifferenceDomestic BranchForeign Branch
LocationEstablished and carried out in the SAME country as its H.O.Always established and carried out in a country OTHER than the H.O.'s country
NatureCan be EITHER dependent or independentALWAYS independent
CurrencyH.O. and Branch both follow the SAME currency for recording transactions and preparing accountsTransactions and accounting for foreign branches happen in a DIFFERENT currency from H.O., requiring translation
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ONE RATE FOR EVERYTHING WHEN TRANSLATING A FOREIGN BRANCH TRIAL BALANCE

THE TRAP: a candidate applies the CLOSING rate to every single line of the foreign branch's Trial Balance — opening stock, sales, fixed assets, everything — because it's the "current" rate given for the year-end.

THE TWIST: the source's own worked illustration uses DIFFERENT rates for different items: Opening Stock at the OPENING rate; revenue items (Sales, Salaries, Taxes & Insurance, Rent) at the AVERAGE rate; monetary Balance Sheet items (Cash, Bank, Expenses Outstanding, Debtors) at the CLOSING rate; Fixed Assets at the HISTORICAL rate ruling on the date of acquisition (which may be neither the opening nor closing rate for the CURRENT year); and the H.O. Account plus "Goods from H.O." at the FIGURE ALREADY RECORDED in the H.O.'s own books (not re-translated at all). The resulting Dr./Cr. mismatch in the translated Trial Balance is the balancing "Difference in Exchange," carried to the Branch P&L Account as an expense (or income, if the branch gains on translation).
