⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING AN INDEPENDENT (OR FOREIGN) BRANCH LIKE A DEPENDENT ONE

THE TRAP: a candidate opens a Branch Stock A/c / Branch Adjustment A/c or writes Debtors-Method journal entries for every micro-transaction of an independent (or, since a foreign branch is ALWAYS independent, a foreign) branch — exactly as done for a dependent branch under the Debtors or Stock-Debtors System.

THE TWIST: an independent branch keeps its OWN complete set of books and passes its OWN entries through a Head Office Account, ending the year with its OWN Trial Balance. H.O. never records the branch's day-to-day transactions at all — it only INCORPORATES the branch's Trial Balance (First Method or Abridged Method) once, at year-end, into a Branch Account. Applying Debtors-Method-style entries to an independent branch either double-records transactions or produces a Branch Account that will never reconcile with the branch's own Head Office Account.

CONCEPT

6.2 Departmental Accounting ★★★ HIGH

For effective operation, efficient management and adequate control, many large organisations dealing in various products, services or specialised activities treat each product/service/activity as a separate segment or unit — technically referred to as a Department.

IndustryIllustrative Departments
BankForex, Underwriting, Credit Card
HospitalsRooms, Medical Store, Cafeteria
HotelsRooms, Restaurants, Confectionery, Gym and Spa
Departmental StoreStationery, Electronics, Grocery
AutomobileTwo-wheelers: Motorcycles, Scooters

Management wants to evaluate the operating results (profit/loss) of each department separately. On the basis of Responsibility Accounting, the idea of Departmental Accounting has emerged and been widely implemented.

The branch of accounting that gives emphasis on the assessment of the financial performance of each department of a large organisation is referred to as Departmental Accounting.

Responsibility Accounting: for better performance and control, responsibility and authority are decentralised to each department. A manager/supervisor is assigned to each department, to whom targets and budgets are provided for carrying out operations. Although all departments are "Cost Centres," all may not be "Revenue Centres." At the end of a period, the performance of each Department/Centre is assessed and suitable measures are taken for betterment.

Branch vs Department

Point of DifferenceDepartmentBranch
ConceptA segment or unit into which an entity is rationally divided.An establishment of a large organisation, located at different places.
PurposeEnhancement of effective operations, efficient management and adequate control.Primary objective is to boost up sales.
LocationGenerally, Departments are not separated by location.Each branch is set up at a different geographical location.
InterrelationA department can never have a branch on its own.A branch may consist of numerous departments.

Features and Objectives of Departmental Accounting

Features:

  • Transactions are recorded department-wise; all expenses and incomes are recognised separately for each department.
  • It is an application of the Responsibility Accounting system — each department is a Responsibility Centre.
  • Both external as well as internal transactions are recorded.
  • It involves the drafting of a Departmental Trading & Profit & Loss Account.

Objectives:

  • To get an analytical idea about the affairs of each department.
  • To ascertain the true operating result and efficiency of each department (department profit/loss).
  • To compare the financial performance among different departments.
  • To provide data and information to management for decision-making and policy-formulation.

Methods of Maintaining Departmental Accounts

An organisation follows either ONE of two approaches for obtaining individual figures of expenses and incomes department-wise.

BasisColumnar / Tabular MethodUnitary Method
MeaningSame set of books maintained, with items gathered in a tabular/columnar format.Separate set of books maintained independently by each department.
Who maintains recordsA centralised Accounting Department maintains the entire records.Each department maintains its own records independently.
Cost / AdoptionComparatively less expensive — widely accepted.Very expensive — usually practised only by large-sized firms.

Glossary Additions — Departmental Accounting Terms, in Plain Words

DepartmentA segment or unit into which ONE entity's own operations are rationally divided (e.g. Stationery vs Electronics within one departmental store). Never a separate location — a department can never have a branch of its own.
Cost Centre / Revenue CentreEvery department is a Cost Centre (it incurs costs); not every department is also a Revenue Centre (earns revenue directly) — both labels feed into Responsibility Accounting.
Columnar (Tabular) MethodOne centralised set of books, with a separate column per department — cheaper, and the most widely used approach.
Unitary MethodEach department keeps its own completely separate books — expensive, used mainly by large firms.
Departmental Trading AccountColumnar account debiting direct expenses and crediting direct incomes of each department, to find each department's Gross Profit/Loss.
Departmental Profit & Loss AccountColumnar account debiting allocable indirect expenses and crediting allocable indirect incomes, after Gross Profit/Loss, to find each department's Net Profit/Loss.
General Profit & Loss AccountA normal (non-columnar) account debiting/crediting expenses and incomes that CANNOT be rationally apportioned to any department, after departmental Net Profits/Losses, to find the entity's Overall Net Profit/Loss.
Common / Joint (Indirect) ExpensesExpenses shared by more than one department (rent, wages, depreciation, etc.) that must be apportioned on a suitable basis rather than debited wholesale to one department.
Basis of ApportionmentThe rational yardstick (floor area, number of employees, sales, purchases, etc.) used to split a common expense or income fairly across departments.
Inter-Departmental TransferGoods/services moving from one department to another — treated as "Sales" of the sending department and "Purchases" of the receiving department.
Transferor / Transferee DepartmentTransferor = the department sending the goods/services (books it as a sale/transfer-out). Transferee = the department receiving them (books it as a purchase/transfer-in).
Loading (on Transfer)The profit margin built into an inter-departmental transfer price when goods move above cost — must be reversed out of any transferred stock still unsold at period end.
Provision for Unrealised ProfitThe adjustment (via the General P&L A/c) that removes the transferor's booked-but-not-yet-earned profit sitting inside a transferee department's unsold closing stock.
Stock Reserve (Departmental)The account that carries the unrealised profit adjustment forward — created on closing stock, reversed on the following year's opening stock.

Components of Departmental Final Accounts

  • Departmental Trading Account — columnar format, one column per department. Direct expenses are debited and direct incomes credited, to ascertain Departmental Gross Profit/Loss.
  • Departmental Profit & Loss Account — columnar format, one column per department. Indirect expenses are debited and allocated indirect incomes credited, after considering Gross Profit/Loss, to ascertain Departmental Net Profit/Loss.
  • General Profit & Loss Account — NOT columnar (like a normal income statement). Indirect expenses/incomes that cannot be rationally apportioned between departments are debited/credited, after considering departmental Net Profits/Losses, to ascertain the Overall Net Profit/Loss of the entity.
Format — Departmental Trading & Profit & Loss Account for the year ended…

Steps for Preparation of Departmental Final Accounts

Step I — Determination of Departmental Gross Profit/Loss:

ItemTreatment
Directly allocable Direct ExpensesDebited to Departmental Trading A/c
Direct Expenses that cannot be directly allocatedApportion on a suitable basis and debit to Departmental Trading A/c
Directly allocable Direct IncomesCredited to Departmental Trading A/c
Goods transferred from one department to anotherDebited to Transferee (Receiving) Department; credited to Transferor (Sending) Department

Departmental Gross Profit/Loss is then transferred to the Departmental Profit & Loss A/c.

Step II — Determination of Departmental Net Profit/Loss:

ItemTreatment
Directly allocable Indirect ExpensesDebited to Departmental Profit & Loss A/c
Indirect Expenses that cannot be directly allocatedApportion on a suitable basis and debit to Departmental Profit & Loss A/c
Directly allocable Indirect IncomesCredited to Departmental Profit & Loss A/c
Indirect Incomes that cannot be directly allocatedApportion on a suitable basis and credit to Departmental Profit & Loss A/c

Departmental Net Profit/Loss is then transferred to the General Profit & Loss A/c.

Step III — Determination of Overall Net Profit/Loss of the concern:

ItemTreatment
Indirect Expenses that could not be allocated to departmentsDebited to General Profit & Loss A/c
Indirect Incomes that could not be allocated to departmentsCredited to General Profit & Loss A/c
Provision for Unrealised Profit (if any)On Closing Inventory — debited to General P&L A/c. On Opening Inventory — credited to General P&L A/c.

By balancing the General Profit & Loss A/c, the Consolidated (Overall) Net Profit/Loss is ascertained.

Apportionment of Common (Joint) Expenses and Incomes ★★★ HIGH

Incomes/expenses directly allocable to a specific department are credited/debited to that department. Incomes/expenses common to more than one department must instead be apportioned rationally across all the departments they relate to — on the basis the source pairs with each item below. This item-to-basis mapping is the single most exam-tested idea in this sub-topic.

Item Common to More Than One DepartmentBasis of Apportionment
Discount ReceivedNet Purchases (Purchases less Returns Outward, if any)
Sales CommissionNet Sales (Sales less Returns Inward, if any)
Commission to Purchase Manager; Carriage InwardsPurchases
Selling Expenses; Commission to Salesman; Bad Debts; Discount AllowedSales
Depreciation, Insurance, Repairs & Maintenance (on assets)Value of Assets*
Rent and Rates, Insurance, Heating (of premises)Floor Area Occupied
PowerHorse Power (HP), or HP × Hours Worked
Other indirect incomes/expenses that are purely FINANCIAL or GENERAL in nature — Dividend Received, Interest Earned on Deposits, Profit on Sale of Fixed Assets (income side); General Charges, Sundry Charges, MD's Remuneration, Miscellaneous Expenses, Bank Charges, Interest on Loan/Debentures (expense side) — relate to the organisation AS A WHOLE and are NEVER apportioned; they go straight to the General P&L A/c.

*Confirmed by the source's own Illustration 14 working notes — Depreciation on Furniture is split 2:2:1, exactly matching the furniture value ratio ₹40,000 : ₹40,000 : ₹20,000 across the three departments.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SWAPPING APPORTIONMENT BASES

THE TRAP: a candidate apportions Rent on the Sales ratio (because Sales is the "default" ratio used for most items), or apportions Carriage Inwards on the Sales ratio instead of Purchases, or Wages on Sales instead of Number of Employees.

THE TWIST: each item has its OWN natural driver — Rent/Rates/Insurance/Heating follow FLOOR AREA (a space-related cost); Wages/Employee Welfare follow NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES (a headcount-related cost); Carriage Inwards/Purchase Manager's Commission/Discount Received follow PURCHASES (a buying-side cost); Selling Expenses/Discount Allowed/Sales Commission/Bad Debts follow SALES (a selling-side cost). Using the wrong driver silently misallocates Gross/Net Profit between departments while the OVERALL total still tallies — making the error invisible unless each department's figure is checked individually.

CONCEPT

Inter-Departmental Transfer ★★★ HIGH

When goods/services are transferred from one department (Transferor Department) to another (Transferee Department), it is known as Inter-Departmental Transfer. Such transfers are treated as "Sales" of the Transferor Department and "Purchases" of the Transferee Department.

Valuation of the transfer can be done on any one of three bases:

BasisDescriptionProvision for Unrealised Profit?
At CostTransferor transfers goods/services to Transferee at "Cost to the Transferor Department."NOT required, even if part of the transferred goods remains in the Transferee's closing inventory.
At Cost Plus ProfitTransferor transfers at a value higher than cost. Departments that produce/render intermediate goods/services usually follow this, so the Transferor gets due credit (profit-booking).Required, if part of the transferred goods remains in the Transferee's closing inventory.
At Normal Selling PriceTransferor transfers at the prevailing Normal Selling Price / Market Price. Departments producing marketable goods/services usually follow this — but the Transferor's actual profit-earning capacity stays undisclosed to stakeholders.Required, if part of the transferred goods remains in the Transferee's closing inventory.
Only "At Cost" needs NO unrealised-profit adjustment. Both other bases ALWAYS need one, whenever any transferred stock is still unsold at the period end.

Provision for Unrealised Profit

Based on Responsibility Accounting, departments are often treated as "Profit Centres," so goods are transferred at a value higher than cost. After receiving the goods, the Transferee Department processes and eventually sells/transfers them onward. At period end, part of the Transferee's closing inventory may still consist of goods received from the Transferor — unsold, although the Transferor has already booked profit on them. This gives rise to Unrealised Profit.

Unrealised Profit is the profit booked (but not earned) by the transferor department out of inter-departmental transfers. Although due credit is given to the Transferor Department and reflected in its profit, this profit cannot be considered earned/realised by the entity as a whole, since it is not yet earned from a sale outside the entity.

As per the Concept of Prudence, unrealised profit must be adjusted. A "Provision for Unrealised Profit" is maintained both on the closing stock AND on the following period's opening stock. It must be noted that such Provision is required on goods received at higher than cost from ALL predecessor departments in the chain — not only the immediately preceding one.

Unrealised Profit in Stock = Value of transferred goods remaining unsold × GP Rate of the TRANSFEROR Department

GP Rate of Transferor = (Gross Profit ÷ (Sales + Transfer)) × 100 — always the rate of the department that SENT the goods, never the rate of the department currently holding them.

Net Stock Reserve (charged to General P&L A/c) = Unrealised Profit on Closing Stock − Unrealised Profit on Opening Stock (using the PRIOR year's GP rate)

Accounting of Transfer:

Transferee Department A/c      Dr.xx
    To Transferor Department A/cxx

(On transfer of goods/services between departments)

General Profit & Loss A/c      Dr.xx
    To Provision for Unrealised Profit A/cxx

(Creation of Provision for Unrealised Profit on Closing Stock)

Provision for Unrealised Profit A/c      Dr.xx
    To General Profit & Loss A/cxx

(Reversal of the prior Provision on Opening Stock, in the subsequent period)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: FORGETTING THE OPENING-STOCK REVERSAL, OR A PREDECESSOR DEPARTMENT

THE TRAP: a candidate creates the Provision for Unrealised Profit only on this year's closing stock and stops there — or, in a multi-department transfer chain, adjusts only for the department that transferred LAST, ignoring an earlier department further back in the chain.

THE TWIST: the Provision must ALSO be reversed on the opening stock (last year's closing stock, using last year's GP rate) — as Illustration 15 shows, the ₹1,380 charged to the General P&L A/c is a NET figure (this year's ₹2,880 less last year's ₹1,500), not the gross ₹2,880. And it is required on goods received at a loaded price from ALL predecessor departments in the chain, not just the one immediately before the department holding the stock.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: VALUING UNREALISED PROFIT AT THE WRONG DEPARTMENT'S RATE

THE TRAP: when valuing the unrealised profit sitting inside Department X's closing stock, a candidate applies Department X's OWN Gross Profit rate (25%) — the rate that is immediately at hand while working through X's own account.

THE TWIST: Illustration 17 shows the goods sitting in X's closing stock were sent BY Y — so the profit margin baked into them is Y's margin (35%), not X's. The rule is always: value unrealised profit using the TRANSFEROR's (sending department's) GP rate, never the rate of the department currently holding the stock. Get the rates crossed and both departments' figures come out wrong, even though the overall Gross Profit may look approximately right.

Managerial Commission and Unrealised Profit — the Correct Sequence ★★ MEDIUM

Commission on profit BEFORE charging such commission = Profit AFTER commission × [Rate ÷ (100 − Rate)]

Used to "add back" an already-charged commission and recover the profit figure before commission. The same rate is then reapplied to the CORRECTED profit (after removing unrealised profit) to find the final commission payable. A stated minimum guaranteed commission is payable even where the department shows a loss.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SKIPPING THE MINIMUM COMMISSION, OR RECOMPUTING IT TOO EARLY

THE TRAP: a candidate assumes a loss-making department (Spares, above) pays NO managerial commission at all — or recomputes the final commission on the ORIGINAL (uncorrected) profit figures, before removing unrealised profit.

THE TWIST: a stated minimum guaranteed commission is payable REGARDLESS of loss or inadequate profit — Spares' manager still gets ₹3,000. And the sequence matters: (1) add back the commission already charged, to find profit BEFORE remuneration; (2) eliminate unrealised profit, charged always to the TRANSFEROR department; (3) ONLY THEN recompute the final commission, on the corrected profit. Recomputing commission before step (2) both overstates the commission expense and understates the correction needed for unrealised profit.

15 EXAM FACTS — BRANCH & DEPARTMENTAL ACCOUNTS (Module 6)

① Debtors (Synthetic) Method: one Branch Account per branch, kept at COST price — branch Net Profit/Loss emerges as the balancing figure on the Branch Account itself.

② Stock and Debtors (Analytical) Method: THREE core accounts — Branch Stock A/c (at Invoice Price), Branch Debtors A/c, Branch Adjustment A/c — the load built into Invoice Price is stripped out via the Adjustment A/c to reveal true (cost-price) Gross Profit.

③ Loading on Opening Stock and on Goods Sent to Branch is credited to the Stock/Branch Adjustment A/c; loading on Closing Stock, on Returns to H.O., and on any Stock Shortage is debited out (reversed).

④ Normal stock loss needs no separate accounting entry; Abnormal loss (fire, theft) is valued at cost, removed from stock, and its Invoice-Price loading is reversed too.

⑤ An Independent Branch keeps its own full set of books and passes its own entries through a Head Office Account; a Dependent Branch's accounts are maintained entirely by the H.O. (Debtors, Stock-Debtors or Final Accounts Method).

⑥ Translating a foreign branch's Trial Balance uses DIFFERENT rates for different items (never one flat rate): Opening Stock/Fixed Assets typically at opening/historical rates, revenue items at the average rate, year-end monetary items at the closing rate, and the H.O. Account/Goods-from-H.O. at the figure already on H.O.'s own books — the resulting mismatch is the "Difference in Exchange," taken to the Branch P&L A/c.

⑦ Department = an internal segment of ONE entity; Branch = a separate location. A department can never have a branch of its own, but a branch can house many departments.

⑧ Two ways to keep departmental accounts: the Columnar/Tabular Method (one set of books, department-wise columns — cheap, widely used) and the Unitary Method (fully separate books per department — expensive, used by large firms).

⑨ Three-tier build-up: Departmental Trading A/c (direct items → Departmental Gross Profit) → Departmental P&L A/c (allocable indirect items → Departmental Net Profit) → General P&L A/c (non-apportionable items common to the whole entity → Overall Net Profit).

⑩ Apportionment bases to memorise: Floor Area → Rent/Rates/Insurance/Heating; Number of Employees → Wages/Staff Welfare; Sales → Selling Expenses/Discount Allowed/Bad Debts/Sales Commission; Purchases → Carriage Inwards/Discount Received/Purchase Manager's Commission; HP (or HP×Hours) → Power; Value of Assets → Depreciation.

⑪ Purely financial/entity-wide items (Dividend Received, Interest on Deposits, Profit on Sale of Fixed Assets, Bank Charges, Interest on Loans, MD's Remuneration, General/Sundry Charges) are NEVER apportioned — straight to the General P&L A/c.

⑫ Inter-departmental transfer pricing: At Cost needs NO unrealised-profit adjustment; At Cost-Plus-Profit and At Normal Selling Price both DO, on any transferred stock left unsold at period end.

⑬ Provision for Unrealised Profit is created on closing stock (debit General P&L) and reversed on the following year's opening stock (credit General P&L) — required on goods received at a loaded price from ALL predecessor departments in a chain, not just the one immediately before.

⑭ The unrealised-profit GP rate is always the TRANSFEROR's (sending department's) rate — never the rate of the department currently holding the stock.

⑮ Company's overall Gross Profit = sum of departmental Gross Profits − unrealised profit in unsold inter-departmental stock; any minimum-guaranteed managerial commission is recomputed only AFTER unrealised profit has been eliminated.

Insurance Claim for
Loss of Stock and Loss of Profit

Fire insurance normally covers two connected but separate risks: the value of stock physically destroyed, and the Gross Profit the business fails to earn (plus any extra cost incurred to keep trading) while operations remain disrupted. Both claims are built the same way — reconstruct what SHOULD have happened using last year's own ratios, compare it with what ACTUALLY happened, and apply the Average Clause if the cover taken was less than the value at risk.

MUST NOT SKIP: the Average Clause formula — Net Claim = Actual Loss × (Sum Insured / Value of Stock or Insurable Value at the date of loss) — applies only when the policy amount is LESS than the value at risk, and is applied ONCE to the whole claim, never separately to its components.

7.1–7.2

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: determine the amount of insurance claim for loss of stock; and ascertain the amount of insurance claim for loss of profit.

Glossary — Module 7, in Plain Words

The technical terms used throughout this module, explained simply.

Loss of StockThe value of stock (goods) physically destroyed or damaged by fire/accident — claimed under a fire policy on stock.
Loss of Profit / Consequential LossThe Gross Profit the business fails to earn, plus any increased cost of working incurred to keep trading, because normal operations were disrupted by the accident — claimed under a separate "Loss of Profit" or "Consequential Loss" policy.
Sum Insured / Policy ValueThe amount for which the insurance cover is taken — compared against the actual value at risk to test whether the Average Clause bites.
Average ClauseThe insurer's protection against under-insurance: if the Sum Insured is less than the value at risk, the insurer pays only a proportionate part of the loss, and the insured bears the rest.
Under-insuranceTaking a Sum Insured that is LESS than the value of stock (or the Insurable Value, for Loss of Profit) at the date of the loss — triggers the Average Clause.
Standing / Fixed ChargesUnavoidable expenses that continue to be paid even when sales fall because of the disruption (e.g. rent, salaries) — distinguished from charges that vary with sales.
Short SalesThe turnover the business failed to make during the disruption — Standard Turnover minus Actual Turnover for the Indemnity Period.
Indemnity PeriodThe period for which the normal activities of the business remain interrupted as a result of the damage.
Gross Profit (for insurance purposes)Net Profit for the previous accounting period plus Insured Standing Charges (or, where the business made a net loss, Insured Standing Charges reduced by a proportionate share of that loss).
Annual TurnoverTurnover during the 12 months immediately preceding the date of the damage, adjusted for any upward/downward trend — used to compute the Insurable Value.
Standard TurnoverThe turnover of the corresponding period in the previous year (i.e. matching the Indemnity Period), also adjusted for trend — the benchmark against which Short Sales is measured.

Both spokes converge on one shared idea, shown at the base: the Average Clause — a single proportionate reduction, applied once, whenever the cover taken is less than the value at risk.

CONCEPT

7.1 Insurance Claim for Loss of Stock ★★★ HIGH

During operations, accidents (fire being the most common) may damage the physical assets of a business — fixed assets and stock. To recover part or whole of such losses, a business takes a fire insurance policy. On a loss, the business computes the loss and files a claim; the insurer appoints a loss assessor to investigate before the claim is met. A fire policy usually covers two types of loss: (1) Loss of Stock, and (2) Loss of Profit. As stock forms a large part of working capital — especially for a trading concern — Loss of Stock cover is the more commonly tested claim.

The amount of claim depends on three factors: the value of stock present at the time of the accident; the value of stock salvaged; and the contents of the insurance policy (policy value, average clause).

Step 1 — Estimating the Value of Stock at the Date of Fire

When stock records are themselves destroyed, an up-to-date stock value is not available. It is then estimated by drafting a Memorandum Trading Account — a statement (not a ledger account) prepared in the proforma of a Trading Account, running from the first day of the accounting period in which the accident occurred, up to the date of the accident.

Memorandum Trading A/c for the period April 1 of year of accident — Date of Accident

Dr.: To Opening Stock (***) · To Purchases (***) · To Gross Profit [Sales × GP rate] (***)
Cr.: By Sales (***) · By Closing Stock (***) — the BALANCING FIGURE, i.e. the estimated stock at the date of fire.

Gross Profit here is NOT a balancing figure taken on faith — it is estimated by multiplying the period's Sales by the rate of Gross Profit (GP). The GP rate is normally the LAST accounting period's own GP rate, found by preparing a regular Trading A/c for the year immediately preceding the accident.

Adjustments before applying last year's GP rate: the Trading Accounts of both the current (stub) period and the preceding year may need adjustment for slow-moving items, abnormal/defective items not fetching the normal GP rate, goods distributed as samples, goods taken by the proprietor, over/under-valuation of stock, and omitted stock records.

Step 2 — Value of Stock Salvaged, and the Average Clause

Stock salvaged is the quantity saved from the accident. Its value is deducted from the estimated stock at the date of accident to arrive at the value of stock actually lost — the Gross Claim.

Average Clause simply states that in the absence of adequate insurance coverage, the insurance company will not shoulder the entire risk. It is a tool of the insurance company to discourage under-insurance. In case of under-insurance, the insured must share a portion of the loss along with the insurance company. Average Clause will NOT be applicable if the policy value is greater than or equal to the value of stock on the date of fire.

Net Claim = Actual (Gross) Loss of Stock × (Amount of Policy / Value of Stock at the Date of Fire)

Applies only when Amount of Policy < Value of Stock at the date of fire (under-insurance). If Amount of Policy ≥ Value of Stock at the date of fire, the clause does not bite and Net Claim = Actual Loss (subject to the policy amount as a ceiling).

Special Situations & Adjustments Before Applying the GP Rate

SituationTreatment in the (Memorandum) Trading A/c
Goods-in-transit / goods sent to branches or a consigneeDeduct the cost of such goods from 'Purchases' (alternatively, credit the cost to the Trading A/c).
Goods sold but not yet deliveredDeduct the sale value of such goods from 'Sales'.
Goods sent on approval basisDeduct the cost from 'Purchases' AND deduct the sale value from 'Sales'.
Change in price level (cost/selling price risen or fallen)The effect of the price change must be nullified from the relevant items before the last year's GP rate is applied to the current period's sales — the stock-pricing method (FIFO, LIFO, etc.) governs how.
Under/over-valued stockIf under-valued, add back the under-valuation to reach cost; if over-valued, deduct the excess to reach cost. The unsold portion of such stock is considered when computing the Gross Claim.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ABNORMAL / DEFECTIVE ITEMS LEFT INSIDE THE NORMAL GP% CALCULATION

THE TRAP: applying the blended (overall) GP rate to the whole of sales/purchases, including goods that could not fetch the usual rate of gross profit (abnormal, defective, obsolete, or heavily-discounted items) — this understates or overstates the normal GP% and throws off the whole stock estimate.

THE TWIST: the source requires such items to be stripped out FIRST. The unwritten-off portion of abnormal goods is deducted from Opening Stock; the cost of any purchased in the current period is deducted from Purchases; the selling price of any sold in the current period is deducted from Sales. This gives a "normal" GP rate. Any portion of the abnormal goods still unsold on the date of fire is then added back to the estimated NORMAL stock at its own agreed/realisable value to reach the total estimated stock at the date of fire (see Illustration 5). The same stripping-out is required for the LAST year's Trading A/c too, if abnormal items existed then.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Basic claim with a change in price level (Sen & Co.)

A fire occurred on 15th September 2023. Stock at cost on 1.1.2022: ₹40,000; Stock at cost on 1.1.2023: ₹60,000; Purchases in 2022: ₹80,000; Purchases from 1.1.2023 to 15.9.2023: ₹1,76,000; Sales in 2022: ₹1,20,000; Sales from 1.1.2023 to 15.9.2023: ₹2,10,000. During the current year, cost of purchase has risen 10% above last year's level; selling prices have risen 5%. Salvage value of stock after fire: ₹4,000.

Trading Account for the year ended 31.12.2022 (to ascertain the rate of Gross Profit)
Dr.       Cr.
Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Opening Stock40,000By Sales (less returns)1,20,000
To Purchases (less returns)80,000By Closing Stock60,000
To Gross Profit (bal. fig.)60,000
Total1,80,000Total1,80,000

GP% on Sales = (Gross Profit / Sales) × 100 = (₹60,000 / ₹1,20,000) × 100 = 50%.

Memorandum Trading Account for the period 1.1.2023 to 15.9.2023
Dr.       Cr.
Particulars₹ (Actual)₹ (Last Yr Level)Particulars₹ (Actual)₹ (Last Yr Level)
To Opening Stock60,00060,000By Sales2,10,0002,00,000
To Purchases1,76,0001,60,000By Closing Stock (bal. fig.)1,32,0001,20,000
To Gross Profit (bal. fig. / 50% of Sales)1,06,0001,00,000
Total3,42,0003,20,000Total3,42,0003,20,000

Purchases are deflated to last year's price level by removing the 10% rise (₹1,76,000 ÷ 1.10 = ₹1,60,000); Sales are deflated by removing the 5% rise (₹2,10,000 ÷ 1.05 = ₹2,00,000). Gross Profit in the "Last Yr Level" column = 50% of that column's Sales = ₹1,00,000; the "Actual" column Gross Profit and Closing Stock are then the balancing figures at current prices.

Amount of Claim: Closing Stock (actual) ₹1,32,000 – Stock Salvaged ₹4,000 = ₹1,28,000. (No policy amount is stated in this illustration, so no Average Clause reduction applies — the claim equals the full stock lost.)

ILLUSTRATION 3 — Average Clause applied cleanly (X Ltd.)

Fire policy ₹1,60,000 on stock. Fire on 31st March 2023. Stock as on 1.4.2022: ₹60,000; Purchases to date of fire: ₹2,60,000; Sales to date of fire: ₹1,80,000; Carriage Inwards: ₹1,600; Commission on purchase: 2% (of Purchases = ₹5,200); Gross Profit Ratio: 50% on cost. Stock salvaged: ₹41,360.

Memorandum Trading Account for the period ended 31st March 2023
Dr.       Cr.
Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Opening Stock60,000By Sales1,80,000
To Purchases 2,60,000 + Carriage Inward 1,600 + Commission on Purchase 5,2002,66,800By Closing Stock (bal. fig.)2,06,800
To Gross Profit (@50% on cost, i.e. 33.33% on sale)60,000
Total3,86,800Total3,86,800

Note: Carriage Inward and Commission on Purchase are direct expenses, so both are added to Purchases before deducting the GP.

Loss of Stock: Stock at the date of fire ₹2,06,800 – Stock Salvaged ₹41,360 = ₹1,65,440.

Amount of Claim applying the Average Clause = Actual Loss × (Amount of Policy / Stock at date of fire) = ₹1,65,440 × (₹1,60,000 / ₹2,06,800)

Net Claim = ₹1,28,000.

ILLUSTRATION 7 — Two fires, mid-year price rise, and a policy reduced after a part-claim (M/s Bad Luck Traders)

Two fires in 2022–23: 31st August 2022 and 30th November 2022. Stock as at 31.3.2022: ₹59,000. Purchases 1.4.2022–31.8.2022: ₹3,45,000. Purchases 1.9.2022–30.11.2022: ₹1,90,000, of which goods costing ₹45,000 were received (goods-in-transit) only on 10.12.2022. Sales 1.4.2022–31.8.2022: ₹4,71,000. WN1 — New GP rate for 2022-23 (selling price up 20%, cost unchanged): Normal: Sale Price 100, GP 20 (Cost 80). After the rise: Sale Price 120, GP 40 (Cost still 80). Rate of GP = (40 × 100) / 120 = 33.33%.

Revised policy value for the 2nd claim = Original policy – Compensation already received = ₹45,000 – ₹30,000 = ₹15,000 (the policy was never topped up).

2nd claim: Stock at date of fire ₹43,000; Less Salvage ₹2,000 = Actual Loss ₹41,000. Revised Policy ₹15,000 < Stock value ₹43,000 → Average Clause applies again.

Net Claim = ₹41,000 × (₹15,000/₹43,000) = ₹14,302 (approx.).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: RE-USING THE ORIGINAL SUM INSURED FOR A SECOND LOSS

THE TRAP: when a business suffers two separate fires within one policy period, students apply the ORIGINAL sum insured to BOTH claims.

THE TWIST: if the insurer pays a claim and the insured does NOT pay an additional premium to restore the policy to its original value, the sum insured for any LATER loss stands reduced by the compensation already paid out (Illustration 7: ₹45,000 → ₹15,000 after the ₹30,000 first payout). The Average Clause is then re-tested against this REDUCED figure.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: APPLYING THE AVERAGE CLAUSE WHEN IT DOESN'T APPLY

THE TRAP: assuming the Average Clause always reduces the claim, or applying it even when the sum insured comfortably covers the stock.

THE TWIST: per the source, "Average Clause will not be applicable if the policy value is greater than or equal to the value of stock on the date of fire." Only genuine UNDER-insurance (policy value strictly less than stock value at the date of fire) triggers the proportionate reduction.

CONCEPT

7.2 Insurance Claim for Loss of Profit ★★★ HIGH

An accident (fire, natural calamity, or a human-induced event) may not just destroy stock — it hampers the organisation's regular operations and, through that, its profitability. To cover this separate risk, a business enters into a "Loss of Profit policy," also called a "Consequential Loss policy." The claim under this policy is for the Gross Profit the business fails to earn due to reduced turnover following the accident, PLUS any increased cost it incurs to keep working and limit the damage.

Indemnity periodThe period for which normal activities of the business remain interrupted.
Standard turnoverThe turnover of the previous year corresponding to the period of indemnity.
Adjusted annual turnoverTurnover during the 12 months immediately preceding the date of damage, taking trend into consideration.
Standing chargesUnavoidable fixed expenses which have to be paid even if there is a reduction in sales.

Calculation of the Net Claim — the Eight Steps

Step 1 — Gross Profit (GP) for the previous accounting period

If Net Profit exists: GP = Net Profit for Previous Period + Insured Standing Charges.
If Net Loss exists: GP = Insured Standing Charges – [Net Loss × (Insured Standing Charges / All Standing Charges)].

Step 2 — GP Rate = (GP / Sales) × 100

Step 3 — Short Sales = Standard Turnover – Actual Turnover for the Indemnity Period

Step 4 — GP Lost = Short Sales × GP Rate

Step 5 — Admissible Additional Expenses = LEAST of:

(i) Actual additional expenses.
(ii) Sales due to additional expenses × GP rate.
(iii) Actual additional expenses × [(Net Profit + Insured Standing Charges) / (Net Profit + All Standing Charges)].

Step 6 — Gross Claim = GP Lost + Admissible Additional Expenses – Savings in Standing Charges

Step 7 — Insurable Value = Adjusted Annual Turnover × GP Rate

Step 8 — Net Claim: if Average Clause applies (Insurable Value > Policy Value): Net Claim = (Sum Insured / Insurable Value) × Gross Claim. If not (Insurable Value < Policy Value): Net Claim = Gross Claim.

  • If the additional sales attributable to additional expenses is not separately given, assume the ENTIRE actual sale during the disruption was achieved because of that additional expenditure.
  • All Standing Charges = Insured Standing Charges + Uninsured Standing Charges.
  • In the absence of specific information, assume ALL standing charges are insured.
  • If sales for past years are given, the trend of sales must first be determined and applied to BOTH the Standard Turnover and the Annual Turnover.

ILLUSTRATION 8 — The eight-step claim in full

Fire on 15th June 2023; business remained disturbed till 15th December 2023. Consequential Loss policy ₹1,40,000 (average clause), indemnity period 7 months. Current year's sales up 25% on last year. Additional expenditure incurred: ₹12,000; saving in insured standing charges: ₹2,000. Actual sales 15.6.23–15.12.23: ₹70,000. Sales 15.6.22–15.12.22: ₹2,40,000. Net profit for the financial year: ₹80,000. Insured standing charges: ₹70,000. Total standing charges: ₹1,20,000. Turnover for last financial year: ₹6,00,000. Turnover 16.6.22–15.6.23: ₹5,60,000.

GP for previous period = Net Profit + Insured Standing Charges = ₹80,000 + ₹70,000 = ₹1,50,000.
GP rate = (₹1,50,000 / ₹6,00,000) × 100 = 25%.

Short Sales = Standard Turnover (trend-adjusted) – Actual Turnover for indemnity period = (₹2,40,000 × 125%) – ₹70,000 = ₹3,00,000 – ₹70,000 = ₹2,30,000.
GP Lost = ₹2,30,000 × 25% = ₹57,500.

Admissible additional expenses — least of: (i) Actual ₹12,000; (ii) Sales due to additional expenses × GP rate = ₹70,000 × 25% = ₹17,500; (iii) ₹12,000 × (80,000+70,000)/(80,000+1,20,000) = ₹12,000 × 1,50,000/2,00,000 = ₹9,000. Least = ₹9,000.

Gross Claim = GP Lost + Admissible Expenses – Savings in Standing Charges = ₹57,500 + ₹9,000 – ₹2,000 = ₹64,500.

Insurable Value = Adjusted Annual Turnover × GP rate = (₹5,60,000 × 125%) × 25% = ₹7,00,000 × 25% = ₹1,75,000. Since Policy ₹1,40,000 < Insurable Value, Average Clause applies.

Net Claim = (Sum Insured / Insurable Value) × Gross Claim = ₹53,118 (approx.), as per source.

ILLUSTRATION 9 — A "special clause" bumping both the GP rate and the turnover trend

Date of fire: 1st September; Indemnity period 6 months (disruption 1 Sept–1 Feb). Sum Insured ₹1,08,900. Sales for preceding FY (ended 31 March): ₹6,00,000. Net profit for preceding FY: ₹36,000, plus Insured Standing Charges ₹72,000. Base rate of Gross Profit: 18%. Turnover during disruption: ₹67,500. Uninsured standing charges: ₹6,000. Annual turnover for the 12 months preceding fire: ₹6,60,000. Standard turnover (corresponding months, preceding year): ₹2,25,000. Increase in cost of working (additional expenditure): ₹12,000, with a saving of insured standing charges ₹4,500 during disruption. Reduced turnover avoided through the increased working expenditure: ₹30,000. Special clause: GP rate to be increased by 2%; Standard AND Annual turnover both to be increased by 10%.

GP rate = 18% + 2% (special clause) = 20%.

Short Sales = (Standard Turnover × 110%) – Actual Turnover for indemnity period = (₹2,25,000 × 110%) – ₹67,500 = ₹2,47,500 – ₹67,500 = ₹1,80,000.
GP Lost = ₹1,80,000 × 20% = ₹36,000.

Admissible additional expenses — least of: (i) Actual ₹12,000; (ii) Sales due to additional expenses × GP rate = ₹30,000 × 20% = ₹6,000; (iii) ₹12,000 × (36,000+72,000)/(36,000+72,000+6,000) = ₹12,000 × 1,08,000/1,14,000 = ₹11,368 (approx.). Least = ₹6,000.

Gross Claim = GP Lost + Admissible Expenses – Savings in Standing Charges = ₹36,000 + ₹6,000 – ₹4,500 = ₹37,500.

Insurable Value = (Annual Turnover × 110%) × GP rate = (₹6,60,000 × 110%) × 20% = ₹7,26,000 × 20% = ₹1,45,200. Policy ₹1,08,900 < Insurable Value ₹1,45,200 → Average Clause applies.

Net Claim = (₹1,08,900 / ₹1,45,200) × ₹37,500 = ₹28,125.

ILLUSTRATION 10 — Standard & Annual Turnover built from a trend in past sales (Omega Ltd.)

Fire on 15th March 2023. Loss of Profit policy ₹80,000, indemnity period 3 months. Net Profit for year ended 31.12.2021: ₹56,000. Standing charges (all insured): ₹49,600. Quarterly sales figures for 2019–2022 were available from sales-tax returns, together with short-period splits at the fire-anniversary dates (16–31 March and 16–30 June, for both 2022 and 2023).

WN2 — GP rate: Net Profit ₹56,000 + Insured Standing Charges ₹49,600 = Insured Gross Profit ₹1,05,600. Sales for the base year = ₹5,28,000. GP rate = (₹1,05,600 / ₹5,28,000) × 100 = 20%.

WN1 — Trend: comparing the last few years' total turnover reveals a fairly steady 10% upward trend year-on-year; this 10% is applied to both the Standard Turnover and the Annual Turnover below.

WN3 — Short Sales: Standard Turnover for the indemnity period (15 March–15 June), built from the corresponding period last year and grossed up by the 10% trend, works out to ₹1,14,400; Actual Turnover for the same period in the fire year works out to ₹34,000. Short Sales = ₹1,14,400 – ₹34,000 = ₹80,400.

WN4 — GP Lost = Short Sales × GP rate = ₹80,400 × 20% = ₹16,080.

WN5 — Insurable Value: Annual Turnover for the 12 months preceding the fire = ₹5,44,000; grossed up by the 10% trend = ₹5,98,400. Insurable Value = ₹5,98,400 × 20% = ₹1,19,680.

Statement of Claim for Loss of Profit
Particulars₹
GP Lost on Short Sales (WN4)16,080
Less: Savings in Standing ChargesNil
Gross Claim16,080

Policy ₹80,000 < Insurable Value ₹1,19,680 → Average Clause applies. Net Claim = Gross Claim × (Policy / Insurable Value) = ₹16,080 × (₹80,000 / ₹1,19,680)

Net Claim = ₹10,749 (approx.).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: MIXING UP WHICH FIGURES GET THE TREND ADJUSTMENT

THE TRAP: forgetting to gross up the Standard Turnover, or wrongly grossing up the ACTUAL turnover for the indemnity period, when a past-years' trend is given.

THE TWIST: per Illustrations 8, 9 and 10, the trend/percentage increase is applied to BOTH the Standard Turnover (Step 3) AND the Annual Turnover used for Insurable Value (Step 7) — because both represent what SHOULD have happened, adjusted for growth. The ACTUAL turnover achieved during the indemnity period is used exactly as recorded — it is never trend-adjusted, since it is already the real, disrupted figure being measured against the benchmark.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SPLITTING THE AVERAGE CLAUSE ACROSS GP LOST AND INCREASED COST OF WORKING

THE TRAP: applying the Sum Insured/Insurable Value ratio separately — once to the GP-lost figure and again to the admissible additional expenses — on the theory that they are two different kinds of loss.

THE TWIST: per Step 6 and Step 8 of the source's own method, GP Lost and Admissible Additional Expenses (less any saving in standing charges) are FIRST combined into a single Gross Claim, and the Average Clause ratio is applied ONCE to that combined Gross Claim (confirmed in Illustrations 8, 9 and 10, where Net Claim = Sum Insured/Insurable Value × Gross Claim, with Gross Claim already netted).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: STANDING CHARGES VS. VARIABLE CHARGES IN THE GP-FOR-CLAIM COMPUTATION

THE TRAP: adding back ALL expenses (or all standing charges, insured and uninsured alike) to Net Profit when computing GP for the previous accounting period (Step 1).

THE TWIST: Standing Charges are specifically the UNAVOIDABLE FIXED expenses that continue even when sales fall — not variable costs, which shrink naturally with reduced sales and need no add-back. Further, only the INSURED portion of standing charges is added to Net Profit at Step 1; the source explicitly separates "Insured Standing Charges" from "All Standing Charges" (used only in the Step 5(iii) test), and instructs that in the absence of specific information, all standing charges should be assumed insured.

Fill in the Blanks:

2. In the absence of specific information, standing charges are assumed to be insured.

3. If the policy value is more than the value of stock lost, it is called over insurance.

12 EXAM FACTS — INSURANCE CLAIM FOR LOSS OF STOCK AND LOSS OF PROFIT (Module 7)

① Fire insurance covers two separate risks: Loss of Stock (7.1) and Loss of Profit / Consequential Loss (7.2) — each needs its own claim computation.

② Stock at the date of fire is estimated via a Memorandum Trading Account, applying LAST year's own Gross Profit rate to the current period's sales.

③ Average Clause: Net Claim = Actual Loss × (Sum Insured / Value of Stock at date of fire) — applies only when the policy value is LESS than the value at risk; not applicable if Sum Insured ≥ value of stock.

④ Abnormal/defective items (can't fetch the normal GP rate) must be stripped out before computing the normal GP%, then added back to closing stock at their own realisable value.

⑤ If a part-claim is paid and the policy is not restored (no extra premium paid), the Sum Insured for a LATER loss in the same period stands reduced by the compensation already received.

⑥ Loss of Profit GP for previous period = Net Profit + Insured Standing Charges (or Insured Standing Charges – Net Loss × Insured SC/All SC, on a net loss).

⑦ Short Sales = Standard Turnover (trend-adjusted) – Actual Turnover for the Indemnity Period; GP Lost = Short Sales × GP rate.

⑧ Admissible additional (increased cost of working) expenses = LEAST of: (i) actual expense, (ii) sales due to that expense × GP rate, (iii) actual expense × (Net Profit+Insured SC)/(Net Profit+All SC).

⑨ Gross Claim = GP Lost + Admissible Additional Expenses – Savings in (insured) Standing Charges.

⑩ Insurable Value = Adjusted Annual Turnover × GP rate; Net Claim = (Sum Insured/Insurable Value) × Gross Claim, applied ONCE to the combined Gross Claim, when Sum Insured < Insurable Value.

⑪ Both Standard Turnover AND Annual Turnover get the trend/% adjustment; the ACTUAL turnover during the indemnity period is used exactly as recorded, never trend-adjusted.

⑫ Standing Charges = unavoidable FIXED costs paid even when sales fall; only the INSURED portion enters the GP-for-claim computation.

Hire Purchase and
Instalment Sale Transactions

Hire Purchase lets a buyer take possession of a high-value asset now and pay for it in staggered instalments with interest, while ownership stays with the seller until the last instalment is paid. Instalment Sale looks identical on the surface — same staggered payments — but ownership passes to the buyer immediately at the time of the agreement, which changes every default, repossession and risk-of-loss rule that follows.

MUST NOT SKIP: Hire Purchase Price = Cash Price + Total Interest, and in Hire Purchase ownership passes only on payment of the LAST instalment (vs. Instalment Sale, where it passes immediately at the agreement) — this single fork drives the comparison table, the repossession rights, and which account format (Asset A/c at cash price vs. an outright Sale) each side uses.

8.1–8.7

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: understand the accounting for acquisition of high-value items under Hire Purchase, in the books of both the hire purchaser and the hire vendor; and account for the acquisition of large quantities of low-value items on hire purchase, under the Debtors Method, the Stock and Debtors Method, and the Final Accounts Method.

Glossary — Module 8, in Plain Words

The technical terms used throughout this module, explained simply.

Hire PurchaseA system where the purchaser (the "hirer") pays the price in staggered instalments — monthly, quarterly or yearly — with interest. Possession passes immediately, but ownership (title) passes only when the LAST instalment is paid.
Hire VendorThe owner/seller who delivers possession under the agreement but keeps ownership until the last instalment is received — and who may repossess the goods if the hirer defaults.
Hire Purchaser (Hirer)The person who takes possession under the agreement. Legally only a bailee until the last instalment is paid — cannot damage, destroy, pledge or sell the goods meanwhile, and must take the care of a prudent person over his own goods.
Cash PriceThe price at which the asset could be bought outright for cash on the date of the agreement — this is the figure the hire purchaser capitalises as the asset's cost, never the higher hire purchase price.
Hire Purchase PriceThe total amount payable under the agreement — Down Payment + all instalments = Cash Price + Total Interest.
Down PaymentThe amount paid at the time of signing the agreement, before any instalment falls due. Carries no interest — it is pure repayment of cash price.
InterestThe excess the hire purchaser pays over the cash price for the privilege of deferred payment. Total Interest = Hire Purchase Price − Cash Price, apportioned across the instalments by one of several methods.
Instalment SaleA sale where BOTH possession and ownership pass to the buyer immediately at the time of the agreement — the price is merely collected over time, in instalments.
RepossessionThe hire vendor taking back possession of goods from a defaulting hire purchaser. Can be Complete/Full (all goods taken back) or Partial (only some goods taken back, the rest retained by the purchaser against the amount he still owes).

Module 8 Mind Map — read it now, redraw it from memory after finishing the module

All four spokes hinge on one fact: WHO owns the goods, and WHEN. Hire Purchase delays ownership to the final instalment; Instalment Sale grants it immediately — that single fork decides the repossession right, the risk of loss, and which account format each side uses.

CONCEPT

8.1 Hire Purchase vs. Instalment Sale — the Legal Distinction ★★★ HIGH

It is not always possible for a purchaser to meet the higher demand for goods through immediate cash payment. To meet this demand, the concept of Hire Purchase is very popular in the market. Under this system the purchaser (the "Hirer") pays the entire amount in a staggered way — monthly, quarterly or yearly — with some interest. Goods are sold subject to conditions: possession of the goods is delivered to the hirer, but the title to the goods (ownership) is transferred only when the last instalment is paid.

Such a hirer has a right to terminate the agreement at any time before ownership so passes — he has the option to return the goods, in which case he need not pay instalments falling due thereafter. However, the hirer cannot recover the sums already paid, as such sums legally represent hire charges for the goods in question. During the period of possession, the hire-purchaser cannot damage, destroy, pledge or sell the goods — he is supposed to take all such care of the goods as a prudent person would take of his own goods.

In case of an Instalment Sale, it is not only possession but also ownership in the goods that is transferred to the buyer immediately, at the time of the agreement. Further, under the instalment system, if the buyer stops paying the dues, the seller does not have the right to seize back his goods.

The Comparison Table (source's own)

ParticularsHire PurchaseInstalment Sale
OwnershipStipulates the time at which ownership passes to the buyer — usually on payment of the LAST instalment.Ownership passes at the time of sale (i.e. immediately).
Default in making paymentSeller CAN repossess the goods. In that case the instalments so far paid are treated as hiring charges.Seller does not have any right except the right of suing the buyer for non-payment of the price.
Right of sale or otherwiseNo right to sell or otherwise transfer the goods, since the legal position of the hirer is that of a bailee.Right to sell or otherwise transfer the goods.
Loss or damage to the goodsSince ownership has not yet passed, any loss falls on the hire vendor as owner — the hirer's own duty (per the source) is only the care a prudent person takes of his own goods, not an owner's risk.Since ownership has already passed at the time of sale, any loss falls on the buyer.
Exam trick: examiners test this table by describing a transaction's FACTS (who can repossess? who bears a fire loss?) without using the words "hire purchase" or "instalment sale" at all — identify the type from the ownership-timing fact first, then apply the right accounting.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING "PAYMENT BY INSTALMENTS" AS PROOF OF HIRE PURCHASE

THE TRAP: assuming any deal where the price is paid in instalments must be a Hire Purchase, and therefore recording the buyer's asset only up to cash price with a Hire Vendor liability, or assuming the seller can repossess on default.

THE TWIST: staggered payment is common to BOTH arrangements — the only thing that tells them apart is WHEN ownership passes. If the question says ownership/title passes immediately at the agreement, it is an Instalment Sale: the seller's only remedy on default is to sue for the unpaid price, never to repossess; and any loss to the goods thereafter is the buyer's problem, not the seller's.

CONCEPT

8.2 Computation of Interest ★★★ HIGH

Every hire purchase instalment is part repayment of cash price and part interest. Which of the following situations a numerical question falls into decides which apportionment method applies — picking the wrong one is the single most common error in this module.

Situation I — Rate, Cash Price and instalments ALL given: Interest for a period = Opening Balance of Cash Price (outstanding) × Rate%

Payment towards Principal/Cash Price = Instalment − Interest. Closing Balance of Cash Price = Opening Balance − Payment towards Principal. Build an "Analysis of Instalments" table, one row per instalment.

Situation II — Rate and instalments given, Cash Price NOT given: work BACKWARDS from the last instalment

Interest embedded in an instalment = Instalment × [Rate / (100 + Rate)]. Cash-price component of that instalment = Instalment − Interest. Add this to the PRECEDING instalment and repeat, peeling interest off each combined figure in turn, until the down payment is added last to give the total Cash Price.

Situation III — Only instalments given (no Cash Price, no rate), but each instalment's cash-price component is EQUAL

Let X = the (equal) cash-price component of each instalment and I = the interest component, which falls by a constant amount each period. Set up one equation per instalment (X + I, X + 2I, X + 3I …, working from the LAST instalment backward) and solve simultaneously by subtraction.

Situation IV — Rate and (equal) instalments given, with an Annuity Table reference, Cash Price not given

Cash Price = Down Payment + (Equal Annual Instalment × Present Value of an Annuity of ₹1 p.a. at the given rate, for the given number of years). The annuity factor converts the stream of future instalments into their present worth, which equals the cash price.

Ratio of Outstanding Balances method — Total Interest known (= H.P. Price − Cash Price), rate NOT given

First find the H.P. Price outstanding at the start of each instalment period (working backward: last instalment's opening balance = that instalment; each earlier one = its instalment + the following period's opening balance). Apportion Total Interest among instalments in the RATIO of these opening balances.

Sum-of-the-Years-Digits method — instalments are EQUAL in amount, Total Interest known

Number the instalments from the LAST (=1) to the FIRST (=n). Sum of digits = n + (n−1) + … + 1. Interest in the k-th instalment (counted from the first) = Total Interest × [its digit / sum of digits] — the FIRST instalment carries the LARGEST share of interest, since the balance outstanding was highest then.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Situation I: rate, cash price and instalments all given

X purchases a car on hire-purchase on 01.01.2021. Total cash price ₹4,50,000, payable ₹90,000 down and three instalments of ₹1,70,000, ₹1,50,000 and ₹1,08,460 at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. Interest charged at 10% p.a.

Analysis of Instalments
DateOpening Balance of Cash Price (₹)Instalment (₹)Towards Principal/Cash Price (₹)Towards Interest (₹)Closing Balance of Cash Price (₹)
01.01.214,50,00090,00090,000—3,60,000
31.12.213,60,0001,70,0001,34,00036,0002,26,000
31.12.222,26,0001,50,0001,27,40022,60098,600
31.12.2398,6001,08,46098,6009,860—

Each year's Interest = that year's Opening Balance × 10% (e.g. 3,60,000 × 10% = 36,000); Principal repaid = Instalment − Interest; Closing Balance carries to next year's Opening Balance — and runs to exactly NIL after the last instalment.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — Situation II: rate and instalments given, Cash Price NOT given

X purchased a T.V. on hire-purchase: ₹3,000 down, ₹4,000 at the end of year 1, ₹3,000 at the end of year 2, and ₹5,000 at the end of year 3. Interest charged at 12% p.a. Find the total cash price and the interest in each instalment.

Step 1 (peel the 3rd/last instalment): Interest = ₹5,000 × 12/112 = ₹536. Cash-price component = ₹5,000 − ₹536 = ₹4,464.

Step 2: Add the 2nd instalment: ₹4,464 + ₹3,000 = ₹7,464. Interest = ₹7,464 × 12/112 = ₹800. Cash-price component = ₹7,464 − ₹800 = ₹6,664.

Step 3: Add the 1st instalment: ₹6,664 + ₹4,000 = ₹10,664. Interest = ₹10,664 × 12/112 = ₹1,143. Cash-price component = ₹10,664 − ₹1,143 = ₹9,521.

Step 4 (add the down payment last): ₹9,521 + ₹3,000 (down) = Total Cash Price ₹12,521.

Total Interest = ₹536 + ₹800 + ₹1,143 = ₹2,479. Check: ₹12,521 (cash price) + ₹2,479 (interest) = ₹15,000 = total of down payment + all three instalments (₹3,000+₹4,000+₹3,000+₹5,000). Balances.

ILLUSTRATION 3 — Situation III: only instalments given, equal cash-price component

X & Co. purchased a motor car on 1.4.2023: ₹60,000 cash down, balance in 4 annual instalments of ₹55,000, ₹50,000, ₹45,000 and ₹40,000 — each instalment comprising an EQUAL amount of cash price. Find total cash price and the interest in each instalment.

Hire-Purchase Price = ₹60,000 + ₹55,000 + ₹50,000 + ₹45,000 + ₹40,000 = ₹2,50,000. Since each instalment's cash-price component is equal, the differences between instalment amounts are entirely due to interest. Let X = cash price per instalment, I = interest. Working from the last instalment: (i) X+I=40,000; (ii) X+2I=45,000; (iii) X+3I=50,000; (iv) X+4I=55,000. Subtracting each equation from the next gives I = ₹5,000; substituting back gives X = ₹35,000.

Hire-Purchase Price split into Cash Price and Interest

Down Payment60,000—60,000
1st instalment35,00020,00055,000
2nd instalment35,00015,00050,000
3rd instalment35,00010,00045,000
4th instalment35,0005,00040,000

Total Cash Price = ₹2,00,000; Hire Purchase Price = ₹2,50,000; Total Interest = ₹50,000.

ILLUSTRATION 4 — Situation IV: annuity table method

On 01.01.2023, X purchased a plant from Y on hire purchase. The H.P. price was settled at ₹60,000: ₹15,000 on 01.01.2023 and ₹15,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. Interest charged at 5% p.a. Present value of an annuity of ₹1 p.a. @ 5% = ₹2.7232. Ascertain the cash price.

Present value of the 3 future instalments = ₹15,000 × 2.7232 = ₹40,848.

Cash Price = ₹40,848 + ₹15,000 (down payment) = ₹55,848.

ILLUSTRATION 4A — Ratio of Outstanding Balances (unequal instalments, rate not given)

Down payment ₹10,000; 1st instalment (after 1 year) ₹20,000; 2nd instalment (after 2 years) ₹10,000; and a last instalment after 3 years. Cash price of the plant ₹43,000. Hire Purchase Price is ₹50,000, so the 3rd instalment = ₹50,000 − ₹10,000 − ₹20,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹10,000.

(i) Total Interest = H.P. Price − Cash Price = ₹50,000 − ₹43,000 = ₹7,000.

H.P. Price outstanding at the beginning of each year
Particulars₹
Hire Purchase Price50,000
Less: Down Payment10,000
H.P. Price o/s at beginning of 1st year (a)40,000
Less: 1st Instalment20,000
H.P. Price o/s at beginning of 2nd year (b)20,000
Less: 2nd Instalment10,000
H.P. Price o/s at beginning of 3rd year (c)10,000
Less: 3rd Instalment10,000

Ratio of (a):(b):(c) = 40,000:20,000:10,000 = 4:2:1.

Interest in 1st instalment = 7,000 × 4/7 = ₹4,000. Interest in 2nd instalment = 7,000 × 2/7 = ₹2,000. Interest in 3rd instalment = 7,000 × 1/7 = ₹1,000.

ILLUSTRATION 4B — Sum-of-the-Years-Digits (EQUAL instalments)

Down payment ₹10,000, followed by 4 annual EQUAL instalments of ₹10,000 each. Cash price of the plant ₹43,000.

(i) Total Interest = H.P. Price (₹10,000 + 4×₹10,000 = ₹50,000) − Cash Price ₹43,000 = ₹7,000.

(ii) Since the instalments are equal, interest can be allocated directly using the sum of the years' digits: 4+3+2+1 = 10.

Interest in 1st instalment = 7,000 × 4/10 = ₹2,800. 2nd = 7,000 × 3/10 = ₹2,100. 3rd = 7,000 × 2/10 = ₹1,400. 4th = 7,000 × 1/10 = ₹700. (Total ₹7,000 — matches.)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: MIXING UP THE SIX INTEREST-APPORTIONMENT METHODS

THE TRAP: applying the Sum-of-the-Years-Digits shortcut to a question with UNEQUAL instalments, or applying the Ratio-of-Outstanding-Balances method when the rate of interest IS actually given (so Situation I's direct calculation applies instead), or trying to "peel" interest backward (Situation II's method) when the cash price is already stated in the question.

THE TWIST: read what is GIVEN before picking a method. Rate + Cash Price + instalments all given → Situation I (direct, forward). Rate + instalments given, Cash Price missing → Situation II (backward peel). Only instalments given, equal cash-price share → Situation III (simultaneous equations). Rate + equal instalments + an annuity factor, Cash Price missing → Situation IV (annuity table). Total Interest already known (or derivable as H.P. Price − Cash Price) but rate NOT given, unequal instalments → Ratio of Outstanding Balances. Same setup but instalments EQUAL → Sum-of-the-Years-Digits (the source explicitly notes this as the shortcut for equal instalments).

CONCEPT

8.3 Accounting in the Books of the Hire Purchaser ★★★ HIGH

The hire purchaser always records the asset at its full CASH PRICE, never at the higher hire purchase price — interest is a separate charge, recognised only as it accrues. Two methods are followed.

Method 1 — Cash Price Method (Proforma)
Particulars       Debit (₹) / Credit (₹)
1.Hire Purchase Asset A/c  Dr. [at full Cash Price]
  To Hire Vendor A/c
2.Hire Vendor A/c  Dr. [Down Payment]
  To Bank A/c
3.Interest A/c  Dr.
  To Hire Vendor A/c
4.Hire Vendor A/c  Dr. [Instalment amount]
  To Bank A/c
5.Profit & Loss A/c  Dr.
  To Interest A/c
  To Depreciation A/c
Method 2 — Interest Suspense Method (Proforma)
Particulars       Debit (₹) / Credit (₹)
1.Hire Purchase Asset A/c  Dr. [Cash Price] & Interest Suspense A/c  Dr. [Total Interest]
  To Hire Vendor A/c [full H.P. Price]
2.Hire Vendor A/c  Dr. [Down Payment]
  To Bank A/c
3.Interest A/c  Dr.
  To Interest Suspense A/c
4.Hire Vendor A/c  Dr. [Instalment amount]
  To Bank A/c
5.Profit & Loss A/c  Dr.
  To Interest A/c
  To Depreciation A/c

Under the Interest Suspense Method, the ENTIRE Hire Vendor liability (at full H.P. Price) is booked upfront against the asset, with the not-yet-accrued interest parked in Interest Suspense A/c and released to Interest A/c only as each period's interest actually falls due — the Cash Price Method instead books the Hire Vendor liability and the Interest charge period-by-period, as they arise. Both methods land on the SAME Asset A/c and the SAME P&L charge; they differ only in how the liability is staged.

CONCEPT

8.4 Accounting in the Books of the Hire Vendor — Sales Method ★★★ HIGH

The Sales Method follows a practical (though not strictly technical) approach: it treats the hire purchaser as though he were already the owner of the asset, on the principle of "substance over form" — since the intention all along is to buy the asset. The asset is recorded at full cash price. Both parties' entries mirror each other transaction-for-transaction.

CONCEPT

8.5 Default and Repossession ★★★ HIGH

If a hire purchaser fails to pay any instalment on the stipulated date, he is said to be "at default." On default, the hire vendor may repossess the goods — taking back their possession. Subject to the agreement, repossession may be Complete/Full (the vendor takes back ALL the goods) or Partial (the vendor takes back only SOME of the goods, adjusting their value against the amount due, leaving the rest with the purchaser).

Complete/Full RepossessionBooks of Hire PurchaserBooks of Hire Vendor
1. Closing the Vendor's/Asset's A/c (Purchaser) & recording repossession (Vendor)Hire Vendor's A/c is closed against the Asset A/c at the amount due to the vendor.Goods Repossessed A/c  Dr. [at the REVALUED amount of the goods]
  To Hire Purchaser's A/c
2. Closing the Asset A/c (i) if Book Value > amount due to vendorProfit & Loss A/c  Dr.
  To Asset A/c		3. For amount spent reconditioning: Goods Repossessed A/c Dr. / To Cash-Bank A/c. 4. On sale of Goods Repossessed: Cash/Bank/Debtors A/c Dr. / To Goods Repossessed A/c. 5. Loss (or, reversed, profit) on sale: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. / To Goods Repossessed A/c.
2. Closing the Asset A/c (ii) if amount due to vendor > Book ValueAsset A/c  Dr.
  To Profit & Loss A/c

Partial Repossession — the practical steps: (1) compute the Book Value of the goods repossessed (Cost − Depreciation to date of repossession); (2) the hire purchaser transfers only the AGREED value of the goods handed back — Vendor's A/c Dr. [agreed value] / To Asset A/c — leaving the balance of his liability (for the goods he RETAINS) still outstanding; (3) any Loss on Default (Book Value of repossessed goods minus their Agreed Value) is separately written off: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. / To Asset A/c. The vendor's-side entries for repossession, reconditioning, resale and loss/profit on resale mirror the complete-repossession entries above.
