⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: REPOSSESSED ASSET RECORDED AT THE WRONG VALUE

THE TRAP: crediting the repossessed asset back into the Asset/Machinery A/c (in the purchaser's books) or recording it into Goods Repossessed A/c (in the vendor's books) at its BOOK VALUE (cost less depreciation) instead of its AGREED/REVALUED value — or the reverse, closing the Hire Vendor's personal A/c at book value instead of at the amount actually due.

THE TWIST: per the source's own rule box, the Goods Repossessed A/c entry in the vendor's books is "passed with the REVALUED amount of goods repossessed" — NOT the purchaser's book value. In the purchaser's books, the Asset A/c is closed against the AMOUNT DUE to the vendor; any gap between the asset's own book value and that amount due is the profit or loss on default (Illustration 7: ₹60,000 profit, since ₹6,60,000 due > ₹6,00,000 book value). Under Partial Repossession specifically (Illustration 8), the Vendor's A/c is closed only by the AGREED value of the goods actually surrendered (₹2,16,000) — never by the full outstanding balance (₹6,60,000) — because the purchaser still owes for whatever he retains.

13 EXAM FACTS — HIRE PURCHASE AND INSTALMENT SALE (Module 8)

① The single fork that decides everything: in Hire Purchase, ownership passes only on payment of the LAST instalment; in Instalment Sale, both possession AND ownership pass immediately at the agreement.

② On default, a Hire Vendor CAN repossess the goods (instalments paid so far are treated as hire charges); an Instalment Sale seller has no such right — his only remedy is to sue the buyer for the unpaid price.

③ Loss or damage to the goods: under Hire Purchase it falls on the hire vendor (owner, since title hasn't passed) — the hirer's own duty is only the care a prudent person takes of his own goods; under Instalment Sale it falls on the buyer, since ownership already passed at the time of sale.

④ Hire Purchase Price = Cash Price + Total Interest = Down Payment + all instalments. The hire purchaser ALWAYS capitalises the asset at Cash Price, never at the higher Hire Purchase Price.

⑤ Six interest-apportionment methods, picked by what the question GIVES: Situation I (rate + cash price + instalments all given) → Interest = Opening Balance × Rate%, forward, via an Analysis of Instalments table. Situation II (rate + instalments given, cash price missing) → peel interest off the LAST instalment backward: Interest = Instalment × [Rate/(100+Rate)].

⑥ Situation III (only instalments given, EQUAL cash-price component each) → simultaneous equations worked from the last instalment backward. Situation IV (rate + equal instalments + an annuity factor, cash price missing) → Cash Price = Down Payment + (Equal Instalment × Present Value of an Annuity of ₹1 p.a.).

⑦ Ratio of Outstanding Balances (Total Interest known, rate NOT given, UNEQUAL instalments) apportions Total Interest in the ratio of each period's opening H.P.-Price balance. Sum-of-the-Years-Digits (same setup but instalments EQUAL) numbers instalments from the LAST (=1) to the FIRST (=n) — the FIRST instalment always carries the LARGEST share of interest.

⑧ Hire Purchaser's books, two methods, same end result: the Cash Price Method books the Hire Vendor liability and Interest charge period-by-period as they arise; the Interest Suspense Method books the FULL H.P. Price liability upfront, parking not-yet-accrued interest in Interest Suspense A/c and releasing it to Interest A/c as it falls due. Both land on the same Asset A/c and the same P&L charge.

⑨ Hire Vendor's Sales Method treats the hire purchaser as already the owner (substance over form): the vendor debits the Hire Purchaser's A/c and credits H.P. Sales A/c at full cash price on day one, then mirrors every subsequent Down Payment, Interest and Instalment entry made in the purchaser's books — but the vendor never records Depreciation (that stays solely in the purchaser's books).

⑩ Balance Sheet disclosure: the Hire Purchaser shows the asset at full cash price less depreciation to date less the balance still due to the vendor; the Hire Vendor shows only a Current Asset — Hire Purchase Debtors, for the balance still receivable.

⑪ Complete/Full Repossession: the purchaser closes the Asset A/c against the AMOUNT DUE to the vendor (any gap between book value and amount due is posted as profit or loss); the vendor records Goods Repossessed A/c at the REVALUED amount of the goods, never at the purchaser's book value.

⑫ Partial Repossession: only the AGREED value of the goods actually surrendered closes the Vendor's A/c — the purchaser's liability for whatever he RETAINS stays outstanding, and any Loss on Default (Book Value of repossessed goods minus their Agreed Value) is written off separately to Profit & Loss A/c.

⑬ After repossession, the vendor's Goods Repossessed A/c also absorbs reconditioning costs (Dr.) before resale; on sale, Cash/Bank/Debtors A/c is debited and Goods Repossessed A/c credited, with any residual loss or profit on that resale charged or credited to Profit & Loss A/c — a SECOND, separate loss/profit event from the repossession itself.

MODULE 8 CLOSING DRILL (retrieval practice — do not skip): put this document down and, on rough paper, write from memory: the ONE fact (ownership timing) that separates Hire Purchase from Instalment Sale, and how that single fork changes the default remedy and the risk-of-loss rule in the comparison table; all six interest-apportionment methods and the exact "what is given" signal that tells you which one to apply; the two methods for the hire purchaser's books (Cash Price Method vs. Interest Suspense Method) and how they differ in staging the liability while landing on the same Asset A/c and P&L charge; the Hire Vendor's Sales Method entries and why the vendor never records Depreciation; how each side discloses the balance in its Balance Sheet; and the difference between Complete and Partial Repossession — which value (book value vs. agreed value) closes which account, and why a partial repossession leaves part of the purchaser's liability still outstanding. Check against the notes only after finishing — answering from memory is what converts today's reading into exam-day marks. Anything you could not retrieve, star it and re-attempt tomorrow morning. Estimated time: eight minutes.

MODULE 9 OF 9 · SECTION F · WEIGHT 20% · ~20 MARKS

Accounting
Standards

This module first frames GAAP, Accounting Standards, and the phased roadmap of Convergence to Ind AS (9.1); it then works through six specified Accounting Standards — AS 1, AS 10, AS 11, AS 12, AS 16 and AS 22 — together with their comparative provisions under the corresponding Ind AS (9.2).

MUST NOT SKIP: the AS-vs-Ind-AS comparison for each standard is the module's core testable idea — AS 10 vs Ind AS 16, AS 11 vs Ind AS 21, AS 12 vs Ind AS 20, AS 16 vs Ind AS 23, AS 22 vs Ind AS 12 — know both columns, not just the AS side.

Module Learning Objectives

SLOB Mapped against the Module: to gain application-oriented knowledge on identifying the impact of various standards on treatment of certain transactions to ensure appropriate reporting (CMLO 4a, c).

After studying this module, the students will be able to: understand the basic concept of Accounting Standards; and get an overview of certain specified accounting standards — namely AS 1, AS 3, AS 10, AS 11, AS 12, AS 16 and AS 22 — along with their comparative provisions with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS). (Note: of these, AS 3 — Cash Flow Statements — is referenced only in passing while scoping AS 11; it is not itself given a dedicated treatment in this module, so it carries no separate sub-topic below.)

Glossary — Module 9, in Plain Words

The technical terms used throughout this module, explained simply.

GAAPGenerally Accepted Accounting Principles — a collection of commonly followed accounting rules, standards and procedures accountants must follow; the framework underneath more detailed Accounting Standards.
Accounting Standard (AS)A written policy document on recognition, measurement, treatment, presentation and disclosure of a specific type of transaction. In India, issued for non-corporate entities/SMEs by the ICAI's Accounting Standards Board; for corporate entities, notified by the MCA based on ICAI's recommendations.
Ind ASIndian Accounting Standards — the Indian version of IFRS, notified under Section 133 of the Companies Act 2013, applied by specified companies in a phased manner from FY 2016-17.
Convergence (vs. Adoption)Convergence = working towards harmonising local GAAP with IFRS over time. Adoption = full-fledged use of IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB. India has converged (Ind AS), not adopted, IFRS.
IFRSInternational Financial Reporting Standards — global standards for public-company financial statements, developed by the IASB.
Accounting Policies (AS 1)The specific accounting principles, and the methods of applying them, adopted by an enterprise in preparing and presenting its financial statements.
Fundamental Accounting AssumptionGoing Concern, Consistency, Accrual — assumed followed unless disclosed otherwise; no specific disclosure needed if followed.
Prudence / Substance over Form / MaterialityThe three considerations governing selection of accounting policies under AS 1 — profits not anticipated but losses provided for; economic reality over legal form; disclose all items that could influence a user's decisions.
Property, Plant and Equipment (AS 10)Tangible items held for use in production/supply/rental/administration, expected to be used for more than 12 months.
Carrying AmountThe amount at which an asset is recognised after deducting accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses.
Depreciable AmountCost of an asset (or amount substituted for cost) less its residual value — the amount that actually gets depreciated.
Fair Value / Recoverable AmountFair value = price in an arm's-length exchange between knowledgeable, willing parties. Recoverable amount = higher of an asset's net selling price and its value in use.
Residual Value / Useful LifeResidual value = estimated amount obtainable on disposal, net of disposal costs, as if the asset were already at end-of-life condition. Useful life = the period (or output units) the asset is expected to be usable by the enterprise.
Monetary ItemMoney held, and assets/liabilities to be received or paid in a fixed or determinable amount of money — e.g. cash, debtors, creditors. Converted at the CLOSING rate every balance sheet date.
Non-Monetary ItemAssets/liabilities other than monetary items — e.g. fixed assets, inventories, equity investments. Carried at historical cost → no further exchange fluctuation; carried at fair value → converted at the rate when that fair value was determined.
Integral / Non-Integral Foreign OperationIntegral = run as an extension of the reporting enterprise (e.g. a dependent branch) — translated like the parent's own transactions, exchange difference to P&L. Non-integral = runs independently — Balance Sheet items at closing rate, exchange difference parked in a reserve until disposal.
Foreign Currency Translation ReserveThe reserve that accumulates exchange differences on translating a non-integral foreign operation's accounts, until the "net investment" in that operation is disposed of.
Government GrantAssistance by government, in cash or kind, to an enterprise for past or future compliance with specified conditions — also called subsidies, cash incentives, duty drawbacks.
Capital Approach vs. Income ApproachCapital approach: grant credited directly to shareholders' funds (no P&L impact). Income approach: grant taken to income over the period(s) it is meant to compensate.
Borrowing CostsInterest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with borrowing funds — e.g. interest, discount/premium amortisation, ancillary cost amortisation, finance-lease finance charges, and forex differences treated as an interest adjustment.
Qualifying AssetAn asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale — the ONLY kind of asset whose borrowing cost can be capitalised.
Capitalisation RateThe weighted average of borrowing costs on an enterprise's general borrowings outstanding during the period (excluding funds borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset) — applied to the qualifying asset's expenditure to find eligible borrowing cost.
Deferred TaxThe tax effect of timing differences — recognised as a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) or Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) in the Balance Sheet, separate from current tax.
Timing DifferenceA difference between taxable income and accounting income that originates in one period and is capable of REVERSING in one or more later periods (e.g. unabsorbed depreciation, carried-forward losses) — these DO create deferred tax.
Permanent DifferenceA difference between taxable income and accounting income that does not reverse the way a timing difference does (e.g. an income-tax penalty) — these NEVER create a deferred tax asset or liability.
CONCEPT

9.1.1 Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) ★★ MED

If full independence were given to accountants over the system and practices to be followed, it would result in lack of uniformity and possible manipulation of accounts. This need for uniformity and comparability led to the framing of GAAP.

Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) is a collection of commonly followed accounting rules and standards meant for accounting of transactions and their reporting — an embodiment of rules and standards accepted and practised by accountants. GAAP contains a set of accounting standards, principles and procedures that accountants must follow; these provide the framework for more detailed and comprehensive accounting rules, standards and industry-specific practices.

9.1.2 Accounting Standards (AS) ★★ MED

Accounting Standards are written policy documents which discuss the recognition, measurement and treatment of specific accounting transactions, along with their presentation and disclosure in an entity's financial statements.

Who issues them, per the source:

  • India (non-corporate entities, incl. SMEs): the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), to establish uniform standards for preparing financial statements in accordance with Indian GAAP.
  • India (corporate entities): the Accounting Standards notified by the MCA — the MCA notifies these, based on ICAI's recommendations, via the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules and amendments thereto, for companies (including SMCs) to whom Ind AS is NOT applicable.
  • US: the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA).
  • The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) is described in the source as the body that sets up the International Accounting Standards.

These standards are mandatory from the dates specified in the respective document or as notified by the ICAI/MCA.

9.1.3 Convergence to Ind AS — Applicability and Scope ★★★ HIGH

Convergence refers to harmonising the accounting standards issued by different countries' regulatory bodies — the goal of a single, high-quality set of accounting standards used internationally, in particular reducing differences between local GAAP and IFRS. Conceptually, "convergence" is different from "adoption" of accounting standards, which means full-fledged use of IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB.

  • International-level Convergence: the process within which the IASB and National Standard-Setters (NSS) converge their respective accounting standards into one global set — a conceptual ideal that would ensure comparability, lower cost of capital, and lower barriers to accountants' movement across jurisdictions.
  • National-level Convergence: adoption of international accounting standards as accounting standards within the country, i.e. the IASB works with the national standard-setter to converge IFRS and local GAAP.

Ind AS, as notified under Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, have been formulated with the Indian economic and legal environment in view, converging with IFRS Standards issued by the IFRS Foundation. The MCA notified the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 in 2015, stipulating a phased adoption from Accounting period 2016-17, since amended by seven Amendment Rules (one each in 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022).

Timeline of Applicability of Ind AS

Entity CategoryPhase / DateMandatory Criteria
A. Companies (other than Banks, NBFCs, Insurance Cos.)Voluntary — 1st April 2015 onwardsAny company, applied voluntarily, along with comparatives.
Phase-I mandatory — 1st April 2016Companies listed/being listed in or outside India with net worth ≥ ₹500 crores; unlisted companies with net worth ≥ ₹500 crores; and holding/subsidiary/JV/associate of the above.
Phase-II — 1st April 2017All companies listed/being listed in or outside India not covered in Phase-I; unlisted companies with net worth ₹250 crores or above but less than ₹500 crores; and holding/subsidiary/JV/associate of the above.
B(1). NBFCsPhase-I — 1st April 2018Listed or unlisted NBFCs with net worth ≥ ₹500 crores; holding/subsidiary/JV/associate of the above (excluding those already covered under the corporate roadmap).
Phase-II — 1st April 2019NBFCs with net worth < ₹500 crores whose equity/debt securities are listed or being listed in India; unlisted NBFCs with net worth ₹250 crores or more but less than ₹500 crores; holding/subsidiary/JV/associate of the above.
B(2). Scheduled Commercial Banks (excl. RRBs)Required from 1st April 2018Presently stands deferred till further notice.
B(3). Insurance Companies/InsurersFY 2018-19Ind AS-based standalone and consolidated statements, with comparatives of FY 2017-18 — per IRDA circular under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, mandating compliance with Ind AS and the MCA's implementation Roadmap.
Once a company starts following Ind AS — voluntarily or mandatorily — it must follow Ind AS for ALL subsequent financial statements, even if it later stops meeting the qualifying criteria. Ind AS applies to BOTH standalone and consolidated financial statements. Companies listed on the SME exchange are NOT required to apply Ind AS mandatorily. NBFCs with net worth below ₹250 crores may not apply Ind AS voluntarily. Companies not covered by any phase continue under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CONVERGENCE ≠ ADOPTION

THE TRAP: students treat "India has converged with IFRS" as meaning India uses IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB.

THE TWIST: convergence and adoption are conceptually different. Ind AS are India's own standards, formulated with the Indian economic and legal environment in view, aimed at converging with (not literally adopting) IFRS as issued by the IFRS Foundation.

CONCEPT

9.2.1 Disclosure of Accounting Policies (AS 1) ★★ MED

This Standard deals with the disclosure of significant accounting policies followed in preparing and presenting financial statements.

Accounting policies refer to the specific accounting principles, and the method of applying those principles, adopted by an enterprise in preparation and presentation of its financial statements.

The view presented of an enterprise's state of affairs and profit or loss can be significantly affected by the accounting policies followed — accounting policies vary from enterprise to enterprise, since more than one accounting treatment can apply in many areas, and choosing among them calls for considerable management judgement. Hence disclosure of significant accounting policies is necessary if the view presented is to be properly appreciated.

Fundamental Accounting Assumptions & Areas of Differing Policy

The following are generally accepted as fundamental accounting assumptions — disclosure is necessary only if they are NOT followed:

  • Going Concern: the enterprise is viewed as continuing in operation for the foreseeable future — with neither the intention nor the necessity of liquidation or of materially curtailing the scale of operations.
  • Consistency: accounting policies are followed consistently from one period to another.
  • Accrual: financial statements are prepared on the mercantile system only — revenues and costs are recognised as they are earned or incurred (not as cash moves), and recorded in the periods to which they relate.

Examples of areas where differing accounting policies are encountered, per the source: (a) methods of depreciation, depletion and amortisation; (b) treatment of expenditure during construction; (c) conversion or translation of foreign currency items; (e) treatment of goodwill; (g) treatment of retirement benefits; (h) recognition of profit on long-term contracts; (j) treatment of contingent liabilities. This list is not exhaustive.

Selection and Disclosure of Accounting Policies

The primary consideration in selecting accounting policies is that the resulting financial statements represent a true and fair view of the state of affairs at the balance sheet date and of the profit or loss for the period. Three considerations govern selection:

  • Prudence: profits are not anticipated but recognised only when realised (though not necessarily in cash); provision is made for all known liabilities and losses even where the amount cannot be determined with certainty — a best estimate on available information.
  • Substance over Form: accounting treatment and presentation should be governed by the substance/economic reality of transactions, not merely their legal form.
  • Materiality: financial statements should disclose all "material" items — those whose knowledge might influence a user's decisions.

Disclosure rule for a change in accounting policy

All significant accounting policies should be disclosed at ONE place, as part of the financial statements. A change with a MATERIAL effect in the current period → disclose the change AND the amount by which any item is affected (to the extent ascertainable; if not ascertainable, disclose that fact). A change with NO material effect in the current period but reasonably expected to have a material effect LATER → disclose the fact of the change in the period it is adopted.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Notes on Accounts for changes in accounting policy

Jivandeep Ltd. had projected a surplus of ₹40 crores for the year ended 31.03.2023; the draft results on hitherto-followed policies showed a deficit of ₹10 crores. The Board made four changes: (i) inventory valuation moved to Works Cost, raising closing inventory to ₹50 crores from ₹30 crores under Prime Cost; (ii) depreciation moved from Reducing Balance to Straight Line, charging ₹27 crores instead of ₹45 crores; (iii) stopped providing 2% of sales (₹600 crores) for after-sales/warranty expenses, expensing actuals instead; (iv) provided ₹10 crores for a permanent fall in investment value accumulated over 5 years.

Per AS 1: a change in accounting policy with a material effect in the current period must be disclosed, along with the amount by which any item in the financial statements is affected, to the extent ascertainable.

Notes on Accounts: (i) Change from Prime Cost to Works Cost valuation increased profit by ₹20 crores (₹50cr − ₹30cr). (ii) Change from Reducing Balance to Straight Line undercharged depreciation, increasing profit by ₹18 crores (₹45cr − ₹27cr). (iii) Discontinuing the 2% warranty provision increased profit by ₹12 crores. (iv) Providing for permanent fall in investment value reduced profit by ₹10 crores.

ILLUSTRATIONS 2–4 — Quick theory checks (source Q&A)

Q2: Which option correctly states the Fundamental Accounting Assumptions per AS 1?

A: Going Concern, Consistency and Accruals (NOT Matching, NOT Prudence, NOT Accounting Period/Entity Concept).

Q3: Explain the AS 1 disclosures relating to Accounting Policies.

A: all significant accounting policies should be disclosed as part of the financial statements, normally in one place; a change with a material current-period effect (or a later material effect) must be disclosed with the amount affected, to the extent ascertainable; if the three fundamental assumptions are followed, no specific disclosure is required — if any is NOT followed, that fact must be disclosed.

Q4: Explain the criteria for selecting and applying Accounting Policies.

A: Prudence (profits recognised only when realised, losses provided for even under uncertainty), Substance over Form (economic reality over legal form), and Materiality (disclose all items capable of influencing a user's decision).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DISCLOSURE IS NOT A CURE

THE TRAP: students assume that disclosing an accounting policy in the notes "fixes" or excuses a wrong treatment applied in the accounts.

THE TWIST: per the source, "Disclosure of accounting policies or of changes therein cannot remedy a wrong or inappropriate treatment of the item in the accounts." Disclosure and correctness of treatment are two separate requirements — AS 1 does not have a comparative Ind AS table in the source; it is examined on its own.

CONCEPT

9.2.2 Property, Plant and Equipment (AS 10) ★★★ HIGH

Objective: to prescribe the accounting treatment for property, plant and equipment (PPE) — principally the recognition of assets, determination of their carrying amounts, and the depreciation charges/impairment losses to be recognised.

Scope: applies to PPE except where another AS requires/permits different treatment. Does NOT apply to: (a) biological assets related to agricultural activity, other than bearer plants (the Standard DOES apply to bearer plants themselves, but not to their produce); (b) wasting assets — mineral rights, exploration/extraction expenditure on minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. It DOES apply to PPE used to develop/maintain assets in (a) and (b). Investment property (AS 13) is accounted for only under the cost model prescribed in this Standard.

Key Definitions

Property, plant and equipment are tangible items that (a) are held for use in production/supply of goods or services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes; and (b) are expected to be used during more than a period of twelve months.

  • Cost: cash/cash-equivalent paid, or fair value of other consideration given, to acquire an asset at acquisition/construction.
  • Carrying amount: the amount recognised after deducting accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses.
  • Gross carrying amount: cost (or substituted amount) WITHOUT deducting accumulated depreciation/impairment.
  • Depreciable amount: cost (or substituted amount) less residual value. Depreciation: the systematic allocation of that depreciable amount over useful life.
  • Fair value: the amount for which an asset could be exchanged between knowledgeable, willing parties at arm's length. Recoverable amount: the higher of net selling price and value in use.
  • Residual value: estimated amount currently obtainable on disposal (net of disposal costs) as if the asset were already at end-of-life age/condition. Useful life: the period, or the number of production units, an asset is expected to be available/usable.
  • Bearer plant: a plant used in production/supply of agricultural produce, expected to bear produce for more than 12 months, with a remote likelihood of being sold as agricultural produce (except incidental scrap sales) — e.g. NOT lumber-harvest trees or annual crops like maize/wheat.

Recognition, Measurement and Depreciation

The cost of a PPE item is recognised as an asset only if it is probable that future economic benefits associated with it will flow to the enterprise. Spare parts, stand-by and servicing equipment are recognised under this Standard only when they themselves meet the PPE definition.

Elements of Cost (measurement at recognition — always at COST)

(a) Purchase price, including import duties and non-refundable purchase taxes, LESS trade discounts and rebates
(b) Any costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for its intended operation
(c) The initial estimate of dismantling, removing and site-restoration costs ("decommissioning, restoration and similar liabilities")

Measurement after recognition — choose ONE, applied to an entire asset class

Cost Model: carried at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment.
Revaluation Model: carried at fair value at revaluation date, less subsequent accumulated depreciation and impairment. An increase on revaluation is credited to Revaluation Surplus (unless reversing a previous P&L decrease of the same asset); a decrease is charged to the P&L (unless offsetting an existing Revaluation Surplus credit balance for that asset).

Components approach: each significant part of a PPE item (cost significant relative to total cost) is depreciated separately — e.g. an aircraft's airframe and engines separately. Land generally has an unlimited useful life and is not depreciated; buildings are depreciable.

Derecognition: on disposal, or when no future economic benefits are expected from use or disposal — gain/loss = net disposal proceeds less carrying amount, included in P&L (gains are NOT classified as revenue). Impairment is assessed per AS 28.

Comparative Provisions — Ind AS 16 vs. AS 10
Ind AS 16AS 10
Does not exclude accounting for real estate developers.Excludes the accounting for real estate developers.
Specific recognition criteria for fixed assets are laid out.No recognition criteria for fixed assets are laid out.
Components approach is followed.Does not require adoption of the components approach.
Requires the organisation to choose either the Cost model or the Revaluation model.Recognises the revaluation of fixed assets.
Change in method of depreciation is treated as a change in accounting estimate.No specific guidance provided.
Does not deal with jointly owned assets.Deals with fixed assets owned jointly with others.
Does not deal with assets held for sale.Deals with fixed assets put up for sale and retired from active use.
Additional costs incurred in construction of a self-generated asset should not be considered.No specific guidance provided.
Revaluation Surplus may be transferred to retained earnings on derecognition of the asset.Guidance note provides recycling to the income statement in the ratio of additional depreciation.
Gain on derecognition should be considered as Revenue.No specific guidance provided.
PPE acquired in exchange of a non-monetary asset is recognised at fair value.PPE acquired in exchange is recorded at the net book value of the asset given up.

ILLUSTRATION 5 — Revaluation cannot be routed through accumulated depreciation

Machinery appears at ₹86,00,000 (accumulated depreciation ₹28,00,000) and is revalued to ₹90,00,000. The accountant suggested adjusting the accumulated depreciation account.

Incorrect. As per AS 10, an upward revaluation of fixed assets must be credited to the Revaluation Surplus Account, not adjusted through accumulated depreciation.

ILLUSTRATION 6 — Component replacement vs. dismantling cost

Jay Ltd. replaced a semi-automatic component with a fully-automatic one for ₹85,000, increasing output by 150%; dismantling and re-erection cost ₹38,000.

Cost of new component (₹85,000): CAPITALISED, since it increases future economic benefits from the machine. Dismantling and re-erection cost (₹38,000): charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

CONCEPT

9.2.3 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates (AS 11) ★★★ HIGH

Objective: to decide which exchange rate to use, and how to recognise the financial effect of exchange-rate changes, when translating foreign currency transactions and foreign operations into the enterprise's reporting currency.

This Standard applies to (a) accounting for transactions in foreign currencies, (b) translating financial statements of foreign operations, and (c) forward exchange contracts. It does NOT specify the presentation currency (only requires disclosure of the reason for the currency used); does NOT deal with restating statements into another currency for user convenience; does NOT deal with cash-flow-statement presentation of foreign-currency cash flows (see AS 3); and does NOT deal with exchange differences on foreign currency borrowings treated as an interest-cost adjustment (see AS 16).

Key Definitions

  • Exchange Rate: rate at which foreign currency is converted into reporting currency (or vice versa).
  • Average Rate: the mean of exchange rates in force during a period (week, fortnight, month, etc.).
  • Forward Rate: an agreed exchange rate between two parties for exchange of two currencies at a specified future date.
  • Closing Rate: the exchange rate at the balance sheet date.
  • Monetary items: money held, and assets/liabilities to be received or paid in a fixed or determinable amount of money — e.g. cash, receivables, payables.
  • Non-monetary items: assets/liabilities OTHER than monetary items — e.g. fixed assets, inventories, equity investments.
  • Foreign operations: operational activities conducted in a country other than the reporting enterprise's own — as a subsidiary, associate, joint venture or branch.

Accounting treatment of Category-1: foreign currency transactions

Initial recognition: transaction-date rate (an average weekly/monthly rate is acceptable if there is no significant fluctuation).
Monetary items → converted at CLOSING rate at every balance sheet date; the difference vs. the rate used at initial recognition (or last reporting date) is an exchange gain/loss to the Statement of Profit and Loss.
Non-monetary items at historical cost (e.g. fixed assets, long-term investments) → continue to be reported at the rate used on initial recognition — NO exchange fluctuation gain/loss arises.
Non-monetary items at fair value (e.g. inventory, current investments) → converted using the exchange rate ruling when that fair value was determined.
Contingent liabilities → reported at the balance sheet date's exchange rate.

Category-2 — Translation: Integral vs. Non-Integral Foreign Operation
Integral Foreign OperationNon-Integral Foreign Operation
Carried on as if an extension of the reporting enterprise's own activities (e.g. dependent branch, sales depot).Carried on largely independently, with little dependence on the reporting enterprise; not decisively defined by AS 11, only indicated by factors — proper judgement applies.
Individual items translated at the ACTUAL rate on the transaction date (average rate acceptable). Fixed assets at cost: rate at date of purchase. Fixed assets at fair value: rate at date of valuation. Inventory cost at the rate when cost was incurred; realisable value at the rate when determined (usually closing rate).Balance Sheet items (BOTH monetary and non-monetary) → CLOSING rate. Income/expense items → actual rate at transaction date.
Exchange difference → charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.Exchange difference → accumulated in a "Foreign Currency Translation Reserve" until disposal of the net investment in that non-integral operation.
A change in classification (Integral → Non-integral, or vice versa) is applied PROSPECTIVELY from the date of change — the non-integral translation reserve is NOT released to income merely because the operation later becomes integral; it stays until eventual disposal.
Comparative Provisions — Ind AS 21 vs. AS 11
Ind AS 21AS 11
Forward exchange contracts are NOT covered.Forward exchange contracts are included within its scope.
Accounting of foreign operations is based on the functional-currency approach.Accounting of foreign operations is based on the integral/non-integral approach.
No specific guidance provided.Option to recognise exchange difference on translating certain long-term monetary items over the period is available.
Presentation currency could be different from the functional currency.No such specification provided.

ILLUSTRATION 7 — Monetary liability at closing rate, both years

Zeds Ltd. incurs a $24,000 fee on 07.12.2022 (rate ₹73.80), paid on 20.05.2023 (rate ₹76.50); closing rate 31.03.2023 was ₹75.45.

Recorded on 07.12.2022 at the transaction-date rate: 24,000 × ₹73.80 = ₹17,71,200.

31.03.2023 outstanding fees reflected at closing rate: 24,000 × ₹75.45 = ₹18,10,800 ⇒ Exchange LOSS for 2022-23 = ₹18,10,800 − ₹17,71,200 = ₹39,600.

On settlement 20.05.2023: 24,000 × ₹76.50 = ₹18,36,000 ⇒ Exchange LOSS for 2023-24 = ₹18,36,000 − ₹18,10,800 = ₹25,200.

ILLUSTRATION 8 — Forex loss on an instalment, entirely to P&L

Subhash Ltd. bought a machine for ₹224 lakhs on 1.4.2022, fully financed by a foreign-currency (US$) loan in 3 equal instalments. Rate: $1 = ₹70.00 on 1.4.2022; $1 = ₹72.95 on 31.03.2023 (first instalment paid).

Cost of machine in US$ = ₹2,24,00,000 ÷ 70.00 = $3,20,000.

Exchange loss on first instalment = 3,20,000 × ₹(72.95 − 70.00) = ₹9,44,000, charged entirely to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

ILLUSTRATION 9 — Loss then further loss across two years

Goods purchased 24.02.2022, US$10,000 @₹76.60; closing rate 31.03.2022 = ₹77.00; paid 5.06.2023 @₹77.50.

Recorded at transaction date: 10,000 × ₹76.60 = ₹7,66,000. At 31.03.2023 (closing rate, monetary item): 10,000 × ₹77.00 = ₹7,70,000 ⇒ loss of ₹4,000 debited to P&L (2021-22 period per source).

On settlement: 10,000 × ₹77.50 = ₹7,75,000 − ₹7,70,000 = ₹5,000 further loss debited to P&L for 2023-24.

ILLUSTRATION 10 — Exception: forex loss on a loan for a FIXED ASSET is added to its carrying amount

MM Ltd. bought fixed assets for US$50 lakhs (₹3,825 lakhs) on 01.04.2022, financed by a foreign-currency loan repayable in 5 equal annual instalments. Rate at purchase: $1 = ₹76.50; first instalment on 31.03.2023 at $1 = ₹81.50. WDV depreciation @20%.

Foreign currency loan = ₹3,825 lakhs ÷ ₹76.50 = 50 lakh US$. Since the loan financed a FIXED ASSET, AS 11 requires the exchange loss on repayment to be ADDED to the carrying amount of the asset, not expensed — unlike the general rule.

Exchange loss on the outstanding loan (40 lakh US$ remaining) = 40 × ₹(81.50 − 76.50) = ₹200 lakhs, added to the fixed asset's cost with a corresponding credit to the outstanding loan. Additional depreciation on the increased depreciable amount = 20% × ₹250 lakhs = ₹50 lakhs (per AS 10).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: MONETARY vs. NON-MONETARY — AND THE ONE EXCEPTION

THE TRAP: students apply "monetary item → closing rate, gain/loss to P&L" mechanically to EVERY foreign-currency loan, including one that financed a fixed asset (Illustration 8 style) — or conversely assume ALL forex loans on fixed assets get added to asset cost.

THE TWIST: the general rule (Illustration 7, 8, 9) IS that monetary items are revalued at closing rate with the exchange difference going straight to P&L. Illustration 10 shows the recognised exception: exchange differences on repayment of a liability incurred SPECIFICALLY to acquire a fixed asset are adjusted into the carrying amount of that fixed asset — read the fact pattern carefully to see which rule the question is testing. Non-monetary items at historical cost (fixed assets themselves, long-term investments) never get revalued for exchange fluctuation at all — only monetary items, and the one named exception, do.

CONCEPT

9.2.4 Accounting for Government Grants (AS 12) ★★★ HIGH

This Standard deals with accounting for Government grants — also called subsidies, cash incentives, duty drawbacks. It does NOT deal with: (i) special problems from Government grants in price-change-adjusted or supplementary financial statements; (ii) Government assistance OTHER THAN in the form of grants; (iii) government participation in the ownership of the enterprise.

Government grants are assistance by Government, in cash or kind, to an enterprise for past or future compliance with certain conditions — excluding forms of assistance that cannot reasonably be valued, and transactions with Government indistinguishable from normal trading transactions.

Capital Approach vs. Income Approach
Capital ApproachIncome Approach
Grant treated as part of shareholders' funds — appropriate for grants in the nature of promoters' contribution (given w.r.t. total investment/capital outlay, no repayment ordinarily expected).Grant taken to income over one or more periods, matched with the associated costs it is meant to compensate — appropriate since grants are earned through compliance with conditions, not gratuitous.
Inappropriate to recognise in P&L since the grant is not "earned" against related costs.Consistent with treating income tax and other fiscal charges through the P&L; income recognised on a RECEIPTS basis is NOT in accordance with accrual accounting.
Grants with promoters'-contribution characteristics → Capital approach (Capital Reserve). Other grants → Income approach is generally more appropriate.

Presentation of Grants

Grants related to SPECIFIC FIXED ASSETS — two acceptable methods

Method 1: deduct the grant from the asset's gross value — recognised in P&L over the asset's useful life via a REDUCED depreciation charge (asset may show at a nominal value if the grant equals virtually the whole cost).
Method 2: treat as DEFERRED INCOME, credited to P&L over the asset's useful life (usually in the same proportions as depreciation is charged). Grants for NON-depreciable assets go to Capital Reserve under this method (unless conditional on an obligation, in which case credited to income over the period of meeting that obligation).

Grants related to REVENUE

Presented as a credit in the P&L, either separately or under "Other Income" — or, alternatively, deducted from the related expense.

Grants of the nature of PROMOTERS' CONTRIBUTION

Given w.r.t. total investment/capital outlay with no repayment ordinarily expected → treated as Capital Reserve — neither distributable as dividend nor treated as deferred income.

Refund of grants (per AS 5, treated as an extraordinary item): a REVENUE grant's refund is applied first against any unamortised deferred credit for that grant, and any excess (or the whole, if no deferred credit exists) is charged immediately to P&L. A SPECIFIC FIXED ASSET grant's refund is recorded by increasing the asset's book value OR reducing the capital reserve/deferred income balance — if the book value is increased, depreciation on the revised amount is provided prospectively over the residual useful life. A refundable PROMOTERS'-CONTRIBUTION grant reduces the Capital Reserve.

Comparative Provisions — Ind AS 20 vs. AS 12
Ind AS 20AS 12
Disclosure required with indication of other forms of government assistance received.No specific guidance, as it does not deal with other forms of government assistance.
Government grants in the nature of capital contribution are NOT recognised as such.Government grants as capital contribution ARE specifically recognised.
Prohibits recognising grants directly to shareholders' funds.Grants for non-depreciable assets are required to be shown as a capital reserve under shareholders' funds.
Non-monetary grants recognised at FAIR VALUE.Non-monetary grants recognised at ACQUISITION COST or nominal value.
No option to deduct the grant amount from the asset's book value.Optional to deduct the grant amount from the asset's book value.

ILLUSTRATION 11 & 14(ii) — Promoters'-contribution grant → Capital Reserve

Illustration 11: Dee Ltd. received ₹80,00,000 from the Central Government as subsidy to set up a factory in a backward area — a promoters'-contribution grant.

Credited directly to shareholders' funds: ₹80,00,000 to Capital Reserve, reflected in the Balance Sheet. (Illustration 14(ii) mirrors this: ₹150 lakhs capital subsidy for a ₹600 lakh plant in a notified backward region → ₹150 lakhs to Capital Reserve, plant shown at the full ₹600 lakhs.)

ILLUSTRATION 12 — Revised depreciation after a refund of grant

Big Box Ltd. bought a machine for ₹44,85,000 on 01.04.2020, receiving a ₹7,35,000 grant (treated as a capital receipt, i.e. deducted from cost). Useful life 4 years, straight line, realisable/residual value ₹15,36,000. The grant became refundable in FY 2022-23.

Calculation of Depreciation (₹ '000)

Cost of machine on 01.04.20204,485
Less: Grant from Government of India735
Net cost of machine3,750
Depreciation p.a. under SLM = (3,750 − 1,536) ÷ 4553.5
Depreciation charged 2020-21 & 2021-22 (553.5 × 2)1,107

ILLUSTRATION 13 — A depreciable-asset grant is NOT straight income, even under losses

Z Ltd. received a ₹25 lakh capital-investment subsidy (25% of ₹100 lakhs invested in capital assets) in January 2023. The accountant wanted to credit it straight to P&L to reduce the year's reported loss.

Not justified. Per AS 12, a grant related to a depreciable fixed asset must be treated as deferred income, recognised in P&L on a systematic basis over the asset's useful life, in the same proportion as depreciation — it cannot be credited to P&L in full in the year of receipt.

ILLUSTRATION 14(i) & (iii) — Net-of-grant asset value; revenue grant

(i) A ₹550 lakh fixed asset with a 40% Government grant (₹220 lakhs).

(i) Shown net at ₹550 lakhs − ₹220 lakhs = ₹330 lakhs, depreciated over the asset's life. (iii) ₹125 lakhs received from a local authority for employee medical facilities is a revenue grant, shown in the P&L — or, if the facilities span more than one year, treated as deferred income taken to P&L on a systematic basis.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CAPITAL vs. REVENUE GRANT — READ THE PURPOSE, NOT THE SOURCE

THE TRAP: students assume ANY subsidy tied to "setting up" or "acquiring an asset" is automatically a capital-reserve item, or that a struggling company can route any grant through P&L to offset a loss.

THE TWIST: the test is the CONDITION attached — a grant given w.r.t. total investment/capital outlay with no repayment expected (promoters'-contribution character, Illustration 11/14(ii)) is Capital Reserve; a grant tied to acquiring a SPECIFIC depreciable asset (Illustration 12/13/14(i)) is deferred income spread over the asset's useful life, matched with its depreciation — never taken to P&L in one shot regardless of how the company's results look that year.

CONCEPT

9.2.5 Borrowing Costs (AS 16) ★★★ HIGH

Objective: to prescribe the accounting treatment for borrowing costs. Scope: applicable to accounting for borrowing costs generally.

Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with the borrowing of funds. A qualifying asset is an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.

Borrowing costs may include: (a) interest and commitment charges on borrowings; (b) amortisation of discounts/premiums relating to borrowings; (c) amortisation of ancillary borrowing-arrangement costs; (d) finance charges on finance-lease assets or similar arrangements; and (e) exchange differences from foreign currency borrowings, to the extent regarded as an interest-cost adjustment.

Examples of Qualifying Assets: manufacturing plants, power generation facilities, inventories requiring a substantial period to reach saleable condition, and investment properties. NOT qualifying: other investments; inventories routinely manufactured/produced in large quantities on a repetitive short-period basis; and assets ready for intended use/sale when acquired.

Recognition: capitalise ONLY the borrowing cost directly attributable to a qualifying asset

Borrowing costs directly attributable to acquiring/constructing/producing a qualifying asset → CAPITALISED as part of its cost, when it is probable they will result in future economic benefits and the cost can be measured reliably. ALL OTHER borrowing costs → expensed in the period incurred.

Specific borrowings vs. General borrowings

Specific borrowing for a qualifying asset: eligible cost = actual borrowing cost incurred during the period, LESS any income on temporary investment of those borrowings.
General borrowing used partly for a qualifying asset: eligible cost = Capitalisation Rate × expenditure on that asset, where Capitalisation Rate = weighted average of borrowing costs on the enterprise's outstanding borrowings during the period (EXCLUDING borrowings made specifically for a qualifying asset).
Capitalised borrowing cost for a period must NEVER exceed the actual borrowing cost incurred in that period.

Commencement, Suspension and Cessation

  1. Commencement — when ALL of: expenditure on the asset is being incurred; borrowing costs are being incurred; and activities necessary to prepare the asset for intended use/sale are in progress (this includes technical/administrative work before physical construction, e.g. obtaining permits — but excludes merely holding an asset with no development activity, e.g. land held without associated development).
  2. Suspension — during extended periods in which active development is INTERRUPTED.
  3. Cessation — when substantially all activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for intended use/sale are complete. Where construction completes in independently-usable PARTS (e.g. a business park of separate buildings), cessation applies part-by-part; where the asset needs to be complete before any part can be used (e.g. a steel mill), cessation is for the whole.

Disclosure: (a) the accounting policy adopted for borrowing costs; (b) the amount of borrowing costs capitalised during the period.

Comparative Provisions — Ind AS 23 vs. AS 16
Ind AS 23AS 16
Qualifying Assets will NEVER include Biological Assets.Qualifying Assets MAY include Biological Assets.
No specific definition of "substantial period of time" — a matter of judgement.Specific definition/explanation of "substantial period of time" is provided.
Inventories produced in large quantities should NOT be Qualifying Assets (only lower-quantity ones may qualify).Inventories MAY be Qualifying Assets if the substantial-period condition is satisfied.
Interest expense capitalised AND not capitalised must be disclosed separately.Disclosure required only if capitalisation was made during the period.
Hyper-inflationary borrowing cost is addressed — increased interest cost from hyper-inflation is written off to the income statement.Inflation in interest rate is not addressed.
Weighted average capitalisation rate on borrowings must be disclosed in Notes.No specific guidance provided.
Consolidated statements: weighted average capitalisation rate of total Holding + subsidiary borrowings is considered.No specific guidance provided.

ILLUSTRATION 15 — Monsoon delay does NOT suspend capitalisation

T&L Ltd.'s bridge construction (project cost ₹125 crores, 40% financed by a 3% ADB loan) was delayed by high water levels during the monsoon (July–September) — a common seasonal condition for the region. The accountant did NOT suspend capitalisation.

Correct treatment. This is a temporary delay that is a NECESSARY part of the construction process, not an interruption of active development — capitalisation continues.

ILLUSTRATION 16 — Only the factory shed is a Qualifying Asset

Pushkar Ltd.'s ₹65 lakh loan: equipment ₹19,50,000; factory shed ₹26,00,000; advance for a delivery vehicle ₹6,50,000; working capital ₹13,00,000. Total interest for the year: ₹11.70 lakhs.

Allocation of Interest (only Factory Shed is a Qualifying Asset)
ParticularsNatureCapitalised (₹)To Income Statement (₹)
Purchase of equipmentNot a QA—3,51,000
Construction of factory shedQA4,68,000—
Advance for delivery vehicleNot a QA—1,17,000
Working capitalNot a QA—2,34,000
Total4,68,0007,02,000

ILLUSTRATION 17 — Weighted borrowing-cost capitalisation

Expenditure to 31.03.2023: ₹5,00,000; interest capitalised for 2022-23 @13%: ₹26,000; borrowed to 31.03.23: ₹2,00,000; assets transferred to construction 2023-24: ₹1,00,000; cash payment 2023-24: ₹75,000; progress payment received: ₹3,70,000; new borrowing 2023-24 @13%: ₹2,00,000.

Total borrowing cost = ₹4,00,000 × 13% = ₹52,000. Expenditure incl. previously capitalised (₹5,00,000 + ₹26,000) + cash payment (₹75,000) + asset transferred (₹1,00,000) = ₹7,01,000; less progress payment ₹3,70,000 = ₹3,31,000. Money borrowed incl. previously capitalised interest = ₹4,00,000 + ₹26,000 = ₹4,26,000.

Borrowing cost to be capitalised = (₹3,31,000 ÷ ₹4,26,000) × ₹52,000 = ₹40,404.

ILLUSTRATION 18 — Only the factory shed qualifies, again

MM Ltd.'s ₹200 lakh loan: shed construction ₹80 lakhs; machinery ₹60 lakhs; working capital ₹40 lakhs; truck advance ₹20 lakhs. Total interest for the year: ₹36 lakhs. Only the shed is a Qualifying Asset.

Interest capitalised = ₹36 lakhs × 80/200 = ₹14.40 lakhs. Balance ₹21.6 lakhs (₹36 lakhs − ₹14.4 lakhs) expensed to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: NOT EVERY RUPEE OF A LOAN QUALIFIES FOR CAPITALISATION

THE TRAP: students capitalise interest on the ENTIRE loan amount, because the whole loan was raised "for the project."

THE TWIST: capitalisation follows the ASSET, not the loan — only the portion of interest attributable to expenditure on an actual QUALIFYING ASSET (a shed under construction, in Illustrations 16 and 18) is capitalised. Equipment already ready for use, an advance for a delivery vehicle, and working capital are NOT qualifying assets even though funded from the same loan — their share of interest is always expensed.

CONCEPT

9.2.6 Accounting for Taxes on Income (AS 22) ★★★ HIGH

Objective: to prescribe the accounting treatment for taxes on income. Scope: applies to determining and disclosing the tax expense/saving related to taxes on income for an accounting period; covers all domestic and foreign taxes based on taxable income. Does NOT specify accounting for taxes payable on distribution of dividends and other distributions.

Key Definitions

  • Accounting income (loss): net profit or loss for a period as reported in the P&L, before deducting income tax expense or adding income tax saving.
  • Taxable income (tax loss): income (loss) for a period determined per tax laws, on which income tax payable/recoverable is based.
  • Tax expense (saving): the aggregate of current tax and deferred tax charged/credited to the P&L for the period.
  • Current tax: the amount of income tax determined to be payable/recoverable for the period's taxable income (tax loss).
  • Deferred tax: the tax effect of TIMING differences.
  • Timing differences: differences between taxable income and accounting income for a period that originate in one period and are capable of reversal in one or more subsequent periods. Unabsorbed depreciation and carried-forward losses that can be set off against future taxable income are ALSO treated as timing differences, resulting in deferred tax assets, subject to prudence.
  • Permanent differences: differences between taxable income and accounting income that originate in one period — the source's own definition of this term is fragmentary in the extraction, but it confirms separately, twice, that permanent differences do NOT result in a deferred tax asset or liability (unlike timing differences, which do).

Recognition and Measurement

Tax expense (current tax + deferred tax) is included in determining net profit/loss for the period. The tax EFFECT of timing differences is included in tax expense in the P&L, and as Deferred Tax Assets (DTA) or Deferred Tax Liabilities (DTL) in the Balance Sheet. Permanent differences create NEITHER a DTA nor a DTL.
DTA recognition is subject to PRUDENCE — recognised and carried forward only to the extent there is REASONABLE certainty of realisation. Where there is unabsorbed depreciation or carried-forward losses, a DTA is recognised only to the extent there is VIRTUAL certainty, supported by convincing evidence, that sufficient future taxable income will be available.
Current tax is measured at the amount expected to be paid/recovered, using applicable tax rates/laws. Deferred tax assets/liabilities use tax rates/laws enacted or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date; where different rates apply to different income levels, AVERAGE rates are used. Deferred tax assets/liabilities are NEVER discounted to present value, and the carrying amount of a DTA is reviewed at each balance sheet date.

Disclosure & Offset

  • Current tax assets/liabilities can be offset only if the enterprise has a legally enforceable right to set off, AND intends to settle on a net basis.
  • Deferred tax assets/liabilities can be offset only if the enterprise has a legally enforceable right to set off current-tax assets against liabilities, AND both relate to taxes levied by the same governing taxation laws.
  • Deferred tax assets/liabilities are disclosed under a SEPARATE heading in the Balance Sheet, distinct from current tax and from current assets/liabilities — with a break-up of major components in the Notes.
  • Where an enterprise has unabsorbed depreciation or carried-forward losses, the nature of the evidence supporting DTA recognition must be disclosed.
Comparative Provisions — Ind AS 12 vs. AS 22
Ind AS 12AS 22
Based on the BALANCE SHEET approach.Based on the INCOME STATEMENT approach.
Recognition based on the difference between carrying amounts of assets/liabilities and their tax base.Recognises the difference between taxable income and accounting income.
Applies to two types of differences: Taxable Temporary Differences and Deductible Temporary Differences.Applies to two types of differences: Timing Differences and Permanent Differences (Permanent Differences are NOT addressed by Ind AS 12).
Deductible temporary differences recognised to the extent future periods are likely to provide taxable earnings.Deferred taxes recognised only when, and to the degree, there is reasonable certainty of realisation; for unabsorbed depreciation/carried-forward losses, virtual certainty backed by convincing evidence is required.
Current and deferred tax recognised in the income statement, EXCEPT tax arising from transactions in Other Comprehensive Income or directly in equity.No specific guidance provided.
Addresses the disparity between the carrying amount of a revalued asset and its tax base.Does not cover the disparity between the carrying amount of a revalued asset and its tax base.
No specific guidance regarding Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) u/s 115JB.Specific guidance provided on tax rates for deferred tax assets/liabilities under MAT u/s 115JB.
No specific guidance on deferred tax for tax-holiday situations and capital-gain cases.Specific guidance provided on deferred tax for tax-holiday situations and capital-gain cases.

ILLUSTRATION 21 — Deferred Tax Liability from excess tax depreciation

Vishnu Ltd.: depreciation per books ₹8,00,000; depreciation u/s 32 of Income Tax Act ₹20,00,000; unamortised preliminary expenditure per tax records ₹1,50,000. Adequate evidence of future profit sufficiency exists; corporate tax rate 40%.

Timing Difference = Additional tax depreciation − Preliminary expenditure allowed = (₹20,00,000 − ₹8,00,000) − ₹1,50,000 = ₹10,50,000.

Deferred Tax Liability = ₹10,50,000 × 40% = ₹4,20,000.

ILLUSTRATION 22 — Deferred Tax Liability, transition adjustment

AB Ltd.: depreciation per accounts ₹8,00,000; per tax records ₹14,00,000; unamortised preliminary expenses per tax record ₹11,200. Adequate future-profit-sufficiency evidence exists; tax rate 40%.

Timing Difference = Excess tax depreciation (₹14,00,000 − ₹8,00,000 = ₹6,00,000) LESS expenses provided in taxable income (₹11,200) = ₹5,88,800.

Deferred Tax Liability = 40% × ₹5,88,800 = ₹2,35,520, credited in the accounts.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TIMING DIFFERENCE vs. PERMANENT DIFFERENCE

THE TRAP: students create a DTA/DTL for EVERY gap between accounting profit and taxable profit — e.g. an income tax penalty, or interest accrued-but-unpaid at return-filing (Illustration 19).

THE TWIST: only TIMING differences (capable of reversing in a later period — e.g. unabsorbed depreciation) create deferred tax. PERMANENT differences (which do not reverse the way timing differences do) create NEITHER a DTA nor a DTL — per Illustration 19, an income tax penalty and unpaid-but-booked bank interest are both Permanent Differences, so no deferred tax entry is passed for either.
